The Morrisites in brief Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, began recording revelations in Utah in the late 1850s. On April 6, 1861, he organized his own church at South Weber, and his followers gathered at Kington Fort on the Weber River. In June 1862 a territorial posse besieged the fort for three days; Morris was killed at the surrender, others died in the siege, and the men were taken prisoner and later tried. After Governor Stephen S. Harding pardoned those convicted in 1863, the Morrisites scattered: to Soda Springs, Idaho, under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor; to Carson Valley, Nevada, and San Francisco; to Omaha and Council Bluffs; to William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla; and to the Deer Lodge Valley in Montana, where the last organized Morrisite church lasted until George Johnson’s death in 1954. This guide gathers the records they left and what has been written about them. Read the chronology and the place pages for the story, the essential works below for the movement’s own texts and its standard history, Teachings for what the Morrisites believed, and Questions for what is still unsettled.
Where to begin

Four ways in History A dated chronology from 1857 to the present, the places of the movement from South Weber to Racetrack, and what the Morrisites taught. Sources Documents to read online, a bibliography, and the archives that hold Morrisite records. People The 430 names on the 1861–62 roll of membership, with FamilySearch links, notes, and pages on individual members. Questions What the record has not settled yet, for students, family historians, and researchers.
Family history

Looking for a Morrisite ancestor? Look up the name. The name index lists everyone on the 1861–62 roll and everyone else the sources name, with links to every place the guide mentions them. Try other spellings: the roll was printed from Danish, Swedish, Welsh and English names, and clerks spelled them as they heard them. The search box at the top of every page searches the whole site. Read what the guide has found. On the roll, a name may carry a note on what the sources say, a FamilySearch link, a tag for the men taken at Kington Fort in 1862, or a link to a person page with a life, family on the roll and sources. Check the family in Family Tree. FamilySearch links marked “probable” are likely but not certain; Family Tree is shared and editable, so check its sources before relying on it. See where the records are. The place pages gather what the guide holds on each place the family lived. Repositories lists the archives that hold Morrisite papers, court files and land records, and Documents lists what can be read online. Share what your family knows. Letters, photographs, family histories and corrections are welcome; see Share records. Descendants have already filled in parts of this guide.

Core texts

Essential works The movement's own scripture, a later compilation from within the movement, a modern collection of its leaders’ writings, and the only book-length history of it. Primary text · 1886 The Spirit Prevails Joseph Morris's revelations, articles, and letters, recorded from 1857 to 1862 and published after his death by his follower George S. Dove. It holds more than 300 revelations, making Morris one of the most prolific revelators in Mormon history. For his followers it was scripture. Read online: Internet Archive · Google Books. Both are free scans of the University of California copy (684 pages). Primary text · 1899 Gems of Inspiration A Collection of Sublime Thoughts by Modern Prophets, compiled by John R. Eardley, a leader of the Montana church after Williams’s death, and printed in San Francisco by Joseph A. Dove in 1899. It shows how the movement kept and passed on its prophetic writings a generation after Morris. Read online: Internet Archive. Primary texts, collected · 2026 The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations Edited by Kirk Watson. Writings of Joseph Morris, George Williams, William W. Davies, George S. Dove and James Dove, among them Davies’s pamphlets, hymns and 1882 interview and James Dove’s Treatise on Re-Incarnation (1892). It is the only collection that puts the later leaders’ writings beside Morris’s, and the main source for the guide’s Teachings page. It also transcribes twelve of Morris’s letters to Brigham Young, 1858–60, his earliest surviving writings; see the dated list with catalog links on the Documents page. Independently published, 267 pages. Buy: Amazon (paperback and Kindle). The standard history · three editions C. LeRoy Anderson's history of the Morrisites 1981 For Christ Will Come Tomorrow: The Saga of the Morrisites 1988 Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites, 2nd ed. 2010 Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited), the final edition. Buy from the publisher · Digital edition (member libraries) Anderson, a sociologist at the University of Montana, built the book on Morrisite papers found in a Deer Lodge attic and on the records of Andrew Hendrikson, who presided over the Montana church from 1886 to 1921, kept by his family. His research files are the core of the Morrisite collection at USU. The 2010 edition is in print in paperback and as an ebook. Please buy it from Utah State University Press, an imprint of the University Press of Colorado; buying from the publisher supports keeping the book in print.
History
Chronology The main events, from Morris’s revelations through the Montana congregations to later claimants and the present.

The movement at a glance How the Morrisite congregations descended from one another, where many members went, and the later groups that drew on the tradition without descending from it. Solid line: organizational succession or movement of members. Dashed line: a later claimant with a documented contact or borrowing, not a line of succession.

The groups over time The same story on a time scale. After 1862 no single leader held the movement together: Anderson counts more than a dozen men who contended for leadership over the next twenty years, and several groups existed side by side. Each lane is a group; the divisions within it are its leaders or phases. Lighter shading means the dates are approximate, and a lane that fades out has no known end. Arrows show members moving from one group to another. Point to or tap the chart to see which groups existed in a given year; select a lane to read more.

t: The groups, with dates and sources Morris’s church 1861–1862. Organize…
s: The groups, with dates and sources Morris’s church 1861–1862. Organized April 6, 1861, later called the Church of the Firstborn (see Glossary); Morris killed June 15, 1862. Soda Springs (Morristown) 1863–1872. Settled May 20, 1863, under Connor's protection. After five frozen harvests most settlers left; a few, among them the Niels Andersons, stayed for life (Anderson, pp. 159–64). Nevada: Carson Valley and Carson City 1863–1878. Livingstone, Parson, the Doves and Eardley organized here in 1863–64; Cainan made Parson president at Carson in August 1864. The Carson Valley News still wrote of “the Morrisites” of the valley in 1877 (Anderson, ch. 13; Carson Valley News, 1877). Cainan’s claim to lead 1862–1882. Claimed the succession from the autumn of 1862 on the strength of visions of April and August 1862; led by correspondence, never visited Montana, and died in England in 1882 (Anderson, ch. 12). Omaha and Council Bluffs 1868–1880. Fifteen members at Omaha and twelve at Council Bluffs in January 1869; forty-two and twenty-seven by October 1871. Many later moved on to Montana (Anderson, ch. 15). Saints of the Most High, Montana 1866–1969. Morrisites arrived from 1863 and gathered under Cainan in the late 1860s and 1870s; the council called itself the Saints of the Most High by 1873. William James presided until 1886; George Thompson was then elected president, though he spent much of his time in England, and Andrew Hendrikson presided in Montana from 1886 to 1921 and George Johnson to his death in 1954, with which the church came to an end (Anderson, pp. 212, 214); survivors still gathered at the Lord’s House in 1969, the year USU’s finding aid gives for its formal disbanding. Kingdom of Heaven 1864–1888. Davies, in Montana from 1864, claimed a divine call in January 1866 and led about forty followers to Walla Walla in 1867. The community broke up after members sued him in 1880–81 (Anderson, ch. 14). Parson’s kingdom 1874–1885. Parson visited Davies in 1872–73, was impressed, then set up his own kingdom in San Francisco on April 7, 1874. How long it lasted is not known (Anderson, chs. 13–14). Church of the Firstborn (the Doves) 1874–1910. George Dove claimed leadership from 1874; the Doves published from 1879 to 1892, including The Spirit Prevails (1886), and visited Montana in 1885. Holzapfel, cited by Anderson, says the church lasted until 1910 (Anderson, ch. 13). Later claimants. James Brighouse’s Order of Enoch (1884) has no traced Morrisite link; Leland Jensen’s Missoula group (from the 1970s) drew on Cainan’s Deer Lodge prophecy without descending from the church. Neither is drawn.

t: 1857–1862Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Latter-day Saint chu…
s: 1857–1862Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Latter-day Saint church, records the revelations later gathered as The Spirit Prevails. He writes repeatedly to Brigham Young. No written reply is known; Anderson reports that the first letter, dated December 7, 1857, bears a penciled note on its margin, “He’s weak minded.” The church’s answer comes in February 1861 (next entry).

t: 11 Feb 1861The apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff hold a meetin…
s: 11 Feb 1861The apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff hold a meeting at South Weber to “regulate” the branch. On Taylor’s motion, seconded by Woodruff, sixteen of Morris’s followers are cut off from the church, among them Bishop Richard Cook, his brother John Cook, John Parson and Robert Farley (Woodruff’s journal, February 11, 1861). Morris’s name is not on the list Woodruff recorded. 6 Apr 1861Morris organizes his church at South Weber with six members and calls his followers to gather at Kington Fort, an abandoned 1853 settler fort there (Anderson, Revisited, p. 66). On its name, see the Glossary. 1861–1862The community holds its goods in common and awaits the Second Coming. On December 30, 1861, a revelation promises that Christ will come “to-morrow morning” if those present consecrate all their property; when he does not, later revelations blame those who gave unwillingly and decline to set another time (The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 188–199, pp. 338–59). As appointed days pass, some members grow discontented and try to leave, and in April 1862 a revelation forbids letting them take back what they consecrated (No. 254, p. 490). See Teachings.

t: 11 Jun 1862Acting Governor Frank Fuller orders General Daniel H. Wells…
s: 11 Jun 1862Acting Governor Frank Fuller orders General Daniel H. Wells to furnish the territorial marshal, Henry W. Lawrence, and his deputies, Robert T. Burton and Theodore McKean, “a sufficient military force” to act as a posse in serving Third District Court writs for the arrest of “Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis County.” The order survives in a copy Wells made in 1871 (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, document 1,215, Utah State Archives; page image on FamilySearch). 13–15 Jun 1862A territorial posse under Robert T. Burton besieges the fort. Morris is killed at the surrender, and John Banks, wounded, dies in custody that evening. The posse loses two young men, Jared Smith (June 13) and Peter Wahler (June 15). Accounts differ on the number of Morrisite dead (see Who died at Kington Fort?). 18–19 Jun 1862Before Judge Kinney in Salt Lake City, Richard Cook is fined and jailed for contempt, Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson are held in prison, and ninety-five other men are bound over on $1,500 bail each for the March 1863 term (Deseret News, June 25, 1862).

t: Mar 1863In Salt Lake City, seven Morrisites are convicted of second-de…
s: Mar 1863In Salt Lake City, seven Morrisites are convicted of second-degree murder: Peter Klemgard is sentenced to fifteen years, Christian Neilsen to twelve, and Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason to ten; John Parson and John E. Jones are acquitted. The other prisoners are fined $100 each for resisting arrest (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The new territorial governor, Stephen S. Harding, pardons them all a few days later. May 1863Many Morrisites leave Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, commanding the District of Utah. On May 5 a party of 160 (53 families, seven single men, and four widows) sets out with a company of California Volunteers; it reaches Soda Springs on May 20, where Connor has a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River beside a new military post, Camp Connor (established by order of May 23). The Morrisites call their town Morristown. Connor also gives 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City, Nevada, in an empty supply train. Others settle in California. (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 1, 226–29.) 1860s–Some Morrisites return to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, in Utah and elsewhere. The 2006 monument at South Weber notes that a few were rebaptized and remained there. Others find a home in the Reorganized Church (RLDS): the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt joins it in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear (Johann Lebrecht Bär, 1838–1919), a Swiss convert from Affoltern am Albis who emigrated from Zürich in 1860 and lost his wife and child at Kington Fort, later serves as an RLDS missionary to Switzerland and Germany, dies in Independence, Missouri, and publishes his autobiography in the RLDS Journal of History. In 1865 RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptize several people who appear on the roll. Others join only after years in the Morrisite groups: Erick and Caroline Eliason are baptized together at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870; Margaretta Cook leaves the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and is baptized RLDS in 1873; and Lena Hanson, at Soda Springs and then Deer Lodge, in 1895 (see the roll). 1865–66Morrisites are meeting in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana. On March 4, 1866, Sven Olson Hagg writes from Deer Lodge City that he has spent the winter with L. C. Larsen and his family, and helped Larsen build a new house “hvori vi nu holder forsamlinger” (“in which we now hold meetings”). God has begun “to pour out the power of his Spirit upon some of his children right here in Deer Lodge Valley, where the beginning (of the Kingdom) shall be founded.” The first to receive it, he says, was “his servant William D.”, president of the Aaronic priesthood, standing “in Abel’s place” by birthright. This was William W. Davies, whose community later dated its era from January 24, 1866. Hagg also notes that Williams, in an epistle of August 26, 1865, had told J. P. Lorentzen, S. P. Guhl and George Thompson to winter in the valley (Hagg to A. Hanssen, March 4, 1866, Church History Library, MS 31876, folder 22; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

t: 1867–1881William W. Davies, who in an 1867 pamphlet declared that a th…
s: 1867–1881William W. Davies, who in an 1867 pamphlet declared that a third dispensation had been opened through him on January 24, 1866, setting baptism aside for a covenant vow (Watson, p. 124), leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of Heaven, near Walla Walla, Washington. He declares his infant son Arthur to be Christ returned, the “Walla Walla Jesus.” Lawsuits by former members end the community: in 1881 a court awards three of them $3,225, and the sheriff sells the community’s livestock and its eighty acres to satisfy the judgment. 1868From Salt Lake City George Williams writes to “Bro. James & Saints of the Most High in Montana” (December 14, 1868): William James’s group is already in Montana and uses the name later borne by the Montana church. Williams wishes to visit “my beloved brethren & sisters in Montana” but says he is “called to travel to the States & Europe” (Church History Library, MS 31876). 1869George Williams leaves Utah for England, passing through Omaha from January 18 to February 5, where the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations are organized on his authority (see Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places); a year later he writes from Loughborough that it was “now one year since I left the continent of America”; his wife and children stay in Salt Lake City, and he asks the Montana members to send help for “my little ones” (Williams to the Saints of the Most High in Montana, January 10 [?], 1870, Church History Library, MS 31876). By June he is at Ashwicken, near King’s Lynn, Norfolk, writing to the Saints at Omaha and Council Bluffs, where Rasmus Rasmussen is “the presiding Bishop.” George Thompson is with him at Ashwicken that summer, and William P. Thomas and a Brother James come to England too: Thompson writes on July 29, 1869, to “Beloved Brethren W. P. and D. J.,” one at Llanybyther in Wales and the other at Derby. The Omaha minutebook names him: on June 2, 1869, Guhl left for Denmark with “2 Welsh brethren, William P. Thomas, a High Priest, and an Aaronic Priest Daniel James,” called “to go to Wales on mission.” In March 1870 Williams writes that “Bro Thomas & Bro James,” having “attended the heavenly call,” are “now permitted to return to their families in Montana” by way of Omaha. In September 1870 he gives his own account of Almerin Grow, who had walked from California to Salt Lake on hearing of him, was told of “his mission to the Sultan & Priesthood of Mahommet,” and was later “sent to Constantinople & Jerusalem,” returning “without my consent” (Williams to the Omaha church and to Andrew Hendrikson, 1869–70; George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869; and the Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876). Danish-language congregations keep membership and account books in Omaha, Nebraska, and Council Bluffs, Iowa.

t: 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under Ge…
s: 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under George Williams, the “Prophet Cainan,” who claims to be Morris's successor. In July 1874 the Montana church is divided into two stakes: Stake No. 1 on Warm Spring Creek, which met at a meeting house at Willow Glen under William James, and Stake No. 2 at Race Track under Andrew Hendrikson (Church History Library, MS 32226; see Repositories). Stake No. 2’s own minutes record its founding general meeting on July 12, 1874. Hendrikson spoke to “the brothers and sisters who had chosen to be under his presidency”: they lived in two places, Warm Spring and Deer Lodge, about equally many in each, and Jens Jensen was appointed to preside over the meetings at Deer Lodge. From then on only members of “our organization” were to sit in its councils, not those of “the other organization” (general meeting, July 12, 1874, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Hendrikson was living at Race Track by February 1878. A local history of Anaconda dates the first Morrisite settlers in the valley to 1863, among them William Price Thomas on Warm Springs Creek, east of the later townsite; has a group under William James arriving in 1867 as others left; and describes a caravan of thirteen covered wagons that came in June 1871, part of a larger migration from Iowa, Nebraska, Utah and Idaho: Scandinavian families, mostly Danes, with English, Scottish and Welsh believers. It places the two congregations in the upper valley near Lost Creek and near Race Track Creek, with about eighty members in all (Patrick F. Morris, Anaconda, Montana, 1997, pp. 15–17). Williams’s letters from England direct the move from Omaha: in September 1871 “Bro Merrick” sets out for Montana “with his cattle,” in the spring of 1872 Williams sends “instructions for gathering up to Montana,” and by December 1872 Andrew Hendrikson’s mail goes to the Warm Spring Creek post office (Williams to Hendrikson and the Omaha church, 1871–72, MS 31876). Not everyone left Nebraska at once. A branch at Fremont met in Andrew Peterson’s house in November 1871, and in March 1873 Peterson wrote to Hendrikson that the Fremont members hoped to come to Montana that summer and were trying to sell their place (MS 31876, folders 37–38). Williams himself was in England, living by 1876 in George Thompson’s house at Walthamstow, Essex: “I am now writing in Bro Thompson’s house where I have been tarrying some weeks” (to William James, July 13, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876). 1873The Montana council minutes, kept in English this year, show the church at Warm Springs while its leaders are away. William James is on “his Mission in Nevada.” Williams calls William P. Thomas “on a Mission to Salt Lake,” and he appoints Andrew Hendrikson by letter “to take the Presidency, assisted by the Bishop and his Counselors,” while both are absent (May 5, 1873). In March a committee of four tries a quarrel between Thomas and Daniel James over the line between their lands and Daniel James’s cattle, set on by dogs as they passed Thomas’s place. It tells the two to forgive each other, but Thomas rejects the ruling as “Develish talke.” In July, Damander, who had hosted the Council Bluffs councils, turns against Williams, saying “Cainan was a Man like Brigham Young to lead the People astray.” James takes back the presidency on July 20. In September the council meets privately at Rasmus Rasmussen’s house to keep Thomas out and agrees to report him to Williams; Thomas, Williams’s appointed first counselor and “our second man in authority,” is to be left alone until Williams answers. In December the sisters in the town of Deer Lodge complain that Margaret Thomas did not invite them to the sisters’ feast at Warm Springs (council minutes, March–December 1873 and January 12, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876). In California the same year, George Dove, who with his father James had followed Williams and then Davies, begins receiving communications and organizes a Church of the Firstborn of about thirty people (Watson, p. 198). 1878–79Montana Morrisites build a wood-frame church, the Lord’s House, a mile or so below Racetrack, south of Deer Lodge. About 1877 Williams wrote from England that he was glad the church “is to have a House and the workmen all in the covenant” (MS 31876, folder 8), but the site was settled only on February 24, 1878. That day a joint council of both stakes met in Andrew Hendrikson’s house at Race Track, with William James presiding. Some wanted the house on Warm Spring Creek or on Peder Jansen’s land, and Rasmus Rasmussen cited “Cainan’s letter that it was to be build on Land of some faithful Brother.” By ten votes to five the council chose “H. Land,” Hendrikson’s land (council minutes, February 24, 1878). Peder Jansen superintended the building (“havde forestaaet Bygningen”). In July 1879 the Race Track council moved its public Sunday meetings into the Lord’s House at 10:30 a.m., with the brethren to sit on the right and the sisters on the left (council minutes, July 24, 1879). The House was dedicated on August 9, 1879: in July 1882 the council planned to celebrate August 9, “som var 3de Aarsdagen siden at Herrens Huus blev indviet” (“which was the third anniversary of the dedication of the Lord’s House”; council minutes, July 29, 1882). The first council minuted “i Herrens Huus” met on September 27, 1879. A special council for both stakes on October 25, 1879, found that the brothers and sisters had given $634.70 in cash, with $76.73 still owing, to be paid by November 10 (council minutes, 1878–82, Church History Library, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). 1879Robert T. Burton, indicted for the killing of Isabella Bowman during the surrender (in 1870, an indictment voided in 1872, and again in 1877), is tried and acquitted. 6 Jan 1879Writing from Walthamstow to William James and the “Saints of the Most High in Stake No. 1 on the Sides of the North in Mo

t: 1882–83Williams dies in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 ye…
s: 1882–83Williams dies in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 year,” after about two years of great pain from “an enlargement of the bone” in his shoulder joint; George Thompson, who had done his writing for him, still knew of no one “appointed to fill his place” in August 1883 (Thompson to William P. Thomas, August 9, 1883, MS 31876). The movement splits among rival successors. In Montana, where the church is known as the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High, Williams had directed that William James, its local president, be put before the church a year after his death: “Let the organisation remain as it is, for twelve months after my decease, then let brother James be placed before the whole Church when assembled at the years end, and if sustained by uplifted hand, there let him remain, and so on, from year to year” (Williams to the Montana brethren, January 29, 1882, Church History Library, MS 31876). An envelope he addressed to James, postmarked at New York on March 26, bears the words “I leave you in charge after my decease.” In his last weeks George Thompson, who lived near him in Walthamstow, answered the Montana church’s questions for him: on March 23, 1882, he wrote that “Bro Cainan is no better but gradually getting weaker & weaker,” and that if Williams named no one to replace a Sister Rasmussen in her office, the church should choose someone “and we will confirm your choice” (MS 31876). On April 25, 1883, a general assembly in the Lord’s House sustains James by 19 votes to 10, and he chooses Andrew Hendrikson and John R. Eardley as counselors. Several of the minority, among them Erick Eliason and Lars Beck, refuse to accept the vote, and the Race Track bishop, Rasmus Rasmussen, who will not sustain James, keeps the church’s records and is suspended (Church History Library, MS 32226; see Repositories). (Eardley, later a stake president, leaves Montana about 1900.) In the Danish-speaking stake at Race Track, the council minutes record the other side of the vote: in December 1882 Andrew Hendrikson read Williams’s last instructions that, if no new servant of the Lord came before the anniversary, the church might “selv … vælge en Leder for Kirken” (“itself choose a leader for the church”); in February 1883 he said that since “Cainan havde recommenderet Wm. James” he would uphold him, while Lars Beck said he could not see that choosing a president would do them any good (Race Track council minutes, December 30, 1882, and February 24, 1883, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). George Dove leads the California congregation. 1884A later claimant. James Brighouse, breaking from the RLDS Church, organizes the Order of Enoch in Independence, Missouri, a small commune with Lars Peterson whose main tenet is celibacy. After breaking with the Petersons and returning to Utah he proclaims himself the embodiment of the Second Coming and the “One Mighty and Strong,” and only then, as far as Kirk Watson can tell, teaches reincarnation. Brighouse had been brought into the RLDS Church in 1880 by the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt (see 1880), but Forscutt opposed the doctrine, calling it Morris’s “strange theory of repeated embodiment” (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702, p. 12). Watson, who has researched Brighouse, has found no connection between him and the Morrisites beyond shared ideas and language, and notes that the two men meant different things by the “seventh angel”: for Morris a stage in the soul’s ascent through the angelic ranks, for Brighouse a figure taken from Revelation 11. Watson also points out that the title was in Latter-day Saint use before either man took it up. The 1832 revelation now Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 speaks of “Michael, the seventh angel, even the archangel,” and in his funeral sermon for Joseph and Hyrum Smith in 1844, W. W. Phelps cast Joseph as the angel who would pour out the “vials of wrath,” an allusion to the seventh angel of Revelation 16; Latter-day Saints of the time often saw their prophet as the Seventh Angel (Kirk Watson, correspondence with the editor, November 2026, following Christopher James Blythe, “‘Would to God, Brethren, I Could Tell You Who I Am!’” Nova Religio 18, no. 2 (2014): 18–19; Phelps’s sermon as reconstructed in 1855, in Van Wagoner and Walker, “The Joseph/Hyrum Smith Funeral Sermon,” BYU Studies 23, no. 1 (1983): 15–16). One online account (Lost Mormonism) says the Order honored Morris as a prophet and martyr, but the standard references do not: Shields’s entry on the Order (Divergent Paths, 5th ed., §5.4) and Kraut’s note on Brighouse both omit Morris. Wikipedia describes the Order as the one Morrisite-related body that survived 1969; its later activity has not been confirmed for this guide.

t: 1886At the yearly general assembly in the Lord’s House at Race Track, …
s: 1886At the yearly general assembly in the Lord’s House at Race Track, Montana, on April 25, George Thompson of London is elected president of the church; William James, who had claimed the presidency for life “by birthright,” resting on Williams’s envelope “I leave you in charge,” stays away. Eleven members who decline to sustain Thompson are given thirty days to do so. At a court meeting on May 10 James is suspended “for the crimes of usurpation of authority, and heresy,” and John R. Eardley is put over the Warm Spring Creek stake (Church History Library, MS 32226; see Repositories). That December Thompson was living in England, writing to the Montana brethren from Thornwood Common, Epping, Essex (MS 31876). Thompson is probably the last general president. Andrew Hendrikson, a Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint, presides over the Montana Morrisites from 1886 until his death on July 3, 1921. 1886The Spirit Prevails, a collection of Morris's revelations, articles, and letters, is published by George S. Dove & Company. 1892In San Francisco, James Dove publishes A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites for the California congregation, and A Treatise on Re-Incarnation or Re-Embodiment, which Kirk Watson calls the earliest book on the subject in the wider Mormon tradition (Watson, pp. 199, 208–64).

t: 1921–1954George Johnson, Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty yea…
s: 1921–1954George Johnson, Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty years and likewise never a Latter-day Saint, presides at the Lord’s House until shortly before his death on April 29, 1954, at ninety-eight. Anderson calls him the last official Morrisite leader: by the 1940s fewer than a dozen members were active, and with Johnson’s death the church came to an end and the Lord’s House was boarded up (Revisited, pp. 212, 214). His funeral was conducted by an Episcopal priest, and the local paper called the Morrisite church “almost extinct these days” (Silver State Post, May 7, 1954, p. 7; see Newspapers).

t: 1969Surviving Morrisites, all of the second or third generation, gathe…
s: 1969Surviving Morrisites, all of the second or third generation, gather at the Lord’s House on August 9, the anniversary of its dedication and one of the church’s two feast days; by then, Anderson writes, the gatherings were more social than religious (Revisited, p. 218). Utah State University’s finding aid for the Morrisite collection says the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High officially disbanded in 1969, and the description of Anderson’s papers says meetings were held irregularly until then; Anderson himself dates the end to 1954. See How and when did the Montana church end? Its records, its descendants, and the Racetrack church remain.

t: 1981–1988C. LeRoy Anderson publishes For Christ Will Come Tomorrow (19…
s: 1981–1988C. LeRoy Anderson publishes For Christ Will Come Tomorrow (1981) and Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (1988), the first book-length histories. 1990A later claimant. Neal Chase, interpreter for Leland Jensen’s Missoula-based sect, the Bahá’ís Under the Provisions of the Covenant, publishes Ezekiel’s Temple in Montana. Drawing on Anderson’s book, he cites George Williams’s prophecy that Christ would come in the Deer Lodge Valley, identifies the Montana State Prison at Deer Lodge (where Jensen was held from 1969) as Ezekiel’s temple, and dates the fulfillment to August 9, 1969, Jensen’s first full day in prison. Jensen already taught that the prison was Ezekiel’s temple; his followers say they first learned of the Morrisites and Williams on a trip to Deer Lodge in 1990. Anderson finds that the book attributes far more prophetic ability to Williams than he had, and that there is no substantive proof the 1969 gathering anticipated the Second Advent (Revisited, pp. 216–18). The sect was not Morrisite in origin; it adopted Morrisite prophecies as confirmation of its leader’s mission. 1996–2010After Jensen’s death in 1996 the sect divides over leadership, with Chase leading one faction; lawsuits continue to about 2010.

t: 2006A monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site is dedicated at …
s: 2006A monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site is dedicated at South Weber. 2010Anderson’s final edition, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited), is published. July 2012Descendants of Morrisite families hold a reunion in Deer Lodge; the property owners allow them to visit the Racetrack church. 2026Kirk Watson publishes The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations, collecting writings of Morris, Williams, Davies, and the Doves. The Racetrack church still stands, in declining condition (see the condition record under Images).
History
Places Sites connected with the movement, and what can be seen at each today. MO-IMG-001 · Monument, December 2008

Kington Fort South Weber, Utah Built in 1853 and abandoned in 1858, then reoccupied by the Morrisites. Nothing of the fort survives; a monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site, Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, was erected in August 2006 at 6600 South and 475 East (N 41.14677, W 111.96884), sponsored by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping, with the site designed by Douglas B. Stephens (Barlow, 2022). The fort was named for Bishop Thomas Kington, and “Kington” is the correct spelling. The monument itself notes that the earliest sources (the notebook kept by Kington’s wife, his gravestone, Wilford Woodruff’s journals, and early church records) all spell it that way; recent scholarship such as Holley (2008) follows them. Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts, and some modern references, including the Utah History Encyclopedia and Wikipedia, write “Kingston Fort.” Insiders used both: Forscutt, who lived in the fort, wrote “Kingston’s Fort” and called it “the proper name” of the place (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702). Search under both spellings. Not all the people in the fort were from South Weber. Holley (2008) names eleven men from Slaterville and Marriott, about nine miles to the northwest, among the prisoners of June 1862, and two of the family groups on the roll, Cowan–Bull and Higham, were Slaterville families (see “Families on the roll” on the roll page). A log cabin nearby, which the local historian Ed Cooper, from oral accounts of older South Weber residents, identified as the building Morris used to hold the three departing members whose detention led to the siege, is shown in MO-IMG-046–049; it has been moved from its original site, and the identification rests on local tradition. About 200 yards south, on the west side of the road, in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery, a marker reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021). The name lingered locally. In the early 2000s, while the editor was going door to door in South Weber, a woman then in her sixties said that elementary-school classmates had called her “Morrisite” as a taunt because of where in South Weber she lived; she said her family had no Morrisite connection. (Editor’s memorandum of recollection, written November 1, 2026; the conversation was not recorded at the time.) A cannonball from the siege was kept by the family of Al Peek, together with a portrait of Mary Christoffersen Anderson (MO-IMG-051–053; the portrait is MO-IMG-062). VisitThe monument is public. The Pioneer Cemetery appears to lie on private land but is reached by a public easement; stay on the access route. The cabin is on private property. MO-IMG-061 · Anderson gravestone, October 2018

Morristown Soda Springs, Idaho The Morrisites were among the founders of Soda Springs, one of the oldest towns in Idaho. Connor reported bringing 160 settlers (53 families, seven single men, and four widows), who arrived May 20, 1863, and were given building lots on a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River, beside the military reservation of Camp Connor (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). A later marker describes a 200-acre survey west of Soda Creek, lots of 25 by 130 feet, and one-room log homes with dirt floors. The Morrisite “Lower Town” stood below the military “Upper Town”; Soda Springs was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. After the troops left in 1865, hard winters and failed crops thinned the settlement. Many Morrisites moved on, some north to the Blackfoot area, and others sold to miners and to Latter-day Saint settlers, whose new town site dates from Brigham Young’s visit of 1870–71. Most of the old town now lies under Alexander Reservoir. Those who stayed, led by Niels Anderson, carried their quarrel with the Mormon hierarchy into territorial politics; the Niels Anderson Homestead marker credits his anti-polygamy campaign with helping deny Mormons the vote in Idaho. Accounts differ on some details: most give 160 settlers (one popular account says about 325), Camp Connor’s founding is dated May 20 or May 23, and the National Park Service marker wrongly calls Morris Welsh-born. Markers stand in town, including the Park Service’s Morrisite settlement marker in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse (HMDB), the state’s Camp Connor marker (HMDB), and “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor’s probable site near the hospital (HMDB). Descendants held a reunion in Soda Springs on August 3, 2013. Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson, married at Morristown on July 20, 1863 (the date on their gravestone; some accounts give July 30), are buried in Fairview Cemetery at Soda Springs. Their gravestone carries a long bronze inscription giving a Morrisite account of the 1862 siege, in which Mary, then fourteen, lost her jaw to the first cannon shot fired into the fort. Forscutt, who was present, described her lower jaw “hanging only by a narrow strip of skin,” with two women dead beside her (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702; MO-IMG-061, with transcription; MO-IMG-062; HMDB; see also the Niels Anderson Homestead marker). VisitThe markers and the Anderson gravestone in Fairview Cemetery are publicly accessible. The townsite is largely under Alexander Reservoir.

Carson City & California Nevada · California The western congregations, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails and led the California church after 1882. In May 1863 Connor gave 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City in an empty quartermaster’s train bound there for stores (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). VisitNo surviving sites identified for this guide. Information welcome.

Omaha & Council Bluffs Nebraska · Iowa Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive in translation. Their own minutebook, written up at Omaha in May 1871, tells how they began. Jens Jacob Poulsen, “a High Priest of the Weber House,” was sent ahead by George Williams to gather the scattered Morrisites, and spent about a year there. Williams himself arrived in Omaha on January 18, 1869, “from his home in South Cottonwood in Utah,” on his way to England, held meetings in Omaha and Council Bluffs, and left on February 5 with Poulsen and a Brother Mortensen, who went on to Denmark. On February 7, 1869, at Council Bluffs, S. P. Guhl, newly come from Montana, organized the church on Williams’s authority: Council Bluffs City Congregation No. 1, under Carlton Fellows, with Hans Nielsen over the Scandinavians at Crescent City, since the Danes “were not satisfied” to have an American president; and Omaha City Congregation No. 2, for all the Saints west of the Missouri, under Jens Jensen, with a district at Florence under Niels Jensen. Rasmus Rasmussen became the first bishop. A conference at Omaha on April 6, 1869, sustained “George Williams, called of the Lord Cainan,” as “our Prophet, Seer and Revelator,” and on May 30, as Guhl left on a mission to Denmark, Andrew Hendrikson was appointed to preside, with Jens Jensen and Hans Nielsen as counselors (minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In March 1871 the church gave up its yearly conferences, which Hendrikson said Guhl had brought in “in likeness with the Mormons’ custom” and Williams had never commanded, and met instead in councils in members’ houses and in “social gatherings.” That May one of its leaders, Sister Marie Mortensen, joined the Reorganized Church, and Hendrikson had the early records copied into a book, “for many of us must be called hence and go to other places.” The last entry is dated June 4, 1871, at Jens Jensen’s house in Omaha. Most of the congregation moved to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1871–72. VisitNo sites identified; the record survives in documents only. MO-IMG-014 · Racetrack church, November 2018

Deer Lodge Valley Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana The longest-lived center of the movement. The wood-frame Morrisite church, built in 1878–79, still stands on private land at Racetrack, about 8 miles south of Deer Lodge: on the north side of Dempsey Road, just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (Exit 195; about 46.29° N, 112.75° W; NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County; until 1901 this was Deer Lodge County, the county named in older records and in this guide’s photograph captions). The county lists it as a frame building of 18 by 36 feet (Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026). It was last photographed for this guide in August 2020. Called the Lord’s House, as the panel over its doors reads, it was the church’s meeting place: George Thompson was elected president of the church there in 1886, and Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954) presided over the Montana church from it. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive, and its condition has worsened markedly since 2009. See the condition record under Images. The Deer Lodge paper, the New North-West, spoke well of its Morrisite neighbors. In June 1878 it reported that the post office at Gwendale, Deer Lodge County, had been renamed Morristown, and that “as many of the people are Morrisites” they would likely take to the name. In 1883 it called the settlements on Warm Springs Creek and the upper Deer Lodge River “largely composed” of Morrisites and praised them as industrious, hospitable and law-abiding; in 1885 it noted “a large number of Morrisites in this valley” (New North-West, June 7, 1878, p. 3; April 13, 1883, p. 2; October 30, 1885, p. 3; see Newspapers). The paper’s notices place Gwendale in the upper Deer Lodge valley, near Warm Springs and Lost Creek. It was school district No. 6; in April 1875 “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” met at the Gwendale school house on the railroad question, with Morgan Evans in the chair and a W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee; Gwendale primaries were held at Wier’s store; and a smelter there began work in August 1877 (New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2; June 18, 1875, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3). Morgan Evans, whose land later became Anaconda, gave Gwendale as his address. By 1883 the same school district, No. 6, was called Willow Glen, with Peter Jessen, a Gwendale man since the 1870s, as a trustee and J. I. Eardley as clerk (New North-West, May 4, 1883, p. 3). In March 1880 the land office listed Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims were held up while it decided whether the ground was mineral land; among them were Daniel James and William P. Thomas, on Warm Springs Creek east of where Anaconda was built (secs. 33 and 34, T5N R10W), and Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen, in sec. 9, T4N R10W, near today’s Opportunity (New North-West, April 30, 1880, p. 4); all four claims were patented as homesteads in 1880–81. In January 1882 the paper reported that John R. Eardley, formerly of San Francisco, had built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and that the neighborhood had petitioned for a post office there “to be called Willow Glen”; in March it reported his appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was” (New North-West, January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3). Gwendale, renamed Morristown in 1878, and Willow Glen were thus successive post offices for the same neighborhood, between Anaconda, Opportunity and Warm Springs. The exact site of the Gwendale school house is still not known. View onlyThe church is privately owned, unsafe and not open to the public. View it from Dempsey Road or the frontage road; do not enter the property.

Kingdom of Heaven Walla Walla, Washington William W. Davies's commune near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. Its site lay on the west side of Mormon Grade Road, a few hundred yards south of Scenic Loop Road, near Russell Creek (Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). An interpretive sign that Walla Walla 2020 put up at the corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. The road name and Davies’s grave in Lyons Cemetery remain. VisitLyons Cemetery is public. The colony site is not marked.

Names and terms The names of the churches, places, offices and titles that readers meet across this guide, in brief. Each entry links to where the guide says more.

t: Church of the Firstborn The name by which Joseph Morris’s church, orga…
s: Church of the Firstborn The name by which Joseph Morris’s church, organized on April 6, 1861, at South Weber, Utah, is now usually known; its members are usually called Morrisites. It was not the church’s first name. Morris’s revelations call it simply “my Church,” and the revelation on baptism of April 3, 1861, speaks of members of “the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, under the fullness of the gospel” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 55, p. 78). Anderson, following Richard W. Young (1890), gives the name at the organization as the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High, and says it “later on” became known as the Church of the Firstborn. The Prophet Cainan declared that the church would “also be called The Church of the Firstborn,” and the Doves’ California congregation used the name from the 1870s (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 57, 66, 182). See more

t: Morrisites Followers of Joseph Morris, and members of the churches tha…

It was named for Bishop Thomas Kington; “Kington” is the correct spelling, but many accounts write “Kingston.” Search under both. See more

t: Prophet Cainan George Williams (born February 14, 1814, at Thorpe, Sur…
s: Prophet Cainan George Williams (born February 14, 1814, at Thorpe, Surrey), who claimed to be Morris’s successor and led the church that gathered in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, from the late 1860s; he was writing to “Saints of the Most High in Montana” by December 1868. In a letter of January 6, 1879, he told the Montana Saints that the region where they lived was “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming; he set no date. He left America for England about January 1869. His letters from England are headed from Loughborough, London and Ashby by Brigg, Lincolnshire (1870–74) and Walthamstow, Essex, where he lived near and then with George Thompson (1875–82) (Church History Library, MS 31876). Thompson explained to the Montana church in 1882 that Williams “was not really Cainan the son of Enos, but that he represented him, & so with Joseph first and second” (MS 31876). He died in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 year,” after two years of pain from a diseased shoulder (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1883, MS 31876). His birth date is given in FamilySearch Family Tree (KWJ8-P3L); the Race Track council kept February 14 as “Herrens Tjeners Fødselsdag,” the Lord’s Servant’s birthday (minutes, December 30, 1882, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude), and it was still one of the church’s two feast days in the twentieth century (Anderson, Revisited, p. 218). t: Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High According to Anderso…
s: Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High According to Anderson, following Richard W. Young (1890), the name Morris’s church took at its organization on April 6, 1861 (Revisited, p. 66; see Church of the Firstborn). It was the name of the Montana church, used by its council by 1873 and kept after Williams’s death on April 25, 1882, when it was led in turn by William James, George Thompson, Andrew Hendrikson and George Johnson. By Anderson’s account it ended with Johnson’s death in 1954 (Revisited, pp. 212, 214); USU’s finding aid gives 1969 for its formal disbanding. See more

t: Lord’s House The Montana Morrisites’ wood-frame church near Racetrack,…
s: Lord’s House The Montana Morrisites’ wood-frame church near Racetrack, built in 1878–79 on Andrew Hendrikson’s land and named for the panel over its doors. It was dedicated on August 9, 1879 (Race Track council minutes, July 29, 1882, Church History Library, MS 31876), and the church kept the day as its anniversary and one of its two feast days, on which surviving Morrisites still gathered there in 1969 (Anderson, Revisited, p. 218); in 1884 John R. Eardley paid to have it painted (Church History Library, MS 32226). It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive. See more

t: Walla Walla Jesus A later popular name for Arthur Davies (1868–1880), …
s: Walla Walla Jesus A later popular name for Arthur Davies (1868–1880), son of William W. Davies. Davies said that on the eighth day after the boy’s birth he proclaimed the Messiah come again in him and named him “Messiah Son of David”; the boy later took the name Arthur (1882 interview, Watson, p. 192). His younger brother David was held to carry the spirit of God the Father. Both died of diphtheria in February 1880 (Watson, pp. 191–93). The belief spread beyond Walla Walla: in 1877 the Carson Valley News reported that R. J. Livingstone had sold his property at Genoa, Nevada, to live near a child born at Walla Walla who was to be the Savior (May 29, 1877, p. 3). Who first called Arthur the “Walla Walla Jesus,” and when, is not known; the name is used in the Washington State Archives’ index to the 1880 lawsuit against Davies, in Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 paper and in the Fort Walla Walla Museum’s collection description. See the question · See more

t: Seventh Angel A title Joseph Morris claimed, after the angel who sound…
s: Seventh Angel A title Joseph Morris claimed, after the angel who sounds the last trumpet in Revelation. For Morris it marked a stage in the soul’s ascent through the angelic ranks. The phrase was already in Latter-day Saint use: Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 names “Michael, the seventh angel, even the archangel,” and in 1844 W. W. Phelps’s funeral sermon for Joseph Smith alluded to him as the seventh angel who pours out the last vial of wrath (Revelation 16). James Brighouse later used it for the title of his tracts. In Morris’s “Order of Sevens” the seven angels of the seven churches are Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch and Methuselah, and Seth, the seventh, presides (Gems of Inspiration, 1899); George Williams’s writings call Morris “Seth” (Watson, p. 90). s: Sides of the North George Williams’s name for the Montana Saints’ region, from Psalm 48:2 (“the city of the great King” on “the sides of the north”). He wrote in 1879 to the “Saints of the Most High in Stake No. 1 on the Sides of the North in Montana” that the City of the great King would come down there before the Lord’s coming, and called the Lord’s House “my first House of Prayer on the Sides of the North” (MS 31876, Church History Library). s: Reincarnation The teaching that spirits return to the earth in new bodies. Morris dated it to a revelation of 1859; Forscutt called it Morris’s “strange theory of repeated embodiment.” Davies’s community taught it too. George Williams told the men he anointed at Council Bluffs and Omaha in 1869 who they had been: Carlton Fellows “was the Father to Simon Peter; Jonas was your name,” Hans Nielsen had been Eliab, David’s brother, and Jens Jensen had been Titus (record book, 1869, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Teachings

What the Morrisites taught A summary of the movement’s teachings, period by period, with the sources for each. It describes what the Morrisites and their successors believed; it does not argue for or against it. Where scholars disagree, both readings are given.

How we know The sources are uneven. Joseph Morris’s revelations were published only after his death, by a follower, as The Spirit Prevails (1886). His letters to Brigham Young survive in Young’s office files, and Kirk Watson’s The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026) prints them with other manuscripts of Morris, George Williams, William W. Davies and the Doves, many for the first time. Gems of Inspiration (1899) shows what the later church chose to keep. Mark H. Forscutt, an insider who later left, wrote a sketch of Morris; the newspapers of 1862 were hostile; and C. LeRoy Anderson’s history is the only book on the movement. For the later church there are Williams’s letters and the Montana minutes at the Church History Library (MS 31876 and MS 32226), and for Davies’s community the sworn testimony of 1880–81 (see Repositories). As Watson notes, almost everything written on the Morrisites has been about the siege, and almost nothing about their beliefs (Watson, p. 6). Teachings also changed over a century, so this page takes them period by period. Translations from the Danish are generated by Claude.

Joseph Morris (1857–1862) A prophet with a message for Brigham Young. Morris, an English convert, believed the Lord spoke through him, and he recorded more than 300 revelations. His letters to Young, from 1858 to 1860, show him first offering to work with Young and then, as no answer came, growing desperate; he believed he had been called to lead the church (Watson, pp. 5, 11–49). A revelation of January 1860 charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door; a clerk docketed it “Balderdash” (see Documents and Did Brigham Young ever answer Morris?). His followers later claimed that church leaders drew on the revelations he had sent and presented them as “new truths” (Watson, p. 11, citing Dove’s preface). Moses, and Seth, the seventh angel. Morris claimed to be the reincarnation of Moses (Watson, p. 6). He also taught an order of seven angels who preside over the last dispensations of each earth: Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch and Methuselah, with Seth, the seventh, presiding (“The Order of Sevens,” in Gems of Inspiration). Morris called himself the Seventh Angel, and George Williams’s writings call the prophet of South Weber “Seth” (Watson, p. 90). Both identities appear in the sources. Gods, angels and Holy Ghosts. In a revelation on the Holy Ghost, an early form of “Keys of the Priesthood” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 2), Morris taught that Holy Ghosts are men who once lived on a mortal earth, “millions” of them, made one as the Father and the Son are one, and that each god is subject to the one above him, up to “the first God of all” (Watson, pp. 50–53). Forscutt later remembered the theology as monotheistic at its root but wide enough to find a place for the faithful of every religion (Forscutt, Sketch, pp. 17–18). Reincarnation. Morris taught that spirits return to the earth in new bodies; Joseph Dove dated the teaching to a revelation of 1859, and Forscutt called it Morris’s “strange theory of repeated embodiment.” Where it came from is disputed: see Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from? and the Glossary. The coming of Christ, and consecration. Morris taught that Christ would come soon to deliver his people, and he tied the coming to the consecration of their property. On December 28, 1861, a revelation promised that the Lord would not delay once the people were prepared; on December 30 another promised that he would come “to-morrow morning” if those present consecrated all their property in the way appointed (The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 186 and 188–189, pp. 336–39). When the morning passed, a revelation of January 6, 1862, blamed those who had consecrated unwillingly, and one of January 11 refused to set another time (Nos. 195 and 199, pp. 350, 359); in February deliverance was promised after the people had taken an oath (No. 224, p. 419). Revelations of January and April 1862 forbade using the property of “the rebellious” and forbade letting those who left take back what they had consecrated (Nos. 202 and 254, pp. 368, 490), the dispute that led to the writs and the siege. John Parson, speaking at South Weber in September 1861, set consecration against Brigham Young’s church, whose apostles, he said, had promised that land would not be monopolized and that all would have equal rights, and had not kept the promise (Watson, pp. 64–67). See How did believers survive failed prophecy? Judgment. The revelations of 1861–62 also foretell judgment on the wicked. A revelation read at South Weber on September 29, 1861, says Christ will come “as a thief in the night” and as a refiner, and will destroy his enemies, among them the leaders of his former church (Watson, pp. 60–64; The Spirit Prevails, No. 104). In a tongue of June 8, 1862, the “3rd Captain of the Lord’s Host,” an angel from an earlier earth, told of a camp like Kington Fort whose faithful, at “the test,” killed the hypocrites among them, and whose prophet then enforced the law of God on pain of death (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 638–42; Watson, pp. 72–79). Watson reads such passages as showing that Morris expected human as well as divine agents of judgment, including against dissenters in his own community (Watson, p. 8); Anderson held that the judgment Morris foretold was God’s alone (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 108, 111). Spiritual gifts. Speaking in tongues and their interpretation, and messages from angels, were part of worship at Kington Fort. An interpretation of June 7, 1862, taught that the gifts are given to mortals and cease only at the resurrection, when the faithful become angels who give them to others, and that they had left the older church because a council in Brigham Young’s house decided to put them down (Watson, pp. 70–72). See What became of the spiritual gifts? Church order and ritual. Morris organized his church on April 6, 1861, at South Weber, with a First Council and apostles (Glossary). Scepters, a robe and crown, and a ceremony at Kington Fort in May 1862 belong to its ritual life; what Morris taught they meant is little documented (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 116–17; see Where did the rituals come from?). Marriage. Later writers often say that Morris opposed plural marriage; Watson argues that he held it to be part of the heavenly order (Watson, pp. 7–8). Morris’s own article of June 4, 1861, explaining Joseph Smith’s revelation on celestial marriage, says something between the two: the biblical law of many wives and concubines was given for this life, “not being a celestial law,” and the kings and prophets who had many wives “can have but one sealed to them each for eternity” (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 651–52). The same article defines a concubine as a fallen spirit “of the seed of Cain.” The 3rd Captain’s testimony calls polygamy true “in its proper time and place.” It was not practiced at Kington Fort (Watson, p. 8). By 1899 the movement’s own history condemned polygamy outright (Gems of Inspiration), which may be where the later tradition began. See What did M

George Williams, the Prophet Cainan (1863–1882) His calling. Williams, the Prophet Cainan, told of visions in 1862. On April 15, near a canyon in Salt Lake Valley, he saw the armies of heaven and the Father and the Son; from August 25 to 27, on a mountain east of the valley, John the Revelator baptized him, and Seth and Enos, who had “sealed our testimony with our blood,” declared him “Cainan, then Melchisedec, now George Williams” and gave him the keys of the priesthood, among them the keys of birthright and of sealing (“Interviews with Celestial Beings,” Watson, pp. 81–90; Gems of Inspiration). Seth and Enos are very probably Morris and John Banks, both killed in June 1862. Williams also claimed the use of the Urim and Thummim and said he had met Muhammad, Joseph Smith and Morris (Watson, pp. 80, 92–96). From 1869 he led from England, by letter (see Chronology). New records. Williams said he had translated ancient records from St. Ann’s Hill in Surrey; the chapters that survive describe the origin of the gods, their dwellings, their incarnations and reincarnations, and the making of worlds (Watson, pp. 96–110). Earlier lives and birthrights. At Council Bluffs and Omaha in 1869 Williams told converts who they had been in earlier lives: Carlton Fellows had been Jonas, the father of Simon Peter, and Maren Fellows had been Abigail (record book, 1869, MS 31876). A single typescript fragment says that the Prophet read men’s priesthood by feeling their heads, and that no descendant of Cain would be let into the church; it is the only source for this (see Did the Prophet Cainan read birthrights by phrenology?). The Sides of the North. In a letter of January 6, 1879, Williams told the Montana Saints that the region where they lived was “the Sides of the North” (Psalm 48:2), where “the City of the great King” would come down, after wise men had first come to make ready for the Lord’s coming: “you are the pioneers.” He described a land made new, with a milder climate, no beasts of prey and a pure language, but he set no date (Andrew Hendrickson’s 1883 copy, letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881, MS 31876). The same letter calls the Lord’s House, then being built, “my first House of Prayer on the Sides of the North,” and tells the Saints to keep his letters, which would one day be gathered and bound “as our old Bible was gathered up.”

The Montana church (1882–1954) From prophet to vote. Before he died in 1882 Williams wrote that the organization should stay as it was for twelve months and that William James should then be put before the whole church and, if sustained “by uplifted hand,” remain from year to year. After him the church chose its presidents at general assemblies (1883, 1886); Andrew Hendrikson presided from 1886 to 1921 and George Johnson until shortly before his death in 1954, with which, Anderson writes, the church came to an end; USU’s finding aid gives 1969 for its formal disbanding (see How did a prophet’s movement become a church run by vote?). Worship and neighbors. The Lord’s House near Racetrack, built in 1878–79 and dedicated on August 9, 1879, held Sunday meetings. The council kept the sacrament open to non-members who came as “friends for the gospel’s sake,” and in 1886 it accepted an invitation to use the Reorganized Church’s meeting house in Deer Lodge City (see How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another?). What the later church kept. Gems of Inspiration, compiled by John R. Eardley and printed by Joseph A. Dove in 1899, is the movement’s own selection a generation after Morris. About a third of it is a history of the Morrisites, written against the Mormon church; the rest is Morris’s articles, among them “Keys of the Priesthood” and “The Order of Sevens,” and Williams’s visions, letters and records, including two letters to the Saints in Montana. It keeps the order of gods, angels and birthrights and the line from Morris to Williams, condemns polygamy, and does not use the word reincarnation. What was taught in the church’s last decades is not yet known.

t: William W. Davies and the Kingdom of Heaven (1866–1881)
s: William W. Davies and the Kingdom of Heaven (1866–1881) Davies, who had been with Morris, began his own community in Montana in 1866 and led it near Walla Walla, Washington, from 1867; many of its members were converts from San Francisco and Portland who had never been Morrisites. Watson calls it “a novel and mystical Christian sect” with roots in Morris and Joseph Smith (Watson, p. 111). Davies declared in 1867 that a third dispensation had been opened through him on January 24, 1866, in which baptism was set aside for “the Holy Vow of THE COVENANT”; members gave their labor and property to a common fund, and he signed himself the Standard of Israel and dated his papers by the Millennial Era (Watson, pp. 124, 128, 184). He testified in 1881 that reincarnation was “taught & believed” (Watson, p. 186), and he taught that his sons Arthur, later called the “Walla Walla Jesus,” and David carried the spirits of the Son of God and of God the Father; both died of diphtheria in February 1880 (Watson, pp. 191–93). His own pamphlets, hymns and interviews, which give his side, are in Watson, pp. 111–97. See William W. Davies and the Kingdom of Heaven.

Other branches The Doves. James Dove and his son George followed Morris, then Williams, then Davies; in 1873 George began receiving communications and organized a Church of the Firstborn in California of about thirty people, seeing himself as the publisher and organizer of Morris’s revelations rather than a prophet (Watson, pp. 198–99). The Doves published The Spirit Prevails and the roll of membership in 1886, and James Dove’s Treatise on Re-Incarnation (1892), which Watson calls the earliest book on the subject in the wider Mormon tradition (Watson, pp. 199, 208–64). The Montana council disowned them as “pretenders” in 1885. James Brighouse. His Order of Enoch in Independence, Missouri (1884), taught celibacy; no Morrisite source for its ideas has been traced (see the lineage chart under History).

Later echoes What follows shows how Morrisite teaching has been read and borrowed since, not that it was carried on. Leland Jensen’s Missoula sect already held that the Montana State Prison at Deer Lodge was Ezekiel’s temple; after its members came on the Morrisites in 1990 through Anderson’s history, they took Williams’s 1879 letter as confirmation, and Neal Chase set out the connection in Ezekiel’s Temple in Montana (1990). Anderson finds that the book credits Williams with far more prophetic ability than he had (Revisited, pp. 216–18). Chad Daybell’s assignment of past lives and talk of marriages across lives have invited comparison with Williams’s practice, but no line of descent has been shown, and both draw on older Latter-day Saint ideas; Israel A. J. Dennis’s Church of the First Born (1889) shows how readily the name and the doctrine could arise on their own. See Is there a line from Morrisite teaching to Chad Daybell’s?

Common misreadings “Morris opposed polygamy.” His own article treats plural marriage as a law for this life, at God’s time, with one wife sealed for eternity; it was not practiced at the fort (see Marriage, above). “Reincarnation came from Charles B. Thompson.” Anderson proposed it; Watson disputes it (see the question). “Church of the Firstborn” as Morris’s own name for his church. It is later usage (Glossary). “Williams prophesied that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming.” His letter names the region where the Saints lived, “the Sides of the North,” and sets no date. Davies’s community as a Morrisite congregation. It was a new movement led by a former Morrisite, made up largely of new converts.

Read the teachings yourself The Spirit Prevails (1886): Morris’s revelations. Free online; see Start here. Gems of Inspiration (1899): what the later church kept. Free online; see Start here. Kirk Watson, ed., The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026): Morris, Williams, Davies and the Doves in one volume, with an introduction; the place to start for most readers. C. LeRoy Anderson, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited) (2010): the standard history.

t: Cilley, Evans and Courtney v. Davies, 1880
s: Cilley, Evans and Courtney v. Davies, 1880 Frontier Justice WAL-3153 Held by Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, Cheney, Washington Contents Case file of the Washington Territorial District Court for Walla Walla County, original case no. 2373, 1880: a civil suit to collect wages and debts brought by Asa B. Hagg and Broer Sorenson of the 1861–62 roll, and Davies himself; a list of the forty-three members in March 1881, with their ages; printed tracts, hymns and letters by Davies filed as exhibits, among them his printed “Synopsis of Remarks” at a meeting of January 2, 1876; lists of donations to the community from 1866 to 1878; the referee’s report; the judgment of May 25, 1881, for $3,225 (Evans $2,700, Courtney $400, Cilley $125), with interest and costs; and the sheriff’s returns: Davies’s livestock and equipment were sold on June 11, 1881, and the community’s eighty acres, the west half of the northwest quarter of section 34, township 7 north, range 37 east, on July 16, 1881. Bowman, 1885 (WAL-4626, original no. 4262; 28 pages): nine promissory notes of November 14, 1879, totaling $1,770, made by William W. Davies and his son William A. Davies to Lewis H. Bowman, who sold them to the bank the same day. The bank sued in February 1885 and took judgment by default on May 21, 1885, for $4,141.60 with attorney’s fees. The son was served in Lincoln County, near Sprague. Zbaraschuk (1989) lists two more suits by the same bank in the territorial district court: case 3093 (1882), against William A. and William W. The papers are not online; copies may be ordered from the Eastern Region Branch, which scanned both files for this guide in November 2026. Pages 158–195, the depositions of five defense witnesses, were missing when the county microfilmed the file; Whitman College Library later found them among its own holdings and returned them, and they are now with the case file (notes by the Walla Walla County clerk and by the archivist, 2002, filed with the case). Pages 133–157 are not in the file. The archivist who scanned it for this guide confirms that the whole file, several folders, was scanned and sent, and that these pages were evidently already missing when it came to the archives; he suspects they left the courthouse the same way pages 158–195 reached Whitman, perhaps when the clerk’s office reported the records “checked out” (Lee Pierce, Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, email to the editor, November 9, 2026). Using the secondary literature Most of what has been written about the Morrisites rests on a small number of earlier works. Later histories, theses and articles often take their account of 1862 from Anderson, from the 1880s and 1890s retellings in the Salt Lake Tribune and the Contributor, or from one another, so an error made early can travel a long way. The theses listed below are valuable for what their authors saw or heard themselves, such as Don Cornelius’s 1962 interviews in Montana and Julie A. Wright’s use of mission records, and weaker where they summarize events at second hand. Where a fact matters, follow it back to a record made at the time: the court records, the cemetery sexton’s book, the 1886 roll, land and census records, and the newspapers, read in the original rather than in reprints. This guide is held to the same rule; it has its own unsettled points, which are listed on the Questions page, and corrections are welcome.

Common errors in print Claims that recur in published and unpublished accounts, and now in online videos, with what the records show and where to check. They are listed to help readers, not to fault the authors, most of whom were relying on what they had been told. The siege at “Manti” or “Knight Fort.” The siege of June 13–15, 1862, took place at Kington Fort, the Morrisites’ settlement on the Weber River at South Weber, Weber County, Utah. “Kingston Fort” is a common spelling of the same place. See Kington Fort. Kington Fort as a military post. It was a settlers’ fort, built in 1853 and abandoned about 1858, not an army post. See Glossary. Morris excommunicated by Taylor and Woodruff in February 1861. At South Weber on February 11, 1861, the apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff cut off sixteen of Morris’s followers, among them Bishop Richard Cook; Morris’s name is not on the list Woodruff recorded (Woodruff’s journal, February 11, 1861). See Chronology. A skirmish with the militia. It was a three-day siege, June 13–15, 1862. The force was a posse comitatus under the deputy U.S. marshal Robert T. Burton, raised from the territorial militia on Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11 to serve the court’s writs for the arrest of Morris and others. See Morrisite War. A single, settled death toll. Accounts differ on how many died and on some of their names and dates; no list has yet been checked against all the sources. See Who died at Kington Fort? One posse man killed. The posse lost two: Jared Smith on June 13 and Peter Wahler on June 15. The sexton’s record lists Wahler, as “Walden,” next to Morris. One account of how Morris died. Morris was killed at the surrender on June 15, but the Morrisite and posse accounts of the moment differ. Read them side by side rather than taking one as fact. Morris buried beneath a street. The Salt Lake City Cemetery sexton’s record lists him as no. 1469, June 15, 1862, in the pauper ground; the street story has no published source yet. See Where is Joseph Morris buried? Mark H. Forscutt as an RLDS apostle. Forscutt was an apostle in Morris’s church and clerk of its First Council; in the Reorganized Church he was a minister. Dates and names taken from reprints. The first dispatch from Salt Lake City, of June 16, 1862, was reprinted across the country, and its wording drifted as it was copied: “the prophet Moses” became “Prophet Morris,” and “the 15th” became “the 5th.” Cite the earliest printing. See Newspapers. The Montana church ending with George Williams, or with no leaders after him. It was led by William James, George Thompson (from 1886), Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954), until his death in 1954, with which, by Anderson’s account, the church came to an end (Revisited, pp. 212, 214); USU’s finding aid gives 1969 for its formal disbanding. See How and when did the Montana church end? John R. Eardley, called an apostle in 1861, was still called “Apostle Eardly” by Latter-day Saint missionaries in 1896. The Lord’s House built in 1877. The council minutes show that the site on Andrew Hendrikson’s land at Race Track was chosen only on February 24, 1878; the House was built in 1878–79 and dedicated on August 9, 1879 (Church History Library, MS 31876). This guide gave 1877 until November 2026. See Lord’s House. Morris as a simple opponent of polygamy. Morris’s own article of June 4, 1861, treats plural marriage as a biblical law for this life, with one wife sealed for eternity, and it was not practiced at Kington Fort; the movement’s 1899 history condemned it outright. See Teachings. Williams naming Deer Lodge County as the site of the Second Coming. His letter of January 6, 1879, names the region where the Montana Saints lived, “the Sides of the North,” and sets no date. The reading of the Montana State Prison at Deer Lodge as Ezekiel’s temple is not Williams’s or the Morrisites’: it was Leland Jensen’s, and his Missoula sect tied it to Williams’s letter only after reading Anderson’s history, in 1990 (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 216–18). See Teachings. Some differences are matters of memory rather than error, and are noted where they arise: Willow Glen’s founding is remembered as 1881 but first appears in the papers in 1882 (see Deer Lodge Valley). Morgan Evans’s family remembered coming to the valley in 1865 (In the Shadow of Mount Haggin, p. 134); Patrick F. Morris dates his arrival to 1866 (Anaconda, Montana, p. 16). Both rest on later accounts, and no record from the time has yet been found to settle it. The family account also has Morgan Evans freighting from “Corrine, Utah, then the terminus of the Union Pacific Railroad” before the family came; Corinne was founded only in 1869, when the railroad reached Utah, so at least that detail belongs to a later time than 1865. The same family account has the Evanses living in a dugout near Gregson Springs until the spring of 1875, ten years after their arrival. That long stay is not confirmed, but it fits the land record: Evans received the patent for his homestead in 1881, after his claim had been held up in 1880 (see the Gwendale entry on the Deer Lodge Valley map). Some differences come from changed boundaries. Racetrack lay in Deer Lodge County when the Lord’s House was built in 1878–79, and stayed there until 1901, when Powell County was created from Deer Lodge County. Records from before 1901 therefore place the church in Deer Lodge County, and so do this guide’s photograph captions, which keep the county the church was built in. Today it is in Powell County, as the place descriptions say. Searches for Racetrack and the lower valley should cover both counties.

Morris’s new church, 1861 Joseph Morris’s revelations reached the national press a year before the siege, through letters from Utah correspondents. Chicago Tribune, July 17, 1861, p. 3. The siege, 1862 The first reports went out by telegraph from Salt Lake City and were reprinted across the country and abroad within weeks. The Deseret News told the story its own way and never used the word “Morrisite”: in 1862 it wrote of a “band” and “the Davis County bandits.” Sacramento Bee, June 16, 1862, p. 3. “[Second Dispatch.] … Rebellion in Utah—The Prophet Moses, or ‘the Prophet Figgs.’” The original telegraphic dispatch from Salt Lake City, dated June 16. The Outlaws.” Credits “the Deseret News of June 18,” and adds the affidavits of H. O. Hanson and Philo Allen.
