t: Trials, pardons and the removal to Soda Springs, 1863
s: Trials, pardons and the removal to Soda Springs, 1863 Brooklyn Eagle, February 6, 1863. Deseret News, April 1, 1863, p. 4. “Third District Territorial Court.” The court’s report of the March 1863 term, with the seven convicted of murder. Transcription on the Documents page Chicago Tribune, April 24, 1863, p. 2. “Our Utah Correspondence. History of the Morrisites. How the Mormons Treat Apostates. The Siege of Morristown.” A long letter from the paper’s Salt Lake correspondent, written after the trials and Governor Harding’s pardons. Newspapers.com holds two scans of this page. Newspapers.com subscription Boston Herald, July 27, 1863. “From Washington,” summarizing Connor’s report of the Soda Springs expedition. New York Herald, August 2, 1863, p. 2. “The Utah and Idaho Expedition. The Trip from Camp Douglas, Utah, to Soda Springs, Idaho—The Morrisites, or Seceding Mormons.” A correspondent’s account of the journey to Soda Springs with Connor’s command. Newspapers.com subscription ↑ Back to the chart

Soda Springs and after, 1864–1869 Idaho World (Idaho City), November 12, 1864, p. 2. Editorial on county organization and the Soda Springs country. Claims that Connor and a Salt Lake judge took up the Soda Springs land and let it to the Morrisites. A partisan charge, not yet checked against land records. Newspapers.com subscription Missouri Republican (St. Louis), November 15, 1867, p. 3. “A Strange Sect. Mormonism Improved Upon.” On Morrisite belief and a married woman of Cairo, Illinois, who joined. Credited to the Cairo Democrat of November 14, 1867, which has not been found. The story ran in about nineteen papers that month. Newspapers.com subscription New York Herald, December 12, 1869, p. 8. Article on Utah, with the subheads “Bobby Burton’s Pedigree” and “A Crusade for the Faith.” Robert T. Burton’s part in 1862, retold while he was in New York. Newspapers.com subscription ↑ Back to the chart

Who was in command? 1870–1876 Corinne Daily Reporter, January 27, 1870, p. 2. J. H. Beadle, “Home Papers. XIX. Gentiles in Utah (continued).” Beadle’s retelling of 1862–63, including the story of Bill Hickman signing the petition to pardon the Morrisites. Newspapers.com subscription Deseret Evening News, October 29, 1870, p. 2. “Correspondence between Lieutenant-General D. H. Wells and Governor J. W. Shaffer,” with “Letter from Lieutenant-General D. H. Wells.” A quarrel over the territorial militia. Governor Shaffer had banned musters and refused to recognize Wells as its lieutenant-general. To show that earlier governors had recognized him, Wells printed Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, requiring him to furnish Marshal Henry W. Lawrence and his deputies Burton and McKean with “a sufficient military force” to arrest Joseph Morris. That is the earliest printing of the order found for this guide. Fuller’s order on the Documents page · Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Weekly Tribune, November 5, 1870, p. 5. “The Morrisite Campaign. Letter from Henry W. Lawrence.” Lawrence’s answer to Wells, a week later, on the Fuller order and on who directed the force at Kington Fort. It reprints Fuller’s letter of June 11, 1862. The same issue is also on Utah Digital Newspapers. Newspapers.com subscription Corinne Daily Journal, July 26, 1871, p. 2. An anti-Mormon editorial complains that the 1862 grand jury indicted about a hundred Morrisites but refused to indict Burton. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Herald, February 4, 1876, p. 3. “Legislative Assembly.” In the territorial legislature, John Taylor opposed a bill on criminal prosecutions and defended Burton’s part in 1862: Burton, he said, was serving a writ from Judge Kinney and was resisted. Utah Digital Newspapers ↑ Back to the chart

Burton’s arrest and trial, 1877–1879 Burton was arrested in July 1877 and tried in Salt Lake City in February and March 1879 for the killing of Isabella Bowman, one of the women shot at the surrender. The jury acquitted him. Carson Valley News (Genoa, NV), May 29, 1877, p. 3; June 15, 1877, p. 3; June 22, 1877, p. 3. A preacher calling himself the Prophet Daniel tells “the Morrisites” of Carson Valley of a Savior born at Walla Walla, and R. J. Livingstone sells out and leaves to join William W. Davies. Reprinted in the Salt Lake Herald, June 16, 1877, and other papers. Douglas County digital archive New North-West (Deer Lodge, MT), June 15, 1877, p. 2. “The Morrisites. A Good Immigration Story.” The Carson Valley News item on the “Prophet Daniel,” reprinted in Montana; it says the Morrisites “flourish largely in Carson Valley, Nevada.” Chronicling America New North-West, July 13, 1877, p. 4. “The Second Christ.” A description of Davies’s colony “between Mill creek and Russell creek,” about seventy people, “an off-shoot from the Mormon church” whose leader’s young son was claimed to be the second Christ. Chronicling America Salt Lake Herald, July 27, 1877, p. 3. “Arrest of Gen. Burton.” Burton’s arrest on July 26, on a warrant sworn by the foreman of the grand jury. Utah Digital Newspapers New York Herald, August 9, 1877, p. 2. “Murder Territory. Awful Revelations Made to the Utah Grand Jury.” A Salt Lake City letter of July 31 on the indictment of Burton and Dr. Jeter Clinton, naming the witness S. D. Sirrine. Newspapers.com subscription Reprinted in The Sun (New York), August 10, 1877, p. 4. “Killing the Morrisites.” Credited “From the Herald.” Newspapers.com files this page under the New York Herald. From the Sun the story passed to about twenty papers, most of them Kansas weeklies. Newspapers.com subscription Salt Lake Herald, February 21 – March 6, 1879. “The Burton Trial,” daily reports of Burton’s trial for the murder of Isabella Bowman. The fullest account in the free archives. Former Morrisites testified for the prosecution and gave their homes in 1879. Among them were James Bowman (of Soda Springs since 1863), Mrs. Mary Anderson (of Soda Springs), Caroline Eliason, Mrs. Emma Just (of the Snake River valley, Oneida County, Idaho), Jacob Johnson, Thomas Williams (of Ogden since 1865), Philip Hewitt (Salt Lake City) and a man from Hyrum whose name the scan garbles. Men of the posse also took the stand, among them Christopher Sproat, William H. Hunt and Dan Camomile. The defense called Thomas Abbott of Farmington, Robert W. Burton of Kaysville, John C. Thompson of Riverdale and Burton himself. Abraham Taylor, one of the seven convicted in 1863, testified near the close (reported March 4). The text of these scans is poor, and the names are as read from it. Feb. 21 · Feb. 22 · Feb. 25 · Feb. 26 · Feb. 27 · Feb. 28 · Mar. 1 · Mar. 2 · Mar. 4 · Mar. 6 Also reported in The Deseret Evening News and the Ogden Junction (daily reports); the Salt Lake Weekly Tribune, March 1, 1879, pp. 1–5. Search Utah Digital Newspapers New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2. “Railroad Meeting at Gwendale.” Also June 18, 1875, p. 3; September 8, 1876, p. 3; July 6, 1877, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3; April 30, 1880, p. 4; January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3; May 4, 1883, p. 3. Notices that place Gwendale, later Morristown, in the upper Deer Lodge valley. The April 1875 mass meeting of “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” at the Gwendale school house was chaired by Morgan Evans, with W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee. Primaries were held at Wier’s store (1875); the 1876 election judges for Gwendale were Morgan Evans, Peter Jessen and Wm Wier; a W W Thomas of Gwendale paid a subscription (1877); and a fifty-ton smelter at Gwendale began work in August 1877. A land-office notice of March 1880 lists Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims awaited a hearing on whether the land was mineral, among them Daniel James, William P. Thomas, Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen. In January 1882 John R. Eardley built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and in March he was appointed postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was.” By 1883 school district No. 6 was called Willow Glen. None of these items calls anyone a Morrisite. Apr. 16, 1875 · June 18, 1875 · Sept. 8, 1876 · July 6, 1877 · Aug. 31, 1877 · Apr. 30, 1880 · Jan. 20, 1882 · Mar. 10, 1882 · May 4, 1883 New North-West, June 7, 1878, p. 3. The post office at Gwendale, Deer Lodge County, renamed Morristown; “as many of the people are Morrisites, we do not doubt that they will eventually take kindly to Morristown.” Chronicling America San Francisco Chronicle, February 27, 1879, p. 2. “The Morrisite Massacre. Burton, the Mormon Assassin, on the Witness Stand.” Burton’s own testimony at his trial. Newspapers.com subscription ↑ Back to the chart

1880–1900 and the 1891 letters Thirty years on, a series of letters in the Salt Lake Tribune retold the siege from the Morrisite side. They are partisan, and their numbers and quoted speech should be checked against the court records. Salt Lake Democrat, November 24, 1885, p. 2. “Their Destiny.” An anecdote about an elderly man, once a Morrisite in Utah, meeting an old friend. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Herald, January 27, 1889, p. 7. “In Undimmed Glory,” with a letter from Boise headed “Morrisite Bugaboo.” The Herald’s Boise correspondent on the Morrisite affair being raised in Idaho’s territorial legislature. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Herald, July 1, 1894, p. 14. “How to Spend Summer.” A resort piece on Soda Springs that recalls the Morrisites settled there by Connor. Utah Digital Newspapers Helena Weekly Herald, April 22, 1880, p. 7. “A Little Girl Burned to Death.” Reprints the New North-West’s account of the death of the five-year-old daughter of Andrew Hendrickson, later president of the Montana Morrisites, at the family’s farm a few miles from Deer Lodge: her clothes caught fire from burning rubbish in the yard, and she lived twelve hours. A county obituary index gives the death as April 15, 1880, aged 5, and the child is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge, as Maggie Hendrickson (1875–1880). In England George Williams heard of it within weeks: on June 21, 1880, he wrote to William James of the “general mourning & sorrow” the news had cast and sent his sympathy to the Hendricksons (Church History Library, MS 31876). Chronicling America New North-West, April 13, 1883, p. 2. On the RLDS conference at Kirtland, taking that church to be of the same faith as the Morrisites; the settlements on Warm Springs Creek and the upper Deer Lodge River are “largely composed of them,” and the editor praises them as industrious, hospitable and law-abiding. Chronicling America New North-West, July 11, 1884, p. 3. “Reorganized Latter-day Saints.” Notice of W. W. Blair’s RLDS preaching at the Deer Lodge courthouse; the church, “like that of the Josephites and Morrisites,” is distinct from Brigham Young’s and opposed to polygamy. It names the church’s Montana congregations: at Rees Creek near Bozeman, at Willow Creek near Gallatin City, and “near Stuart, in upper Deer Lodge valley.” The Reese Creek branch in Gallatin County was the first in Montana, founded in 1868 by the missionary Joseph W. Morgan, who baptized John E. Reese there (Don Cornelius, “Mormonism in Montana, 1847–1898,” M.A. thesis, 1962, p. 56). Chronicling America New North-West, October 30, 1885, p. 3. “The preachers from California, to speak at the court house next Sunday afternoon, are Morrisites”: almost certainly James and George Dove, who visited the Morrisites at Deer Lodge, Race Track, Willow Glen and Anaconda that October and November (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 182, 207). “There are a large number of Morrisites in this valley.” Chronicling America New North-West, November 13, 1885, p. 3. “Notice. To all Whom It May Concern.” The Montana church disowns the Doves: two men “calling themselves ‘Doves,’” claiming to be Morrisites, are warned against as “pretenders” by the leaders of the church organized in the county “under the name of the ‘Church of the Saints of the Most High,’” who “utterly repudiate their claims, teachings and practices.” Signed William M. James, Andrew Hendrickson and John R. Eardley. The council had ordered the notice at its meeting of November 10 (Church History Library, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 25–27). Chronicling America New North-West, September 3, 1886, p. 3. Also February 19 and March 26, 1886, p. 3. “A Mormon Church, of the Morrisite branch, we are informed, is being constructed under the superintendence of Elder Clapp on the Cottonwood road about a half mile east of town.” An Elder J. C. Clapp had preached at the Deer Lodge court house in February and March 1886, once on the “Origin of the American Indians,” a Book of Mormon theme. The Morrisites’ own minutes settle the question: in November 1886 their council recorded an invitation from “Elder Clapp of the Reorganized Church” to use that church’s meeting house at Deer Lodge City while he was preaching in Utah (Church History Library, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 37–38). The building was the Reorganized Church’s, not a Morrisite church; Clapp was very probably the RLDS missionary Joseph C. Clapp. Chronicling America · Chronicling America · Chronicling America Salt Lake Tribune, July 12, 1891, p. 3. “The Morrisite Movement. Motives That Led the Brighamites to Crush It in Blood.” Signed “The Elder.” The companies that marched on the camp and Howard Egan’s attack and withdrawal. Also the writer’s own sight of Morrisite families being carried west to Nevada in 1863, and where the Morrisites settled: Soda Springs, the Deer Lodge Valley, Walla Walla and Salt Lake County. Newspapers.com subscription Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891, p. 3. “Massacre of Morrisites. The Inside History of That Dreadful Deed.” The ninth letter. The surrender and the deaths of Morris and Banks, and the seven sentenced and pardoned. Also where some survivors went: Soda Springs, Reese River and Carson Valley. Newspapers.com subscription Anaconda Standard, July 26, 1891, p. 11. “The Morrisite Tragedy: A Thrilling Incident in the History of Mormonism.” An unsigned account sympathetic to the Morrisites, from Morris’s arrival at South Weber through the surrender. It appeared the same day as the Tribune’s ninth letter, but the text differs. Newspapers.com subscription San Francisco Chronicle, June 19, 1892. ↑ Back to the chart

Early twentieth century, 1901–1950 Truth (Brisbane, Australia), May 5, 1907, p. 2. “Morrisite Murders. The Case for the Mormons.” Letter of J. F. Nash. A Latter-day Saint’s reply to the paper’s article “Murdered Morrisites,” which drew on Fanny Stenhouse. Nash dates that article April 14, 1907 (the NZ reprint of his letter says April 11); it has not been found on Trove. The exchange between Nash and J. W. Barkus of Coorparoo ran in Brisbane Truth through the summer, and John Norton’s Truth in Wellington reprinted it. Trove (free) · Newspapers.com subscription Reprinted in NZ Truth (Wellington; free on Papers Past) April 27, 1907. The article drawn from Mrs. Stenhouse. Papers Past May 25, 1907, p. 7. “Morrisite Murders. The Case for the Mormons.” Nash’s letter. Papers Past July 20, 1907, p. 8. “More Mormon. Brigham Young’s Words Explained.” Nash’s answer to Barkus. Papers Past Truth (Brisbane), May 26, 1907, p. 2. “‘Morrisite’ Murders. Another Side to the Story.” J. W. Barkus’s reply to Nash. He recalls the Morrisite men in the penitentiary in the winter of 1862–63 and their pardon, and says his company escorted the Morrisite colony to Soda Springs in the spring of 1863. He later took up a ranch on the Blackfoot River. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Tribune, November 13, 1907, p. 4. “Gen. Burton’s Death.” An editorial on Burton’s death that names the suppression of the Morrisites as one of the two chief acts of his career. Utah Digital Newspapers Washington County News (St. George, UT), June 26, 1924, p. 1. “Veteran Pioneer is Called Home.” Obituary of Schuyler Everett, who was called out with the force sent to the Morrisite fort in 1862. t: The end of the Montana church, 1954–1962
s: The end of the Montana church, 1954–1962 The Deer Lodge Silver State Post records the last Morrisite minister’s death and, within a few years, speaks of the church in the past tense. See How and when did the Montana church end? Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), January 15, 1954, p. 2. A feature on George Johnson, then 97. Johnson’s own story as the paper told it: born near Copenhagen in 1856, he came to Council Bluffs at fifteen, became a Morrisite minister, crossed to Montana by wagon train with Andrew Hendrickson, reaching it “early in 1874,” and preached in family homes as Hendrickson’s assistant before he was ordained and the two led in building the church. His obituary and a 1956 article give 1873 for the journey. Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), May 7, 1954, p. 7. “George Johnson Sr’s Last Rites Sunday, Burial in Hillcrest.” Johnson died on the morning of Thursday, April 29, 1954, at ninety-eight. An Episcopal priest conducted the funeral, quoting the words Johnson had used at funerals “as a minister of the Morrisite faith,” and he was buried in Hillcrest cemetery beside his wife, who died in 1907. The paper calls the Morrisite church “almost extinct these days.” Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), August 10, 1956, p. 7. An article on Johnson’s surrey and buggy, recalling him as a Morrisite minister who with Andrew Hendrickson built the little white church west of U.S. Highway 10. Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), March 28, 1958, p. 12. Obituary of Mary Ann Goldie (1873–1958), daughter of Andrew Hendrickson. It describes the Hendricksons as members of the Morrisite denomination “known as the House of the Lord Church, which is no longer active here.” Newspapers.com subscription Also reported in Montana Standard (Butte), March 26, 1958, p. 7. “Mary Ann Goldie Called by Death.” The same obituary, two days earlier. Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), July 27, 1962, p. 7. “Early Day Records Sought By Valley Historical Society.” At the new Deer Lodge Valley Historical Society’s organizing meeting, interest focused on “the Morrisite church which was located at one time” in the south valley. Recent retellings, 1951 to the present Ogden Standard-Examiner, June 29, 1975, p. 22B. “Morrisite War Touche[d] …” (headline only partly read). An anniversary retelling. Newspapers.com subscription Salt Lake Tribune, February 26, 1981, pp. D-1–D-2. “‘Morrisite War’ Disappears in H[istory] …” (headline only partly read). Local memory of the siege at South Weber. Newspapers.com subscription Missoulian, May 8, 1982, p. A-8. Bryan Di Salvatore, “Morrisite Saga Transcends Its Subject.” Review of C. LeRoy Anderson’s For Christ Will Come Tomorrow. Newspapers.com subscription Montana Standard (Butte), June 19, 1982, p. 5. “Deer Lodge Once Thought to Be Site of Second Coming.” With photographs, including the church. Brought to this guide’s attention by Kris Pozega, a great-great-niece of George Johnson. Not yet read for this guide. Montana Standard (Butte), July 2, 1989, pp. 69–71. Roger Kelley, “From Morrisites to Marcus Daly.” An interview with the Anaconda historian Alice Finnegan. She calls the Morrisites the area’s first settlers, says they wintered at Gregson (now Fairmont Hot Springs) before homesteading, and names Morgan Evans, who bought the land for Daly’s town and smelter, as a Morrisite. Morris’s Anaconda, Montana (1997) describes Evans’s arrival in 1866 without calling him one, and he is not on the 1861–62 roll; the claim is unconfirmed. Bonner County Daily Bee, July 9, 2013. “Descendants of Morrisites Sought.” On a descendants’ reunion at Soda Springs, August 3, 2013. Website Caribou County News (Soda Springs, ID), December 18, 2025. “The Morrisites and Founding of Morristown.” Website ↑ Back to the chart

Searching the newspapers The word “Morrisite” finds only part of the story. The Salt Lake papers of 1862 never use it. To find their reports, search a narrow range of dates for names and places: Morris, Kinney, Burton, Weber, Kington. Newspapers.com treats “Morrisite” and “Morrisites” as the same word, even in quotation marks. A search for either finds about 4,300 pages. Nearly a third of them come from 1871–1900, and more than half from after 1900. Many of the hits are about something else. In the 1850s, Illinois papers called the followers of a politician named Morris “Morrisites”; in 1920 a New Orleans baseball team had the same name. Common surnames (Morris, Fuller) bring in letter lists and war news. In Salt Lake papers of 1905–06, “Morrisites” are the supporters of Mayor Richard P. Morris. In 1908–19 they are the followers of Newfoundland’s premier, Edward Morris; from the 1880s on, papers in Morris, Illinois, Oklahoma and Minnesota use the word for their own townspeople. Adding Mormon, Utah or Brigham to a search screens out most of these. Utah Digital Newspapers has about fifty more pages from 1927 to 2024 that mention the Morrisites, mostly anniversary pieces and local history; they are not yet listed here. See them on Utah Digital Newspapers. Most reports from 1862, 1867 and 1877 are reprints. Find the earliest printing and note where later texts differ. The Deer Lodge New North-West (1869–97) is free on Chronicling America; a search for “morrisite” in it finds the seven pages listed here. Free sources for the West: Utah Digital Newspapers (the Deseret News, Salt Lake Herald, Tribune and others), Chronicling America, the California Digital Newspaper Collection, and, for Australia and New Zealand, Trove and Papers Past.

Printed by the Morrisites The Spirit Prevails (1886) Joseph Morris What it is The revelations, articles and letters of Joseph Morris, printed in San Francisco by George S. Dove and Company. The fullest source for Morris’s teaching and for the community at Kington Fort. Read it Internet Archive Roll of Membership (1886) Geo. S. Dove & Co. What it is Eight pages listing the people baptized at South Weber in 1861–62, printed in San Francisco in May 1886. Read it Transcribed on this site, with notes and links to FamilySearch Family Tree. Copy: Utah State Historical Society, PAM 9569c1. Gems of Inspiration (1899) John R. Eardley What it is A collection by a former Morrisite of sayings and accounts from the movement, including Eardley’s history of Kington Fort and the surrender. Read it Internet Archive The Voice of the Seventh Angel! (1887–92) James Brighouse What it is Tracts of James Brighouse, whose title echoes Morris’s claim to be the Seventh Angel. Kirk Watson finds the two used the phrase differently, Brighouse drawing it from Revelation 11, and has found no other link between them. He also notes that the title was already in Latter-day Saint use, from Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 (“Michael, the seventh angel”) and W. W. Phelps’s 1844 funeral sermon for Joseph Smith, which alludes to Smith as the seventh angel of Revelation 16 (see the chronology under 1884). Read it HathiTrust · Google Books Not yet online Wanted Pamphlets A Voice from the West (George S. and James Dove, 1879); Articles of Faith (San Francisco, 1887); A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites (James Dove, 1892). A library or family that holds one of these could make it available to everyone; the editor will help arrange scanning and an Internet Archive copy.

t: Written by a Morrisite: Mark H. Forscutt
s: Written by a Morrisite: Mark H. Forscutt

“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” undated Mark H. Forscutt · CHL MS 702 Original Church History Library, Salt Lake City, MS 702. Manuscript, 54 leaves, in Forscutt’s hand. Catalog record and images Copy Morrisite collection, Utah State University, USU CAINE COLL MSS 10, box 3, folder 1 Date Written some years after Forscutt joined the RLDS Church Contents An insider’s history of the movement: the setting in Utah after Joseph Smith’s death, Morris’s call and claims, the organization of the church in April 1861, its theology and revelations, its relations with the Reorganized Church, the mounting conflict with the territorial authorities, and the opening of the siege of Kington Fort on June 13, 1862, which Forscutt witnessed. The narrative ends with the first cannon shot. Utah State University’s description says the last page refers to an earlier history Forscutt wrote; this is being checked against the original. Edition A documentary edition by the editor is in preparation; the text is not reproduced here. Short passages are quoted and cited elsewhere in this guide. About Forscutt Forscutt (1834–1903) was clerk of the Morrisite First Council and an apostle in Morris’s church, and later a minister in the Reorganized Church. Eric Paul Rogers, “Mark Hill Forscutt: Mormon Missionary, Morrisite Apostle, RLDS Minister,” John Whitmer Historical Association Journal 21 (2001): 69–100. Author’s copy (Zenodo)

Government records Order calling out the posse, June 11, 1862 Utah State Archives, series 2210 What it is Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order to Gen. Daniel H. Wells to furnish the marshal a military force to arrest Joseph Morris. The original has not been found; this copy is in a letter from Nauvoo Legion headquarters of January 14, 1871 (document 1,215), which copies it among “communications … from predecessors of Governor Shaffer.” Text Executive Department Great Salt Lake City June 11th 1862 To Genl D H Wells Commanding Militia of Utah Territory: Sir— A requisition has been made upon me this day, by Henry W. Lawrence, Esqr.— Territorial Marshall for the Territory of Utah, through his deputies, R. T. Burton, Esqr. and Theodore McKean Esqr. for a military force to act as a posse comitatus in the service of certain writs issued from the Third Judicial District Court of said Territory, for the arrest of Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis County, in said district. It appears that said Joseph Morris and his associates have organized themselves into an armed force to resist the execution of said writs, and are setting at defiance the law and its officers. I therefore require you to furnish the said Henry W. Lawrence Esqr. or his Deputies aforesaid a sufficient military force for the arrest of the offenders, the vindication of justice and the enforcement of law. Frank Fuller Acting Governor and Commander-in-Chief. Newspapers “Fatal Resistance to the Laws,” June 18, 1862 Deseret News, p. 404 What it is The Salt Lake paper’s first account of the siege, written the day after the prisoners reached the city. It traces the writs from Enoch M. King’s complaint of May 22, served on the 24th by J. L. Stoddard, to the affidavits of H. O. Hanson and Philo Allen on June 10, and names Morris, Cook, Banks, Klemgaard and John Parsons as the men the writs were against. It reports two young men of the posse killed, “Smith and Wahler” (see Questions), and Cook, Parsons, Klemgaard and some ninety others brought in as prisoners on June 17. Read it Utah Digital Newspapers (search the Deseret News for June 18, 1862)

“The Davis County Bandits,” June 25, 1862 Deseret News, p. 412 What it is The result of the hearing before Judge Kinney in chambers, June 18–19, 1862. Richard Cook was fined fifty dollars and jailed thirty days for contempt and held to bail; Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson were remanded to prison; the other ninety-five men were held to bail of $1,500 each for the March 1863 term of the Third District Court, and stood surety for one another. It is the only list found so far of the men taken at Kington Fort, and a check on the roll: 78 of the 95 match a man on the roll, 8 more probably do, and 9 are not on it (marked * below). On the roll Every man on this list who matches a name on the 1861–62 roll of membership is tagged 1862 prisoner there: the 78 held to bail, with Richard Cook, Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson. Hover over or tap a tag to see the name as the paper printed it and what happened to him. The 8 uncertain matches are not tagged. The men not on the roll are an open question (see Questions); for the trials of March 1863, see the next entry. “Third District Territorial Court,” April 1, 1863 Deseret News, p. 4 What it is The court’s own report of the March 1863 term at Salt Lake City, Chief Justice Kinney presiding, in which the Morrisites taken at Kington Fort were tried. It names the seven convicted of murder, whom the Morrisites’ own histories name differently, and the eighty-five men tried for resisting an officer. The murder trial In People v. Peter Klemgard and others, for the deaths of the two posse men, the prosecutor entered a nolle prosequi for Richard Cook. Robert T. Burton, Judson L. Stoddart, Theodore McKean, David J. Ross and James Hales testified for the prosecution; Margaret Cook, Jens Christian Sorensen, Mrs. Dove, James Bowman, Joseph Marsh, James Mather, Mrs. Banks, David Thomas, Mrs. Gray, John O. Mather, Mrs. Garrett, Philip Hewit, Peter Swenson and Lebrecht Bar for the defence. On Friday, March 27, the jury found Peter Klemgard, Christian Neilsen, Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason guilty of murder in the second degree, and John Parsons and John E. Jones not guilty. The sentences were fifteen years at hard labor for Klemgard, twelve for Neilsen and ten for each of the others. On Saturday Richard Cook, John Parsons and John E. Jones pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and were fined $100 each, and Cook’s $50 fine for contempt in June 1862 was remitted. Two lists of the seven The Spirit Prevails (p. 7) and Eardley’s Gems (p. 31) name the seven as Peter C. Klemgard, John Nielson, Abraham Taylor, George Lee, Christian Nelsen, Jens Christiansen and John E. Jones. The court report agrees on four, but has Kadrup Neilsen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason where they have John Nielson, George Lee and John E. Jones, and it records John E. Jones as acquitted. The report was printed within days of the verdict, and its sentences (fifteen, twelve and five of ten years) agree with Stenhouse; the Morrisite accounts were written decades later. Resisting an officer On Thursday, March 26, in the case of Peter L. McCue and others, the jury found the defendants guilty of resisting an officer and fined each $100. Chief Justice Kinney told them the court had been disposed to look with mercy on men who had acted under the direction of leaders they trusted. Of the eighty-five names called, sixty-eight match a man on the 1861–62 roll, nine more probably do, and eight are not on it (marked * below). The court found several defendants absent, so not all need have been fined; Stenhouse and Bancroft give sixty-six fined. Names called, March 26 Peter L. The Wells–Shaffer correspondence, October 29, 1870 Deseret Evening News, p. 2 What it is A quarrel over the territorial militia. Governor J. W. Shaffer had banned musters by proclamation on September 15, 1870. When Daniel H. Wells, signing as lieutenant-general of the militia, asked him to suspend the ban, Shaffer refused to recognize the rank and called the militia “an unlawful military system.” Wells answered in a letter to the editor and, to show that earlier governors had recognized him, printed two letters from 1862. The first is Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order for the posse sent to Kington Fort, the earliest printing of it found for this guide. Fuller’s order, June 11, 1862 EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT, Great Salt Lake City, June 11, 1862. TO GEN. D. H. WELLS, Commanding Militia of Utah Territory: Sir:—A requisition has been made upon me this day, by Henry W. Lawrence, Esq., Territorial Marshal for the Territory of Utah, through his Deputies, R. T. Burton, Esq., and Theodore McKean, Esq., for a military force to act as a posse comitatus in the service of certain writs issued from the Third Judicial District Court of said Territory, for the arrest of Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis county, in said District. It appears that said Joseph Morris and his associates have organized themselves into an armed force to resist the execution of said writs, and are setting at defiance the law and its officers. I therefore require you to furnish the said Henry W. Lawrence, Esq., or his Deputies aforesaid, a sufficient military force for the arrest of the offenders, the vindication of justice and the enforcement of law. FRANK FULLER, Acting Governor and Commander-in-Chief. The rest of the page Wells’s request of October 25 (signed with H. B. Clawson, adjutant-general), Shaffer’s refusal of October 27, and Wells’s letter to the editor, which also encloses Governor Stephen S. Harding’s letter of November 26, 1862, about arms furnished to the territory since 1861. An editorial in the same issue, “An Extraordinary Letter,” introduces the correspondence. A week later Henry W. Lawrence answered Wells in the Salt Lake Weekly Tribune (November 5, 1870) on who directed the force at Kington Fort; see Newspapers. Transcription Transcribed for this guide from the page image, November 2026; the full text of the correspondence (about 2,700 words) is available on request (Share records). The page is in the public domain. Read it Utah Digital Newspapers (the page image; the text the site provides with it is too garbled to use)

Church records “Niels Anderson matter, 1903” Church History Library, CR 1 191 What it is Letters of Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson to President Joseph F. Smith, January–March 1903, asking help for Mary, wounded at Kington Fort in 1862, with the office’s draft reply and related correspondence. Read it Church History Catalog (24 images)

Joseph Morris’s letters and revelations Church History Library, CR 1234 1 What it is Morris’s letters to Brigham Young and manuscript revelations, 1858–1862, in the folders “Revelations of Joseph Morris” in Brigham Young’s office files. Kirk Watson’s edition, The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026), transcribes twelve of them, from October 11, 1858, to November 26, 1860, in its section “Joseph Morris, Letters to Brigham Young,” and gives the catalog link for each. Watson notes that the revelation headed February 18, [1859], is No. 6 of The Spirit Prevails, dated there September 6, 1860. The letters, by date October 11, 1858 · January 1, 1859 · revelation of January 26, 1859 · revelation of February 18, [1859] · February 24, 1859 · April 21, 1859 · June 15, 1859 · September 1, 1859 · April 20, 1860 · June 24, 1860 · November 21, 1860 · November 26, 1860. Dates as Watson gives them, from the manuscripts; links from his notes. Church History Catalog; a free Church Account may be required. Find more Search the Church History Catalog for CR 1234 1. Two more revelations, of January 14 and 16, 1860, are filed elsewhere in the same papers (see below).

George Morris reminiscences, circa 1867–1886 Church History Library, MS 1614 What it is The reminiscences of Joseph Morris’s brother George Morris (1816–1897): his life in England, conversion, Nauvoo, emigration to Utah in 1848 and life in Salt Lake City, with incidents about his brother Joseph, a family genealogy and a photograph. The bound manuscript (321 images) opens “A Short sketch of the Geneoligy and History of George Morris the Son of Joseph and Elisabeth Morris”; George was born on August 23, 1816, at Handley, Cheshire, one of six children, among them Joseph. Brought to this guide’s attention by Kirk Watson, who finds in it valuable evidence of Morris’s personality, theology and life. Read it Church History Catalog (open to research; a free Church Account may be required).

t: Two revelations to the First Presidency, January 14 and 16, 1860
s: Two revelations to the First Presidency, January 14 and 16, 1860 Church History Library, CR 1234 1 What it is Two manuscript revelations, signed “Jesus Christ” and addressed to “the first presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Later day saints and all so to the twelve apostles.” Both demand that the leaders receive “my servant Joseph.” They are filed as anonymous letters among Brigham Young’s incoming correspondence for 1860, outside the folders of Morris’s revelations, and were identified by Kirk Watson in November 2026, after his edition of Morris’s letters was published, so they are not in it. Why they matter They are among the earliest dated revelations of Morris to survive in manuscript. The Spirit Prevails has only No. 2 (“Winter of 1859”) before them; its No. 3 is dated March 1860. Neither is printed there, but both are early forms of later texts. The January 14 revelation opens “when you whas small in your own eyes i took you and i rose you to the apostle ship,” the same opening as No. 18, “Revelation to President Brigham Young” (October 2, 1860). Like No. 18, it charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door and speaks of “the throne of isreal.” But it is addressed to the Twelve as well as to Young, and its warnings to them, which name Jeroboam, promise “fresh apostles” in their place and threaten to cut them off root and branch, are not in No. 18, which is addressed to Young alone. The January 16 revelation requires anyone with “gould and silver and houses and lands and whives” to “lay them at the feet of my servant Joseph,” the test Morris set out again in No. 185 (December 28, 1861). How they were received The office docket on the January 14 letter reads “Jan 14 1860 / Balderdash / About revelations / Rec Jan 20 1860,” and the same clerk wrote “Balderdash” above the heading of each revelation. The letter is addressed “To president Brigham Young grait Sault Lake City.” The hand Kirk Watson, who has transcribed many of Morris’s writings, identifies the hand and spelling as Morris’s. He compared the January 14 revelation with a revelation “to president young” dated October 11, 1858, catalogued as a “Joseph Morris letter” in the folder “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860” of the same office files. The two share the same dating formula (“October the 11 1858,” “January the 14 1860”), the same letter forms and the same phonetic spelling (“speckelating,” “whas”). Read it January 14, 1860 (5 images) · January 16, 1860 (2 images). Church History Catalog; Brigham Young office files, General Correspondence, Incoming, General Letters, A–Bi, 1860, “Anonymous letter.” For comparison, the revelation of October 11, 1858 (9 images; President’s Office Files, General Office Files, “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860”). A free Church Account may be required. Transcription by Kirk Watson: “Missing revelation Joseph Morris to BY 1860” (Google Docs), linked with his permission.

t: MO-IMG-032The slough below the bluffs. Kington Fort stood on the Weber…
s: MO-IMG-032The slough below the bluffs. Kington Fort stood on the Weber River flood plain, in a bowl ringed on the south and west by sandy bluffs about half a mile off and some two hundred feet high. On June 13, 1862, the posse took its position on the bluffs south of the fort, from which it could see into the fort (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 64, 112, 128). The plan of the fort drawn by G. Q. Jones for the Sons of Utah Pioneers (1996) marks a slough just outside the south gate, and its notes say that on June 15 an armored battery made from the rear of a wagon was rolled toward the fort, caught a wheel in the mud and tipped over, and that its crew retreated under musket fire. Jones does not give his source, and Anderson describes the rolling battery as pushed up to the fort wall (p. 135). The editor, from Jones’s plan and the comments of the South Weber historian Ed Cooper on a visit to the site, takes this to be the slough where the battery mired. See the map on the Kington Fort page.South Weber, Utah · before February 2004 (scanned print)

Cooper says the cabin has been moved from its original site. The three, William Jones (probably William J. Jones of the roll), John Jensen and Lars Gurtsen (probably Lars Christian Geertsen), were brought back to the fort by an armed party under Peter Klemgard; their detention led to the writs and the posse (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 99–108). Transcription of the Anderson plaque (MO-IMG-061) NIELS ANDERSON · OCTOBER 3 [?], 1835 – MARCH 4 [?], 1926 MARY CHRISTOFFERSEN ANDERSON · JULY 26, 1847 – JULY 13 [?], 1928 THEY WERE BORN IN DENMARK; JOINED THE MORMONS THERE. IN 1857 MRS. ANDERSON ARRIVED AT BURLINGTON, IOWA; DETAINED THERE UNTIL 1859 ON ACCOUNT OF JOHNSTON’S ARMY HAVING TO BE SENT TO UTAH. THAT YEAR SHE WALKED NEARLY ALL THE WAY TO SALT LAKE CITY. IN 1860 MR. ANDERSON CAME; HE PULLED A HAND-CART FROM FLORENCE, NEBRASKA. THEY SOON SAW THE DECEPTION IN “BRIGHAMISM,” JOINED MORRIS A SECEDER FROM BRIGHAM. MAY 22 [?], 1863, THEY CAME TO SODA SPRINGS WITH THE FIRST SETTLERS; THEY WERE ESCORTED AND PROTECTED BY GEN. CONNOR AND CALIFORNIA VOLUNTEERS. JULY 20, 1863, THEY WERE MARRIED HERE; THEIR MARRIAGE WAS THE FIRST IN IDAHO TERRITORY AS FAR AS THEY KNEW. LATER MR. ANDERSON BECAME “THE FATHER OF THE ANTI-MORMON PARTY” IN IDAHO. AT SOUTH WEBER, UTAH, JUNE 13–15, 1862, MR. AND MRS. ANDERSON WERE IN “THE MORRISITE MASSACRE.” MRS. ANDERSON’S CHIN WAS SHOT AWAY WITH A CANNON BALL, THAT KILLED MRS. BARBARA DE[…]THELM [?] AND MRS. JOSEPH (?) MARSH, FIRED BY GEN. ROBERT T. BURTON’S MORMON MILITIA INTO A BOWERY OF UNARMED “MORRISITES,” JUNE 13, BECAUSE THEY REFUSED TO OBEY “BRIGHAM’S” DECREES, AFTER JOHNSTON’S ARMY HAD LEFT UTAH ON ACCOUNT OF THE CIVIL WAR. MRS. J. L. BEAR AND HER BABY WERE KILLED WITH ANOTHER CANNON BALL. THEN MANY MORRISITES WITH THEIR OLD GUNS TRIED RESISTANCE. ON THE THIRD DAY ALL SURRENDERED UNDER A WHITE FLAG. MRS. ANDERSON SAYS: “WHEN MORRIS CAME BEFORE GEN. BURTON, THE LATTER USED ABUSIVE LANGUAGE AND TRIED TO RIDE OVER MORRIS ON HIS HORSE. THIS ABUSE WAS ON ACCOUNT OF HIS RELIGIOUS TEACHING. I SAW HIM … SHOOT MORRIS.” DOW’S AFFIDAVIT SAYS: BURTON SHOT MORRIS, BANKS, MRS. JAMES BOWMAN AND ANOTHER WOMAN, AFTER THEY SURRENDERED. TEN “MORRISITES” WERE KILLED, AND ONE “MORMON.” THE PRISONERS WERE TO BE TRIED AT THE NEXT TERM OF COURT HELD BY CHIEF JUSTICE KINNEY, A MORMON. IN THE MEANTIME GOV. HARDING, ASSOCIATE JUSTICES WAITE, DRAKE, COL. CONNOR AND VOLUNTEERS ARRIVED. “SEVEN MORRISITES” WERE SENTENCED TO IMPRISONMENT FROM “TEN TO FIFTEEN YEARS.” “SIXTY-SIX” HEAVILY FINED. “WE,” WROTE GOV. HARDING IN 1874, “ATTENDED THROUGH THE TRIAL, WHICH WAS NOTHING BUT A MOCKERY. BURTON ADMITTED HIS SHOOTING THE PRISONERS. … HAD I BEEN ON THE BENCH I SHOULD HAVE HAD HIM ARRESTED … ; BUT IT WOULD HAVE BEEN USELESS. THE JURORS WOULD ALL BE MORMONS, AND RECOGNIZE NO LAW BUT ‘THE COMMANDS OF AUTHORITY.’ “PETITIONS WERE GOTTEN UP FOR THE UNCONDITIONAL PARDON OF THE MORRISITES, WHICH WERE SIGNED BY ALL THE GENTILES, … NOT A MORMON SIGNED THEM. … “I ISSUED THE PARDON; … SOME MOUNTED MORTARS … COMMANDING THE BEE-HIVE HOUSE AND LION HOUSE, MADE THINGS TOLERABLY SMOOTH ON THE SURFACE.” BRIGHAM YOUNG JUNE 15, AS BY H. P. McLANE, SAID, “THAT MORRIS AND BANKS WILL BE TAKEN I HAVE NO DOUBT. … BUT IF I HAD MY OWN WAY ABOUT IT, I WOULD NOT SPARE NEITHER MAN, WOMAN NOR CHILD; BUT AS IT IS A UNITED STATES AFFAIR, THEY CAN HAVE IT AS THEY PLEASE. BUT AS REGARDS THIS YOUNG MAN, HE HAS DIED A MARTYR TO THE CAUSE AND KINGDOM OF OUR GOD. … THIS WAS A MATTER OF NECESSITY. … THE WORST … I [?] DISLIKE … , IS THAT AFTER THEY ARE ROUTED, THE … ACCURSED DEVILS … WILL BE TRYING TO SNEAK BACK INTO THE CHURCH AGAIN. …” R. W. YOUNG WRITING FOR THE “CONTRIBUTOR,” OF 1890, FOR THE MORMON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION SAYS: “THE … ACTION OF THE GOVERNOR WAS FOLLOWED … IN COURSE OF TIME, BY PERSECUTION OF GEN. BURTON. … A GRAND JURY WAS LED IN … 1870, TO BRING IN AN INDICTMENT FOR MURDER … , AND … (HE) THOUGHT HIMSELF COMPELLED BY CIRCUMSTANCES TO EVADE ARREST … LATER, ANOTHER INDICTMENT WAS FOUND AGAINST GEN. BURTON … , HE MADE NO ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE. …” BETWEEN THESE TWO INDICTMENTS A RULING HAD “PROVIDED IN SUBSTANCE FOR JURIES HALF MORMON, AND HALF GENTILE.” THIS YOUNG SAYS, “THE PROSECUTION LABORED LONG, AND,” “CLOUDS OF WITNESSES WERE BROUGHT FORTH,” “TO PERSUADE THE JURY,” “ONE-HALF BEING NON-MORMONS,” THAT BURTON KILLED MRS. BOWMAN. THIS CASE WAS NO. 3109, U.S. VS. BURTON FOR “MURDER 1ST DEGREE,” SET FOR TRIAL 1ST DAY OF FEB. TERM 1879, MARCH 8 — INDICTMENT DISMISSED. THIS WAS ONE OF THE THREE INDICTMENTS AGAINST HIM. IT WAS ASKED: WHAT ABOUT THE CASE FOR KILLING MORRIS? U.S. DISTRICT ATTORNEY VANZILE ANSWERED “WHAT IS THE USE, IF THEY WILL NOT CONVICT FOR KILLING AN INNOCENT WOMAN?” TO FATHER AND MOTHER, AND HISTORIC TO MAN, WE DEDICATE THIS MEMORIAL. ABRAHAM CHRISTOPHER ANDERSON, I[D]A COLLETT, ANNA CHRISTINA ROGERS, DAVID ANDREW ANDERSON, ABELONE LARSEN, PETER WILLIAM ANDERSON, NIELS CHRISTIAN ANDERSON, MARY AMELIA VERHAM. MO-IMG-099Looking out from the ranch toward the Anaconda smelter stack.Deer Lodge County, Montana · July 8, 2013 People and portraits Historical portraits from the editor’s files; their original sources were not recorded. Portraits published in Anderson, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited) (2010), not reproduced here: Joseph Morris, with a man captioned as his older brother William, dated about 1841, England (p. 118). The only photograph identified as Morris; on its date and identification, see Open questions. A later portrait captioned as Mary Christoffersen Anderson, different from MO-IMG-062 (p. 119). The caption makes her seventeen when she was wounded; the birth date on her gravestone, July 26, 1847, makes her fourteen. George Thompson, with two unidentified women, in a pony cart (p. 120). The caption calls him one of the first to join the Morrisite army and a later successor to George Williams, the Prophet Cainan; Anderson’s text dates his election as president of the church to May 1886. John R. Eardley, George Williams (the Prophet Cainan), and George Thompson, England, about 1873, during a Morrisite mission there under Williams (p. 121). George Johnson and Andrew Hendrikson (spelled Henrikson in the caption), Danish immigrants who led the Montana church (p. 124). The caption’s “from 1866” for Hendrikson’s presidency is a misprint; Anderson’s text gives 1886 to 1921. See Chronology.

The 1861–62 Roll of Membership The men and women baptized into Joseph Morris’s church at South Weber, Utah Territory, in 1861–62, as printed in San Francisco in 1886. A work in progress. The names are checked against the printed pamphlet (a photocopy, November 2, 2026). FamilySearch links, notes and later paths are added as sources turn up, so the counts below will grow. Last updated November 4, 2026. Know something about someone on the roll? Write to contact@morrisite.org. 178 names link to FamilySearch (114 probable). Tap or hover over a link, dot or bar for the evidence; 123 names have a notes button with what the sources say about them. 81 men are marked 1862 prisoner: they are on the list of men taken at Kington Fort and brought before Judge Kinney (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). 2 are marked held at the fort: men the Morrisites themselves had captured and held in a log house that spring, whose detention brought the posse. 37 names have a full page with sources. About this roll Roll of Membership: Names of Persons Baptized into the Fulness of the Gospel USHS PAM 9569c1 Published San Francisco: Geo. S. Dove & Co., May 1886. 8 pp. Subtitle: “Names of persons baptized during the administration of Joseph Morris, at South Weber, Utah Territory, in the years of 1861 and 1862.” Copy Utah History Information Center (Utah State Historical Society), Salt Lake City, PAM 9569c1; gift of William Mulder. Larson’s transcription also records the words “Reorganized Church Library,” probably a library mark on the copy. Compiler’s note “All the names that we found in the record book are in this list. We feel assured that there were many persons baptized whose names were not recorded.” Absence from the roll does not show that someone was not a member. Pencil notes In the copy Larson transcribed, someone has totaled the names in pencil at 430 and marked the church’s officers (listed above); a further pencil note reads “174 Scan names,” apparently a count of Scandinavian names. The roll has 430 names, matching that total; Larson’s transcription had left out David Thomas (note 10). This transcription Made from David A. Larson’s transcription of the Utah State Historical Society copy (MORRISITES-L mailing list, RootsWeb, March 25, 2007), then checked name by name on November 2, 2026, against a photocopy of the printed pamphlet in the editor’s files. The check restored one name (David Thomas) and corrected fourteen spellings to match the print. Names follow the order and spelling of the roll; where a name repeats, the roll adds “2.” Notes on doubtful readings are numbered. Links to FamilySearch Family Tree 178 linked, 114 probable What they are Where a person on the roll has been identified with confidence in FamilySearch’s Family Tree, the name carries a link to that record. Hover over a link to see the basis for the identification and who supplied it. Links open FamilySearch’s public page for the person, which needs no sign-in; a free account shows the full record and its sources. Family Tree is open to editing by anyone, so check those sources before relying on it. What counts A shared name is not enough. A match needs something tying the person to the Morrisites or to South Weber in 1861–62, or a name rare enough in Utah Territory then to leave no other candidate. Matches that rest on circumstantial evidence, such as a husband and wife both on the roll and a likely place, or a family whose members on the roll all match one family in Family Tree, are linked but marked “probable”; corrections are welcome. Cases with more than one candidate are explained in the notes instead. Contribute If you can identify someone, send the FamilySearch ID and your evidence to contact@morrisite.org. Contributions are credited. Families on the roll Updated as evidence is added What it shows People on the roll who were related by birth or marriage, grouped by family, with the places they lived after 1862. The groups come from Family Tree, membership records and published histories; a relationship that rests only on a likely guess is left out until it is checked. Many Morrisite families stayed together after the siege and married into one another at Soda Springs, Deer Lodge and in the Carson Valley, so a descendant of one family may find related families in the same group. Contribute If you know of a connection that is not shown, write to contact@morrisite.org. What became of them Updated as evidence is added How it is counted Each person counts as “not yet known” until a source shows where he or she went: the RLDS Church (Reorganized Church, now Community of Christ), back to the LDS Church, one of the later Morrisite groups in Idaho, Montana, Nevada, California, Washington Territory or Iowa, or death at Kington Fort during the siege of June 13–15, 1862. Many Morrisites joined the RLDS Church only after years in the groups at Soda Springs, Deer Lodge, Carson Valley or Walla Walla; when a source shows both stages, the person is counted as “stayed Morrisite, later joined the RLDS Church,” with a half-green, half-blue dot. The sources are RLDS and LDS membership records, FamilySearch, and published histories. Where the source names someone who is probably, but not certainly, the person on the roll, the evidence begins “Probable identification.” A colored dot beside a name shows the category; hover over it, or tap it on a phone, for the evidence. Send additions or corrections to contact@morrisite.org. Reading the roll Spellings vary, especially for Danish and Swedish names: search under Hanson and Hansen, Peterson and Petersen, Christiansen and Christensen, Sorenson and Sorensen. The roll itself spells some families two ways (Peterson and Petersen; Lorensen and Lorentzen). In its own text this guide names people as the roll spells them, or by the fuller name on their person page (Peter C. Klemgard; Sven Olasson Hägg, the roll’s Svend Hegg). Where it quotes or summarizes a document, it keeps the document’s spelling, so the same man may appear as Klemgaard in the Deseret News or Swen O. Hagg in a court file. The roll records baptisms in 1861–62. It does not show who remained in the church, who left before the siege of June 1862, or who later joined the Soda Springs, Carson Valley, Walla Walla, or Montana groups. Later rolls, including those of the Montana church, which lasted until 1954 or, formally, 1969, are cited in Repositories but not published here.
Who they were

The people on the roll Who joined Joseph Morris? This page counts what can be said of the 430 people on the 1861–62 roll of membership. Some figures cover everyone on the roll, judged from their names. The rest come from the people identified so far in FamilySearch Family Tree, and hold only for them. The roll is not a full list of members. Its compiler wrote that “many persons baptized” were never recorded. The lists behind these figures can be downloaded, and counted in other ways, on the Data page. Corrections and new identifications are welcome at contact@morrisite.org.

Paths into the movement What brought Latter-day Saints to Joseph Morris? The members left few accounts of their reasons, so this section tests what the records can show: when people reached Utah, whom they crossed the plains with, where they came from, and whether they joined as families. Companies are known for 98 of the 178 people linked to Family Tree, from the Mormon Pioneer Overland Travel records attached there and from the rosters of the Church History Biographical Database (CHD). These are associations in the records, not reasons the members gave. When they came, against everyone who came 1847–51 0.5 1852 0.5 1853 3.9 1854 3.3 1855 5.3 1856 4.5 1857–58 1.1 1859 11.2 1860 7.3 1861 0.0 Roll members per 1,000 people in the CHD’s pioneer companies of each year. The highest rate is 1859 (18 of 1,606). People who had arrived in 1859 and 1860, a year or two before Morris began baptizing, joined about twice as often as those who came in 1853–56, and far more often than those who came before 1853. Those who arrived in 1861 had little time to join before the roll closed. CHD counts are the names it holds, not every emigrant; the roll members identified so far are not a random sample, and some were found by searching these same rosters. Crossing together Robert F. Companies were made up by language and port of departure, so a shared company partly repeats a shared origin; the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 was Danish and the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 largely Welsh. John Banks, later Morris’s counselor, captained the 1856 company that brought Robert E. Farley. Weighing the factors Factor What the records show How far it goes Recent arrival 63 of 117 identified people with a year of arrival reached Utah in 1856 or later; the rate per 1,000 emigrants peaks in 1859. Strong pattern, the clearest in the records. Why newcomers joined more often (fewer ties to their wards, less property, hardship on arrival) is not yet measured. Crossing together 65 of 98 with a known company shared it with another roll family. Moderate. It overlaps with origin and with how the names were found. Language and origin 168 of 430 names on the roll are Scandinavian. Strong for the roll as a whole, but it overlaps with arrival year; how it compares with the population of Utah in 1861 has not been measured. Family 127 roll names belong to the 30 family groups found so far (see the roll). Strong where known: families often joined together, so one household’s decision accounts for several names. Many relationships on the roll are still unfound. Place 57 of the 91 roll members found in the 1860 census lived in Davis or Weber County, near South Weber. Strong but expected: Morris preached and baptized there. Leaders and wards The South Weber bishop, Richard Cook, and his brother John joined; sixteen were cut off together on February 11, 1861. Not counted. Followed through the roll notes and person pages. The factors overlap: a Danish family who crossed in 1859 and settled near South Weber counts under four of them at once, so they cannot be added up. A fair reading is that Morris drew most on recent emigrants, Danish and British, who came as families and lived near him, and least on Saints settled since the early 1850s.

What became of them Where the people on the roll went after the Morrisite camp broke up in 1862, as far as the sources show so far. Most have not yet been traced, so these counts will grow; the absence of a category means no one has been identified in it yet, not that no one belonged to it. Others named in the sources People whom the sources name as Morrisites, or as followers of a later offshoot, but who are not on the printed roll of 1861–62. Each entry rests on a source that names the person as a member, officer, missionary, donor or prisoner; family tradition alone is not enough, and only people who have died are listed. “Probable” marks an identification or a membership that is not certain. Corrections and additions are welcome at contact@morrisite.org. With Morris, 1861–62 (2) Named as Morrisites in 1861–62 but not on the printed roll.

Morris, Joseph (died June 15, 1862) Morrisite The prophet himself. The printed roll lists his followers, not Morris. His wife Mary Olsen, a Danish convert he married soon after a revelation of August 23, 1861, is probably the roll’s “Mary Morris.” The roll’s “Karen Morris” is not identified. (Anderson, Revisited, 87, 104–5; The Spirit Prevails, 149–51)

Bowman, Isabella (died June 15, 1862) Morrisite Killed at Kington Fort during the surrender, one of the two women shot by Robert T. Burton’s party. Burton was indicted for her killing in 1870 (the indictment was voided in 1872) and again in 1877, tried from February 18, 1879, and acquitted. Alexander Dow’s affidavit of April 1863 calls her “Mrs. Bowman, wife of James Bowman.” The 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letter says she was holding Joseph March’s baby, whom she had taken in after its mother was killed. Wife of James Bowman (below). Not on the printed roll; she may have joined after it was made. (Salt Lake Herald and Salt Lake Weekly Tribune, Feb.–Mar. 1879 (Burton trial); Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman); Anderson, Revisited, 148–49) Taken at Kington Fort, June 1862 (12) Men held to bail after the surrender or tried in March 1863 whose names do not match anyone on the roll. Being taken prisoner does not by itself show membership: Val Holley names eleven Slaterville and Marriott men among the prisoners. See the June 1862 list and the Questions page.

Aggerson, Hans (1863) Kington Fort (probable) Fined $100 for resisting an officer at the March 1863 term; probably the “H. Okensen” held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Edwards, John C. (1862–63) Kington Fort Held to bail as “J. C. Edwards” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Halse, Samuel (1862–63) Kington Fort Held to bail as “Saml. Hulse” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Moffat, Peter (1862–63) Kington Fort Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Neilsen, Kadrup (1863) Kington Fort Convicted of murder in the second degree in March 1863 and sentenced to ten years at hard labor; pardoned by Governor Harding. (Deseret News, April 1, 1863)
Parr, L. (1862) Kington Fort Held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862)
Peterson, James (1863) Kington Fort Fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, April 1, 1863)
Rasmussen, Soren Peter (1862–63) Kington Fort Held to bail as “S. P. Rasmusson” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Reese, John E. (1862–63) Kington Fort Held to bail as “J. E. Reese” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Sorenson, John Peter (1862–63) Kington Fort Held to bail as “J. P. Sorensen” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)
Williamsen, S. (1862) Kington Fort Held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862)

Bowman, James (1862–79) Kington Fort Husband of Isabella Bowman, who was killed at the surrender. Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863; moved to Idaho in the spring of 1863. In 1879 he testified at Burton’s trial that he had lived at Soda Springs since 1863. Not the John Bowman of the roll, who was at Kaysville in 1870 and South Weber in 1880; Anderson also treats them as two men. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863; Salt Lake Herald, Feb. 21, 1879; Anderson, Revisited, 148, 162; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman)) The Montana church (3) Leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High in the Deer Lodge Valley, 1870s–1969, who are not on the roll.

Williams, George (died 1882) Montana church The “Prophet Cainan,” who claimed to be Morris’s successor and led the church that regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s; in January 1879 he prophesied that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming. (Anderson, Revisited; Watson)

Hendrikson, Andrew (died July 3, 1921) Montana church A Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint. Counselor to William James from May 1882; presided over the Montana church from 1886 until his death. His records, kept by his family, are a main source for Anderson’s book. (Anderson, Revisited)

Johnson, George (born in Denmark, 1856; died April 29, 1954) Montana church Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty years, likewise never a Latter-day Saint; presided at the Lord’s House near Racetrack from 1921 until shortly before his death at ninety-eight, the last official leader of the Montana church. A county biography of about 1902 says he came to Montana in the summer of 1873, worked in Deer Lodge hotels, and then took up a stock ranch eight miles south of the town, and that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” On July 1, 1876, he married Josephine V. Oleson, a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. (Anderson, Revisited; Progressive Men of the State of Montana (Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902]), pp. 1092–93) Followers of William W. Davies (24) Members, missionaries and donors of Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven near Walla Walla, 1867–81, as named in the 1880–81 lawsuit against him and the 1880 census. Many were converts made by his missionaries in San Francisco and Portland who had never been Morrisites; one former Morrisite testified that the Davies doctrine was “not like the Morrisite religion.” Those known or said to have been with the Morrisites before are also tagged Earlier a Morrisite. Davies testified that everyone on his list of donations except Niels R. Beck was a member.

Andrews Follower of Davies Foreman and agent of the community; Davies sent him east. A former member called him the “destroying angel”; another said he left of his own accord. Given name not recorded. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Bowman, Joseph Follower of Davies (probable) Called “the first born in the kingdom”; in Davies’s teaching he was counted among Davies’s sons, as Elias reincarnated. Compare Lewis H. Bowman, to whom Davies gave notes in 1879. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Cilley, Asa B. (at the camp 1871–79) Follower of Davies A blacksmith from Stockton, California, who learned the doctrine at Portland, Oregon, in the winter of 1870–71 and came to the camp in November 1871. He left in June 1879 and sued Davies with Evans and Courtney; the court awarded him $125. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Clore, Jesse Y. (born about 1823) Follower of Davies Born in Kentucky; first heard the doctrine at Gold Hill, Nevada, and took the vow at San Francisco about 1869. He lived at the camp, homesteaded four miles away, and testified for Davies in 1881 (“Jesse Y. Close” in the 1880 census). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)
Corbett, Mrs. M. B. (born about 1834) Follower of Davies On Davies’s list of members in March 1881, aged 47; “Mary Corbet” in the 1880 census. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)
Courtney, A. J. (at the camp 1876–77) Follower of Davies At the camp from about 1876 to July 1877; a plaintiff against Davies, awarded $400. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)
Degroot, Mrs. Follower of Davies Credited with gifts of $218, 1869–78. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

Evans, Thomas W. (at the camp 1870–78) Follower of Davies Earlier a Morrisite (probable) A plaintiff against Davies, awarded $2,700, the largest share. Davies said he came in 1870 and left in the spring of 1878. A Davies letter of March 1877 to a T. B. Evans, who was blind, looked for him “to come with Mr. Livingstone,” the roll’s R. J. Livingstone of Carson Valley. Emma Evans also testified. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Hagg, Ola (born about 1808) Follower of Davies Born in Sweden; at the camp from July 1868, and a witness for Davies in 1881. Probably the father of the roll’s Svend Hegg (Sven Olasson). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)
Hollenbeck, Mrs. Follower of Davies Credited with gifts of $195, 1869–74. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

Jones, Rachel D. (born about 1833) Follower of Davies Mrs. John E. Jones, born in Wales; a member from 1866, she came to Walla Walla with Davies in 1867. Her children were born in Utah and Montana. Her husband, sent out as a missionary in 1868 and later at Indian Valley, may be the roll’s apostle John E. Jones; that is not settled. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Kelley, Michael H. (born about 1843) Follower of Davies A sailor, born in Ireland; first came to the camp in November 1868, having learned the doctrine at San Francisco. Testified for Davies in 1881. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Lambert, V. D. (at the camp 1868–70) Follower of Davies A cooper and later a justice of the peace; Davies’s missionary at San Francisco in 1869–70. He left the community and testified against Davies. Sarah Lambert also testified. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Miller, Søren (born about 1817) Follower of Davies Earlier a Morrisite (probable) “Sorn Miller,” born in Denmark, at the camp from July 1868 with his wife and children Christian J., John M. and Christina, who are all on Davies’s 1881 list. Klemgard’s testimony implies that the elder Miller had been with him in Utah or at Soda Springs, that is, among the Morrisites. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Mortensen, James (born about 1825) Follower of Davies “J. Mortezen,” a shoemaker born in Sweden, at the camp from July 1868 with his wife Maria; their daughter Maria and Oscar Olsen are on the 1881 list. Whether the family connects to the Mortensens on the roll is not known. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Parker, Mrs. E. S. J. (born about 1824) Follower of Davies (probable) A widow, a member from 1868, at San Francisco. Probably the widow of Thomas Parker, Davies’s missionary there; whether he is the Thomas Parker on the roll is not settled. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)
Parker, Mary B. Follower of Davies “Mrs. Parker of San Francisco,” credited with gifts of $2,363.40, 1868–77. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

Perkins, Cornelia S. (born about 1850) Follower of Davies Born in New Hampshire; a member from 1869 at San Francisco, at the camp from that fall. She took the minutes of meetings in shorthand, helped print the community’s tracts and taught the district school; later Davies’s second wife. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census; Find a Grave)
Perkins, M. A. C. (born about 1826) Follower of Davies Cornelia’s mother, a member from 1869 at San Francisco, at the camp from 1872. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Roberts, Jane S. (born about 1811) Follower of Davies Born in England; at the camp from 1868, with her daughter Emily J. Roberts. Testified for Davies in 1881. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Roberts, Robert (died January 1881) Follower of Davies Husband of Jane S. Roberts; Davies’s missionary at San Francisco and Portland, who preached the doctrine and administered the vow. He was later expelled from the community and did not return. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)
Smith, Mrs. Follower of Davies Credited with gifts of $122. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)
Turnbull Follower of Davies Named with Robert Roberts as administering the vow at San Francisco about 1869. Given name not recorded. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Wood, S. W. (born about 1823) Follower of Davies A photographer, born in England, who had an upholstery shop in Portland; he heard of Davies at San Francisco in 1868, came to the camp in the fall of 1869, served as a missionary and is credited with $5,921.65 on the list of donations. A defendant in the 1880 suit (“Samuel Woods” in the 1880 census). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)
