t: 11 Nov 2026Building the Lord’s House; Montana in 1873–74. Correction: …
s: 11 Nov 2026Building the Lord’s House; Montana in 1873–74. Correction: the guide said the Lord’s House was begun in 1877. The council minutes (Church History Library, MS 31876) show the site was chosen only on February 24, 1878, when a joint council voted ten to five to build on Andrew Hendrikson’s land at Race Track. The House was built under Peder Jansen, used for Sunday meetings from the summer of 1879, and nearly paid for that October; the Chronology and the Glossary now say so. Also added to the Chronology: Stake No. 2’s founding meeting of July 12, 1874; the church in 1873, with William James on a mission in Nevada and the quarrel between William P. Thomas and Daniel James; a Fremont, Nebraska, branch, 1871–73 (now also shown in a small locator inset on the Omaha & Council Bluffs map, with Lincoln); and Sven Olson Hagg’s letter of March 1866, which shows Morrisites meeting in the Deer Lodge Valley that winter and William W. Davies already claiming spiritual gifts there. See also the roll notes for Hegg, Davies, Thomas, James and Eliason. The Danish passages are translated by Claude and not yet checked.

t: 10 Nov 2026About the Danish translations. The translations of the Dani…
s: 10 Nov 2026About the Danish translations. The translations of the Danish minutes, the 1869 record book and the Omaha minutebook quoted in this guide were generated by Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, from the Church History Library’s page images (MS 31876). No Danish reader has checked them yet, so treat them as provisional. Each citation now says so, and so does the collection’s entry under Repositories.

t: 10 Nov 2026Omaha in 1871. The last pages of the Omaha minutebook show …
s: 10 Nov 2026Omaha in 1871. The last pages of the Omaha minutebook show the congregation giving up Latter-day Saint-style conferences in March 1871, a leader of its sisters, Marie Mortensen, joining the Reorganized Church that May (the earliest such case yet found among Williams’s followers), and the book closing on June 4, 1871, as members prepared to move west. Its companion record book of 1869 records the earlier lives Williams assigned to the men he anointed. See Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places, the LDS and RLDS question under Questions, and Reincarnation in the Glossary.

t: 10 Nov 2026The Omaha minutebook. The Danish minutebook of the Omaha an…
s: 10 Nov 2026The Omaha minutebook. The Danish minutebook of the Omaha and Council Bluffs church (Church History Library, MS 31876) tells how it was organized in February 1869, while George Williams passed through Omaha on his way to England, and names the Welsh missionary who went with William P. Thomas in 1869 as Daniel James, settling the question corrected earlier today. See Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places, the Chronology, and the roll notes for Rasmus Rasmusson, S. P. Guhl and W. P. Thomas.

t: 10 Nov 2026The Lord’s House dedicated August 9, 1879. The Danish counc…
s: 10 Nov 2026The Lord’s House dedicated August 9, 1879. The Danish council minutes of the Race Track stake (Church History Library, MS 31876) date the dedication of the Lord’s House: in July 1882 the council planned to celebrate August 9 as the third anniversary of its dedication. They also show the council keeping February 14 as Williams’s birthday, and the Danish members’ debate before the 1883 vote. Added to the Chronology and the Glossary.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: which James went to England. Earlier today th…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: which James went to England. Earlier today the Chronology said that William James went with William P. Thomas to join Williams in England in 1869–70. George Thompson’s letter of July 29, 1869, addresses the two as “W. P. and D. J.,” so the Brother James was probably Daniel James, not William M. James; the entry is corrected. Thompson’s letters to Thomas (Church History Library, MS 31876) also place Thompson with Williams at Ashwicken in 1869 and give Williams’s age and the cause of his death, now in the Chronology and the Glossary.

t: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams’s letters…
s: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams’s letters of 1869–73 to Hendrikson and the Omaha church (Church History Library, MS 31876) show that William P. Thomas and a Brother James went to England to be with him and returned to Montana in 1870, give Williams’s own account of Almerin Grow’s mission to Constantinople and Jerusalem, and trace the move from Omaha to Montana in 1871–72. Added to the Chronology and to the roll notes for Rasmus Rasmusson, John Merrick and S. P. Guhl; John Merrick’s identification is raised from “Check” to “Probable.”

t: 10 Nov 2026Williams in England, 1869–73. Williams’s letters of 1870–73…
s: 10 Nov 2026Williams in England, 1869–73. Williams’s letters of 1870–73 in the Church History Library (MS 31876) show that he left America about January 1869, leaving his family in Salt Lake City, and that his “Ashby” was Ashby by Brigg, Lincolnshire; they also give his daughter Adelaide’s full name. In 1873 he called “Burton and Lot Smith” “the murderers at Weber”; whether Lot Smith was at the siege is a new open question under Questions.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Montana by 1868. The Glossary said the Montan…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Montana by 1868. The Glossary said the Montana church regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s. A letter of George Williams dated December 14, 1868, is addressed to “Bro. James & Saints of the Most High in Montana,” so William James’s group was there, under that name, by 1868 (Church History Library, MS 31876). The Glossary is corrected and the Chronology has a new 1868 entry, which also notes that Williams was living in George Thompson’s house at Walthamstow by 1876. The roll note for Charles Higham adds his visit to Thompson in England about 1877.

t: 10 Nov 2026Thompson at Williams’s side. In March 1882, as George Willi…
s: 10 Nov 2026Thompson at Williams’s side. In March 1882, as George Williams lay dying at Walthamstow, George Thompson answered the Montana church’s questions for him, explaining that Williams “was not really Cainan the son of Enos” but represented him, and promising to confirm the church’s choice of officers (Church History Library, MS 31876). Added to the Chronology, the Glossary and the Questions.

t: 10 Nov 2026Thompson in England. George Thompson, elected president of …
s: 10 Nov 2026Thompson in England. George Thompson, elected president of the church in Montana in April 1886, was writing to the members that December from Thornwood Common, Epping, Essex, open to Joseph Smith III being “called through our Joseph” but not yet calling him a prophet. The letter is in the Church History Library’s Cainan letters (MS 31876) and is now in the Chronology and the Questions. The same letters show John R. Eardley planning, in February 1880, to open a store in Montana (see the roll note).

t: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s last instructions. The Church History Library’s …
s: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s last instructions. The Church History Library’s Cainan letters (MS 31876) hold George Williams’s own note of January 29, 1882, directing that William James be put before the church a year after his death, and an envelope to James inscribed “I leave you in charge after my decease,” the words James later relied on in claiming the presidency for life. Both are now in the Chronology. The same letters add to the roll notes for S. P. Guhl, who disputed James’s authority from Omaha in 1874, and for John Parson, William White and John Merrick, whom John R. Eardley reported on from California in 1875.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Montana elections. This guide said, follo…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Montana elections. This guide said, following Anderson, that William James was sustained as president in Montana in May 1882 and that George Thompson was elected president of the church on May 10, 1886. The Montana minutebook at the Church History Library records both elections at the yearly general assembly on April 25, the anniversary of George Williams’s death: James in 1883, by 19 votes to 10, and Thompson in 1886. The May dates are those of council meetings. The Chronology and Questions are corrected.

t: 10 Nov 2026The Montana church’s own records. The Church History Librar…
s: 10 Nov 2026The Montana church’s own records. The Church History Library’s Church of the Firstborn records, now on the Repositories page and readable online, include the membership record kept from 1874 and the council minutes for 1881–1890. They give the date of Williams’s death in England (April 25, 1882), the two stakes on Warm Spring Creek and at Race Track, the meeting house at Willow Glen, the schisms of 1883 and 1886, the council’s notice in the New North-West of November 13, 1885, disowning the Doves of the California congregation (now on the Newspapers page), and an invitation in 1886 to use the Reorganized Church’s new meeting house in Deer Lodge City, which settles who built the church a newspaper had called Morrisite, now a first finding on one of the open questions. The membership record also strengthens the notes on several names on the roll: Ole Olsen, W. P. Thomas and Erick Eliason, and new notes for William James, Christian Anderson and Rasmus Rasmusson.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Zbaraschuk paper. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 …
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Zbaraschuk paper. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 paper on William W. Davies was written at Walla Walla College, not Whitman College as this guide said. Its acknowledgments thank his thesis advisor at Walla Walla College, and the Church History Library catalogs it the same way. The Bibliography is corrected.

t: 10 Nov 2026Citations for your reference manager. The Bibliography and …
s: 10 Nov 2026Citations for your reference manager. The Bibliography and the Newspapers list can now be downloaded for Zotero, EndNote or Mendeley, as RIS, BibTeX or CSL-JSON: 109 books, articles, theses and media items, and 66 newspaper articles and reprints, each reprint noting the paper it was copied from. Each record keeps the citation exactly as it appears here.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Johan Peter Lorentzen. Earlier versions of th…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Johan Peter Lorentzen. Earlier versions of this guide gave his death as 1870 in Nevada. Family Tree says only that he died before 1870, probably in Nevada; the date was an estimate misread as a year. His death date is now left blank on the roll, the people and Movements pages and in the data files, and a new roll note explains the evidence, including the 1870 census, which finds his children Charles and Josephine at Treasure City with no father in the household. The same misreading had crept into the new roll note on Ole Olsen’s wife Anne, which gave Family Tree’s date for her death as 1870; the tree, too, says only “before 1870,” with no source, so the 1902 account of her death in Wyoming in 1862 stands uncontradicted. That note is corrected.

t: 10 Nov 2026George Johnson in 1902. A county biography of about 1902, P…
s: 10 Nov 2026George Johnson in 1902. A county biography of about 1902, Progressive Men of the State of Montana, says of George Johnson, later the last leader of the Montana church, that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” It also confirms that his wife, Josephine V. Oleson, was a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. Both entries are updated: Johnson under others named, and Ole Olsen on the roll.

t: 10 Nov 2026Free to reuse, with credit. The guide’s own text and data a…
s: 10 Nov 2026Free to reuse, with credit. The guide’s own text and data are now licensed under CC BY 4.0, and the data files carry a release number and a list of changes, so a figure can be traced to the version it came from. Release 1.0 is archived at Zenodo with a permanent identifier, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24100263. Every name on the roll now has its own link (hover over a name and click #), pages can be saved to Zotero with one click, and pages print without menus and buttons. The About page now explains how corrections are made and what the guide does for accessibility.

t: 9 Nov 2026The guide’s data, to download. A new Data page offers the li…
s: 9 Nov 2026The guide’s data, to download. A new Data page offers the lists behind the roll, the person pages and the Where they went map as CSV files: the 1861–62 roll with FamilySearch matches, birthplaces, emigrating companies and later affiliations; documented whereabouts after 1862; family ties on the roll; and others named as Morrisites. Each comes with a description of its columns and their limits, and all four can be downloaded together. The page also shows how much is known so far about the people on the roll, where they were decade by decade, a table of the roll that can be sorted, filtered, shared by link and downloaded, and a tool for counting the roll by any two characteristics, with the unknowns shown.

t: 9 Nov 2026Birthright by phrenology? A fragment of a letter in the Morr…
s: 9 Nov 2026Birthright by phrenology? A fragment of a letter in the Morrisite collection at USU says that a prophet in hiding at Cottonwood felt men’s heads “Phrenologically” to tell them their priesthood, and that no descendant of Cain would enter the Church. Kirk Watson, who found it, identifies the prophet as the Prophet Cainan. The page also names a Niel Beck. See the new question of interpretation.

t: 9 Nov 2026The Racetrack church in 2020. Ten photographs taken inside a…
s: 9 Nov 2026The Racetrack church in 2020. Ten photographs taken inside and outside the Lord’s House on August 16, 2020, contributed by a reader, extend the condition record between 2018 and the videos of 2026. They show the pulpit, benches and table still in place, and the hymnals and a 1931 Reorganized Church lesson quarterly left in the building. See Images. The Bibliography adds In the Shadow of Mount Haggin (1975), on the Evans family at Gwendale, and an Anaconda Standard article of 1935 that Patrick F. Morris cites.

t: 9 Nov 2026The missing pages of the Davies case. Pages 133–157 of the 1…
s: 9 Nov 2026The missing pages of the Davies case. Pages 133–157 of the 1880 case against Davies are not in the file at the Washington State Archives: archivist Lee Pierce confirms the whole file was scanned and that those pages were missing before it reached the archives. They may have left the courthouse with pages 158–195, which Whitman College later found and returned. See Repositories.

t: 8 Nov 2026Corrections. A check of the guide against its sources led to…
s: 8 Nov 2026Corrections. A check of the guide against its sources led to several fixes. The chronology no longer gives a single death toll for the siege, and now says that John Banks died in custody on the evening of the surrender. The Glossary explains that “Church of the Firstborn” was not the name of Morris’s church in 1861: his revelations call it “my Church,” and Anderson gives the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High. The roll no longer lists Joseph Morris’s wives as Mary and Karen: his wife Mary Olsen is probably the roll’s Mary Morris, and Karen Morris is not identified. Notes on Anne Bar now record that the sources disagree on whether her baby died. Citations of The Spirit Prevails have been checked against the 1886 text; the account of the surrender, the trials and the pardons is on its p. 8, not p. 7, and it names the second woman shot at the surrender “Mrs. O’Hagg” (see Who died at Kington Fort?). The counts on Who they were now include all 178 people linked to Family Tree.

t: 7 Nov 2026Reading the sources. The Bibliography now opens with a note …
s: 7 Nov 2026Reading the sources. The Bibliography now opens with a note on using the secondary literature and a list of common errors in print, from the siege placed at “Manti” to the street burial, with what the records show. A new question on the Questions page asks how the story has been passed down and where those errors come from.

t: 7 Nov 2026Two Montana sources. Henry Hendrickson’s 1962 interview on t…
s: 7 Nov 2026Two Montana sources. Henry Hendrickson’s 1962 interview on the Deer Lodge Valley Morrisites, now online from the University of Montana, is listed under Repositories, and Julie A. Wright’s 2004 thesis “Mormon Movement to Montana” under Bibliography.

t: 7 Nov 2026Where Gwendale was. Notices in the New North-West place Gwen…
s: 7 Nov 2026Where Gwendale was. Notices in the New North-West place Gwendale, the Montana settlement renamed Morristown in 1878, in the upper Deer Lodge valley near Warm Springs and Lost Creek; by 1883 its school district was called Willow Glen. Gwendale is now marked on the valley map, with roll notes for W. P. Thomas and William W. Thomas. The four Warm Springs homestead claims named in a March 1880 land-office notice (Morgan Evans, Peter Jessen, Daniel James and W. P. Thomas) were all patented in 1880–81 and are now drawn on the map. The paper also settles the link between the names: in March 1882 it reported John R. Eardley’s appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was”; his store stood at “Daniel James’ corner.” See Deer Lodge Valley and Newspapers.

t: 7 Nov 2026The Deer Lodge paper. Seven items from the New North-West of…
s: 7 Nov 2026The Deer Lodge paper. Seven items from the New North-West of Deer Lodge (1877–86), free on Chronicling America, are now on the Newspapers page. Among them: a Montana post office renamed Morristown in 1878 because many of its people were Morrisites, a description of Davies’s colony in 1877, and the Doves’ visit to preach at the Deer Lodge courthouse in 1885.

t: 7 Nov 2026The groups over time. A new timeline in the History chronolo…
s: 7 Nov 2026The groups over time. A new timeline in the History chronology shows the Morrisite groups side by side on one time scale, from Morris’s church through Soda Springs, Nevada, Cainan’s claim, Omaha, the Montana church, Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven, Parson’s kingdom and the Doves’ Church of the Firstborn, with their leaders and the movements of members between them.

t: 7 Nov 2026Witnesses at Burton’s trial. Former Morrisites who testified…
s: 7 Nov 2026Witnesses at Burton’s trial. Former Morrisites who testified at Burton’s 1879 trial are now noted on the roll: Mary Christoffersen Anderson and Caroline (Karen) Eliason of Soda Springs, Philip Hewitt of Salt Lake City, Emma Thompson Just of the Snake River valley, and, less certainly, Abraham Taylor and Thomas Williams. Mary Anderson, Emma Just and Philip Hewitt now have an 1879 stop on Where they went.

t: 7 Nov 2026Fuller’s order for the posse. The Documents page now has the…
s: 7 Nov 2026Fuller’s order for the posse. The Documents page now has the Wells–Shaffer correspondence of October 1870, with the text of Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, requiring Daniel H. Wells to furnish a military posse for the arrest of Joseph Morris.

t: 7 Nov 2026Isabella and James Bowman. Isabella Bowman, killed at the su…
s: 7 Nov 2026Isabella and James Bowman. Isabella Bowman, killed at the surrender and the woman Burton was tried for killing in 1879, is now listed among the others named in the sources, with her husband James, who testified at the trial. James was earlier taken to be the John Bowman of the roll; the sources show they were different men. The timeline now gives both of Burton’s indictments: 1870, voided in 1872, and 1877.

t: 7 Nov 2026Newspapers. A new Newspapers page lists the press coverage b…
s: 7 Nov 2026Newspapers. A new Newspapers page lists the press coverage by event, from the Sacramento dispatch of June 16, 1862, and its reprints as far as England and Australia, through the 1870 dispute over who commanded at Kington Fort, Burton’s arrest in 1877 and the Salt Lake Tribune letters of 1891, to recent retellings. It also has tips for searching the newspapers. A first pass through Utah Digital Newspapers added the Salt Lake Herald’s daily reports of Burton’s 1879 trial, where former Morrisites testified and gave their homes at the time, and a 1907 interview with Presto Burrell of Connor’s command, who helped escort the colony to Soda Springs.

t: 6 Nov 2026Where they went. A new animated map follows the people on th…
s: 6 Nov 2026Where they went. A new animated map follows the people on the 1861–62 roll from Kington Fort to Soda Springs, the Carson Valley, the Deer Lodge Valley, Walla Walla and beyond, year by year, as censuses, land patents, testimony and death records place them. Choose a family to follow it, or tap a dot for the person’s sources.

t: 6 Nov 2026Zbaraschuk on Davies, and two more court cases. Tony Zbarasc…
s: 6 Nov 2026Zbaraschuk on Davies, and two more court cases. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 Walla Walla College paper on William W. Davies is now in the Bibliography. Its notes point to two more suits against the Davieses (1882 and 1883), now listed with the Davies case files on Repositories.

t: 6 Nov 2026A map of Morristown. The Morristown page now maps the 1863 s…
s: 6 Nov 2026A map of Morristown. The Morristown page now maps the 1863 settlement at Soda Springs: the Lower Town (mostly under Alexander Reservoir), the probable site of Camp Connor, the markers, the Andersons’ graves in Fairview Cemetery, and the land patents of the families who stayed. Hover over the markers on the Places map to preview each place’s site map.

t: 6 Nov 2026Maps of Kington Fort and the Kingdom of Heaven. The Kington …
s: 6 Nov 2026Maps of Kington Fort and the Kingdom of Heaven. The Kington Fort page now maps the fort and the siege of June 1862 as G. Q. Jones’s plan and Anderson place them: the monument, the fort’s outline, the bowery, the west gate, the slough by the south gate and the posse’s bluffs. The Kingdom of Heaven page maps William W. Davies’s eighty acres, placed from the legal description in the 1881 sheriff’s sale, and Swen O. Hagg’s homestead. Each site is marked as located, approximate or not yet located.

t: 6 Nov 2026Places in the Deer Lodge Valley. The Deer Lodge Valley page …
s: 6 Nov 2026Places in the Deer Lodge Valley. The Deer Lodge Valley page now has a map and a list of the Morrisite sites in the valley, each marked as located, approximate or not yet located: the Lord’s House at Racetrack, the land entries of Morrisite families between Racetrack and Deer Lodge, William Price Thomas’s 1863 settlement on Warm Springs Creek, and Willow Glen, where a reminiscence in the Montana Historical Society places the post office of 1881 beside “an old log church” and the home of William James. Corrections are welcome.

t: 6 Nov 2026Anaconda and Willow Glen. Volunteers at the Marcus Daly Muse…
s: 6 Nov 2026Anaconda and Willow Glen. Volunteers at the Marcus Daly Museum and Archives in Anaconda shared the museum’s Willow Glen photographs, including the Rasmus Rasmussen family in 1915, and pages from Patrick F. Morris’s history of Anaconda on the first Morrisite settlers in the upper Deer Lodge Valley and the wagon train of 1871. See History under the 1870s, Repositories and the Bibliography.

t: 6 Nov 2026The “seventh angel” before Morris. Kirk Watson points out th…
s: 6 Nov 2026The “seventh angel” before Morris. Kirk Watson points out that the title Morris claimed was already in Latter-day Saint use: W. W. Phelps’s 1844 funeral sermon for Joseph Smith alludes to him as the seventh angel of Revelation 16, a connection first made by Christopher Blythe, and Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 names “Michael, the seventh angel, even the archangel.” See History under 1884 and the Glossary.

t: 5 Nov 2026The Walla Walla court files. The Washington State Archives s…
s: 5 Nov 2026The Walla Walla court files. The Washington State Archives scanned the two lawsuits against William W. Davies for this guide. The 1880 case brought by three former followers ended in a judgment of $3,225 and the sheriff’s sale of the community’s livestock and its eighty acres in 1881. Its depositions add to the record of several people on the 1861–62 roll: Peter C. Klemgard, who lived at Davies’s camp from 1870 to 1872; Swen O. Hagg, who came to Walla Walla with the first five families in 1867; Niels R. Beck, probably the “Neil A. [or R.?] Beck of Montana” who sent money toward the land; and R. J. Livingstone, who left the Carson Valley for Walla Walla in 1877, as the Carson Valley News reported. Witnesses also describe the community’s teaching of reincarnation. Thanks to Lee Pierce of the archives’ Eastern Region Branch. See Repositories, the roll notes and the reincarnation question.

t: 5 Nov 2026The man who went for help. Lars Christian Geertsen, one of t…
s: 5 Nov 2026The man who went for help. Lars Christian Geertsen, one of the men the Morrisites held in their log-house jail in 1862, escaped and carried word to Salt Lake City. A Church History Department profile now confirms that he is the same man who settled at Salmon, Idaho, where he ranched at Geertson Creek and built a log house, later listed on the National Register of Historic Places, whose upstairs dance hall served the community into the 1920s. Readers in Salmon pointed the way. See Lars Christian Geertsen.

t: 5 Nov 2026A 1982 newspaper story. The Montana Standard of June 19, 198…
s: 5 Nov 2026A 1982 newspaper story. The Montana Standard of June 19, 1982, ran “Deer Lodge Once Thought to Be Site of Second Coming,” with photographs of the Racetrack church; Kris Pozega, a great-great-niece of George Johnson, brought it to light. See the Bibliography.

t: 4 Nov 2026Where did the reincarnation teaching come from? With help fr…
s: 4 Nov 2026Where did the reincarnation teaching come from? With help from Kirk Watson, the question now sets out C. LeRoy Anderson’s theory that Morris took the idea from Charles B. Thompson, and the case against it: the idea was already current among Latter-day Saints in the 1850s, and Morris dated it to a revelation of 1859. It also adds Israel A. J. Dennis, who founded a reincarnationist “Church of the First Born” with no known Morrisite tie, and corrects the chronology on James Brighouse, whose ideas have not been traced to the Morrisites. See Questions and History.

t: 4 Nov 2026What became of them. The later paths of the people on the ro…
s: 4 Nov 2026What became of them. The later paths of the people on the roll now have their own section on Who they were, beside the paths that brought them into the movement.

t: 4 Nov 2026The 1880 census. One census page at Walla Walla shows Willia…
s: 4 Nov 2026The 1880 census. One census page at Walla Walla shows William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven in the summer it began to break up: Davies, a widower, with Sven Hagg in his house and David Park, Ole Hagg, the Sorensons and others around him, months after the deaths of his sons Arthur and David. The same census finds Erik Eliasson farming in the Deer Lodge Valley while his family stayed at Soda Springs, and settles who John Garrett’s wife was. See William W. Davies and Erik Eliasson.

t: 4 Nov 2026The “Walla Walla Jesus” case. The 1880 lawsuit against Davie…
s: 4 Nov 2026The “Walla Walla Jesus” case. The 1880 lawsuit against Davies, reported missing from the county courthouse, survives in the Washington State Archives as a territorial court case file, and Whitman College holds copies of depositions and an 1882 photograph of the Davies family and home. See Repositories.

s: 4 Nov 2026Land records. Federal land patents traced for about twenty roll members and their families, from David Park’s claim in the Carson Valley in 1864 to Walla Walla in 1890, with the Deer Lodge Valley, Soda Springs and Blackfoot between. See the notes on the roll and Repositories.

s: 4 Nov 2026Three new pages. Niels R. Beck, John Garrett and David Park bring the pages on people of the roll to thirty-seven.

s: 3 Nov 2026The Eliasons and the Christoffersens. A family group sheet and a 1989 Powell County history add Erik Eliasson’s brother Elias, the family’s move to the Deer Lodge Valley, and the Christoffersens’ road north to Montana. See Erik Eliasson.

s: 3 Nov 2026The prisoners and the trials. The Deseret News named the ninety-eight men brought before Judge Kinney after the siege in June 1862, and the seven convicted of murder in March 1863, with their sentences. The posse lost two men, not one. See Documents and Questions.

s: 3 Nov 2026Paths into the movement. Who they were now asks what brought Latter-day Saints to Morris: those who reached Utah in 1859–60 joined at about twice the rate of earlier emigrants. The roll now has 150 names linked to FamilySearch, 30 family groups, and notes on 92 people.

s: Nov 2026Documents and the posse order. A new page gathers the primary documents that can be read online, including Acting Governor Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, calling out the militia. See Documents.

About

About this guide Where the material comes from, how it is checked, and how to cite it. How the guide was compiled The guide brings together work done over more than two decades. Its foundation is the research of C. LeRoy Anderson, whose files at Utah State University (Caine Coll. MSS 10) remain the largest body of Morrisite records. The editor assisted Anderson with the 2010 edition of his history and has studied the Morrisite apostle and later RLDS minister Mark Hill Forscutt since at least 2001, when his first article on Forscutt appeared, including transcribing Forscutt’s journals. Photographs of the sites were taken by the editor from the early 2000s onward. Kirk Watson’s 2026 edition of Morrisite writings, published scholarship, and records shared by descendants fill out the rest. Standards Citations follow The Chicago Manual of Style. Every work in the bibliography has been examined by the editor in at least one edition; where a page reference comes from an edition not seen, the entry says so. A work known only from another source’s citation will be marked Not yet checked. Facts are drawn from published works with citations; their text is not reproduced. Videos and photographs by others are linked, not copied, unless they have been shared for this guide; those are credited. Dates marked provisional, approximate, or “ca.” are flagged as such and revised when better evidence turns up. Membership rolls and other records naming private individuals are cited but not republished, with one exception: the 1861–62 South Weber roll, printed in 1886 and naming only people baptized more than 160 years ago, is given in full on the Roll of membership page. Changes are listed under What’s new. Oral and field sources Records of the editor’s own fieldwork, cited in this guide. Rogers, Eric Paul. “Memorandum of Recollection: South Weber Door-to-Door Visit.” Signed memorandum, November 1, 2026, recalling an unrecorded canvass of South Weber residents made before February 2004 in preparation for the editor’s 2006 John Whitmer Historical Association paper. PDF Privacy The guide counts visits with GoatCounter, an open-source service that uses no cookies and collects no personal information. It records which pages are read, how visitors arrived, and what words are typed into the search box, so the editor can see what readers look for and where the guide falls short. No one is tracked from one site to another, and the counts are not shared or sold. How to cite this guide Rogers, Eric Paul, ed. Morrisite.org: A Research Guide to the Morrisites. Accessed [date]. https://morrisite.org.

Reusing this guide The editor’s own text and the data files on this site are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0): you may copy, adapt and republish them for any purpose, provided you credit Morrisite.org and link to the page or file you used. Photographs, documents and quotations from other people and institutions are not covered; they belong to their owners, who are named in each caption or citation, and permission to reuse them must come from those owners. Photographs taken by the editor (those on the Images page with no other source noted) are also licensed under CC BY 4.0; please credit “Eric Paul Rogers, Morrisite.org.”

Corrections Errors are corrected as soon as they are found. A correction that changes a fact, a date or an identification is listed under What’s new, and person pages show the date they were last updated. Corrections, with the source they rest on, are welcome at contact@morrisite.org, and contributors are credited unless they prefer not to be.

Accessibility The guide aims to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2) at level AA. Pages can be read with a screen reader and used with a keyboard alone, images carry text descriptions, the text can be enlarged without loss, and the layout adapts to phones and to the reader’s light or dark setting. Charts are accompanied by the numbers behind them, and every page prints cleanly. If anything is hard to read or use, please write to contact@morrisite.org, and it will be fixed.
Contribute

Share records and corrections Much of the record is still in private hands. This site is noncommercial and does not ask for or accept money. Write to the editor at contact@morrisite.org. Descendants If your family kept letters, diaries, photographs, or church papers, they can be described here, and digitized or placed in a repository if you wish. Nothing is published without your permission. Researchers Send citations, corrections, and new finds. Theses, conference papers, and local histories are especially welcome, since they are the hardest to locate. Forscutt papers For the forthcoming edition of Forscutt’s “Sketch of Joseph Morris,” the editor would be glad to learn of other writings by Mark H. Forscutt: letters, diaries, sermons, or the earlier Morrisite history he is said to have written, whether in repositories or in family hands.

On the roll Erik Eliasson (1817–1893) A Swedish convert baptized into Joseph Morris’s Church of the Firstborn at South Weber, who stayed with the Morrisites at Soda Springs, joined the RLDS Church in 1870, and died among the Morrisite families of the Deer Lodge Valley. On the roll Eliason, Erick, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886; listed with Eliason, Karen Born May 2, 1817, Västmanland, Sweden Died March 6, 1893, Racetrack, Deer Lodge Valley, Montana Wife Karin Caroline Anderson (1830–1902), on the roll as Eliason, Karen; married 1860 (FamilySearch LHN8-4C5) Children Six: Caroline (born 1861 at Farmington, Utah), then Anna, Joseph, the twins Jacob and John, and Isaac, all born at Soda Springs between 1863 and 1869 (Family Tree) Later path Stayed with the Morrisites, then joined the RLDS Church Family Tree FamilySearch MVRH-QQ6, Erik Eliasson (1817–1893) Places in this guide Kington Fort, Morristown, Deer Lodge Valley Life 2 May 1817Born in Västmanland, Sweden. (Family Tree) 1860Marries Karin Caroline Anderson, who reached Utah that year. (Family Tree) 1861–62Baptized with Karin into the Church of the Firstborn at South Weber; both names are on the roll of membership. His name is not on the list of men taken at Kington Fort and brought before Judge Kinney (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); whether he was at the fort in June 1862 is not known. May 1863Comes to Soda Springs with the Morrisites under General Connor’s escort. Shupe’s early list of those families names “Eric Eliason” and “Mrs. Caroline Eliason,” and also his brother Elias and Elias’s wife. (Shupe, p. 13) 2 Aug 1863Daughter Anna born at Soda Springs; Shupe calls her the first white child born there. (Shupe, p. 29; Family Tree) 1 Sep 1867Son John Eric born at Soda Springs. (family account) 9 Jun 1870Baptized into the RLDS Church at Soda Springs by Lars Edler, on the same day as Karin, who is entered as Caroline Eliasson, born March 7, 1830, in Sweden. (Black, vol. 2) After 1870Takes the twins, Jacob and John, to the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, leaving part of the family at Soda Springs, and settles on the ranch near Racetrack that his grandson still held in 1989. The grandson’s account gives 1868, but the twins were born in 1867 and Isaac at Soda Springs in 1869, so the move came later. (Powell County: Where It All Began, pp. 108–109) 3 Jun 1877At the Race Track stake’s council at Deer Lodge the clerk notes “Bro. O. Olsen og Eliason, som var ankommet fra Soda Spring” (“who had arrived from Soda Springs”; the place name is a probable reading). The date fits the family account: the twins, born in 1867, were ten. (council minutes, June 3, 1877, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude) 24 Feb 1878At a joint council at Race Track he votes with the majority, ten to five, to build the Lord’s House on Andrew Hendrikson’s land. (council minutes, February 24, 1878, MS 31876) Jul 1879Leads the meetings at Race Track until July 24, 1879. That day the council agrees, and Eliason with it, that a brother who speaks English better should lead them, and asks Hendrikson to take them over. (council minutes, July 24, 1879, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude) June 1880The census counts Erik three times: as a married farmer living alone in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana; as a rancher living alone at Soda Springs; and, as “Alexr. Eliasson,” 63, at the head of the family at Soda Springs with “Carrie,” 50, and all six children, including the thirteen-year-old twins. He was already working land in Montana while the family’s home was still at Soda Springs. (1880 U.S. census) 14 Jan 1888Receives the patent for his 40-acre homestead in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T6N R9W, sec. 4), Homestead Certificate 560 at the Helena land office. The Homestead Act required five years’ residence before final proof, so he was on the land by about 1882 at the latest. His son Joseph patented the adjoining 40 acres in 1889. (BLM General Land Office records) 1893Dies at Racetrack, Montana, on March 6. (Family Tree) Karin dies at Soda Springs in 1902. (Family Tree) His brother Elias Erik’s younger brother Elias Eliasson (born 1819) also came to Soda Springs with the Morrisites in 1863; Shupe lists “Elias Eliason” and “Mrs. Elias Eliason” beside Erik and Karin (p. 13). Neither is on the roll of membership. Elias’s wife was Margreta Nilsdotter (1816–1900), and the family was in the Deer Lodge Valley by 1870, some years before Erik. The Family Tree records for Elias are tangled: one (LVXJ-L2R) has his Swedish baptism, and another, which carries his wife and children, has been given Erik’s birth and death dates. An Eliason household in 1889 When Joseph Smith III, president of the RLDS Church, visited Soda Springs in 1889, he stayed in the house of an Eliason family whose head was a widow, then away at Blackfoot (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 437). Erik was still living in 1893, and Elias’s widow lived in Montana, though one of Elias’s daughters later died at Blackfoot. Who that widow was is an open question. Open questions Where were Erik and Karin between the siege of June 1862 and the move to Soda Springs in May 1863? Who was the Eliason widow at Soda Springs in 1889? In what year did Erik move to the Deer Lodge Valley, and did Karin ever join him there? The 1880 census finds him farming there alone, with the family still at Soda Springs. His homestead case file at the National Archives (Helena land office, Homestead Certificate 560) should give the date he entered the land. If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. On the roll John Parson (1829–1892) President of the Morrisite apostles, who gave the order to raise the white flag at Kington Fort in 1862, later a Morrisite leader in Nevada, and joined the RLDS Church. On the roll Parson, John, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born January 1829, England (Family Tree) Died 1892, Montana (Family Tree) June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “John Parsons” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term Later path Stayed Morrisite, later joined the RLDS Church. In the Morrisite presidency with Richard Cook and John Livingstone that worked and baptized in Nevada; at the 1864 meeting of apostles there (Anderson, pp. 178, 180); listed among the contenders for Morrisite leadership (Anderson, p. 181). Later baptized into the RLDS Church at Oakland by Joseph Smith III (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 432). Family Tree FamilySearch L7YM-D5Y, John Parson (1829–1892). Wife Elizabeth (roll: Elizabeth Parson); died at Deer Lodge, Montana, the later Morrisite center. Identified by editor (FamilySearch search). Connected names on the roll Farley, Robert E.; Cook, Richard; Brown, Alonzo; Parson, Elizabeth Places in this guide Kington Fort, Carson City & California, Deer Lodge Valley What the sources say Living up Weber Canyon when Morris began his mission (Gems, p. 16); called by revelation to move to South Weber, February 1861, with Robert Farley (Spirit Prevails, pp. 60–61); president of the apostles (Anderson, p. 65; Spirit Prevails, p. 77). Gave the order to raise the white flag at the surrender (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137); named in the writ and contempt citation (Anderson, p. 108; Gems, p. 20). Carried Governor Harding's pardon to the penitentiary and demanded the seven prisoners' release (Gems, p. 31). Later a leader in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 178–81). A member of the First Council; summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 28, 51). In November 1857 he served as a private in the same Weber District militia company and platoon as Robert Farley, mustered at Ogden in the Utah War call-up (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, Utah State Archives); in July 1860 the two were next-door neighbors near Ogden, both tanners (1860 U.S. census, Weber County, p. 155, as "Jno Parsons"). He later joined the RLDS Church: Joseph Smith III baptized him at Oakland, California, over the protests of some of his brethren, and on July 29, 1889, Parson showed Smith and Brother Anthony the site of the camp at Weber (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, pp. 432–33). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “John Parsons”). At the March 1863 term the jury found him not guilty of murder; he then pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and was fined $100 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). A John Parson received a patent for 40 acres near Genoa in Carson Valley on September 20, 1873 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, sec. 15; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0020__.043). John R. Eardley wrote from Hollister, California, on November 9, 1875, that “John Parson & family have moved to Iron County,” after a “Kingdom building in San Francisco” had failed (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 23). In 1888 and 1889 the Montana council discussed Parson’s mission “as appointed him by a new prophet called Dr. Poulson of Oakland, Cal.,” while he still held membership in the Reorganized Church (Church of the Firstborn records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 40, 44). On the roll Peter C. Klemgard Leader of the armed party that captured the three dissenters in 1862, sentenced in March 1863 and pardoned. On the roll Klemgard, Peter C., in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “Peter Klemgaard” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, remanded to prison Connected names on the roll Jones, William J.; Banks, John; Cook, Richard Places in this guide Kington Fort, Morristown, Carson City & California, Kingdom of Heaven What the sources say Led the armed party of about thirty that captured William Jones and his companions (Anderson, p. 99, as Klemgaard); named in the writs and the contempt citation (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20); appointed to take charge of the firearms (Spirit Prevails, pp. 527–29). He later followed William W. Davies. Testifying at Walla Walla in 1881, he said that he and Davies had withdrawn from the Latter-day Saint church under Morris at Weber, that he next met Davies at Soda Springs in 1865, where there were “about sixty of us Morrisites” and the camp broke up for want of a leader, and that he then went to San Francisco, where Davies’s missionaries won him over. He lived at Davies’s camp near Walla Walla with his wife and four children from April 1870 to April 1872, and added that “the doctrine taught at the Davies camp is not like the Morrisite religion” (Cilley et al. v. Places in this guide Kington Fort, Deer Lodge Valley Kington Fort, 1862 In the spring of 1862 Lars Gurtsen, also called Lewis C. Gurtsen, left the Morrisite camp. A party under Peter Klemgard captured him with William Jones and John Jensen, and the three were held in a log house at the fort. After several days he and Jensen cut a hole through the log wall; Gurtsen got away, and Jensen was caught and brought back (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 98–100, 105). The Church History Department’s profile of Lars Christian Geertsen adds that he went to Salt Lake City and told the authorities that Jones and Jensen were being held against their will, and that the posse followed: the detention of these men is what brought the writs and the siege of June 1862. Salmon, Idaho The spellings of his name trace his road north. A Montana county marriage record calls him L. C. Gurtson, and the 1880 census lists him as Louis C., the “Lewis C.” of Anderson’s account; in Salmon he was known as Lars. He and his Danish wife came to the Salmon area in 1866 or 1867, as the town grew up around the gold strikes of 1866. In 1868 he homesteaded a 160-acre ranch, raising cattle to supply the miners, and a small community called Geertson Creek grew up nearby. He served for a time as a territorial justice of the peace, and he was one of the original shareholders of the Salmon City Cemetery Association. Between 1872 and 1883 he built a two-story house of hewn logs, square-notched and chinked. It also held the ranch commissary, which served settlers and travelers on the Red Rock–Salmon City stage line, and its upstairs dance hall was a gathering place for the community into the 1920s. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 3, 1980, as the Lars Geertson House (later the Herb Aldous House). A Salmon resident reports that it was damaged by fire years ago and torn down in 2025. Lars Christian Geertsen died at Salmon in 1925 and is buried in the Salmon Cemetery. Sources Anderson, C. LeRoy. Davies (1833–1906), born in Denbighshire, Wales, who came to Utah in 1855 (FamilySearch LRMD-8L5). With his wife Anne Elizabeth, also on the roll, he joined Morris; he was held to bail after the siege as “Wm. Davies” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). He was in Montana with the Morrisites by 1864 (an 1882 county history, drawing on Davies, puts him near Virginia City in 1864 and in the Deer Lodge Valley from 1865 to 1867; Watson, p. 189) and from 1867 led the Morrisite community near Walla Walla, Washington, known as the Kingdom of Heaven, until it broke up after the lawsuit of 1880–81 (Anderson, pp. 157, 187–92). He later lived in San Francisco, where James Dove found him in 1892 (Anderson, p. 192), returned to Walla Walla County shortly before his death on November 25 or 26, 1906, and is buried in the Lyons Cemetery above the old community (FamilySearch; Find a Grave 15969383). In 1880 Asa B. Cilley, Thomas W. Evans and A. J. Courtney sued him, his son Alfred (William Alfred Davies, born 1858) and W. Wood in the territorial district court at Walla Walla to collect wages and debts, the case the state archives index calls the “Walla Walla Jesus” case (Washington State Archives, Frontier Justice, WAL-3153). The 1880 U.S. census, taken that June, lists him at Walla Walla as “William W. Davis”, 47, a mason and a widower, with eight children from Grace, 25, to Seth, 4; Arthur and David are not among them. The census mortality schedule for the year records the deaths of Arthur Davis, 12, and David Davis, 10, of diphtheria in February 1880, and, in May, of “Sarah E. Davis”, 43, born in Wales. She was evidently his wife Anne Elizabeth: Family Tree records her birth on March 29, 1836, and her death at Walla Walla on May 19, 1879, which fits her age but falls just before the census year that began June 1, 1879 (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c, and mortality schedule, ED 50, p. 3; FamilySearch LRMD-NG6). His neighbors on that census page include Swin O. Hagg, David Park, Rachel Jones, two McCue boys and Cornelia S. Perkins, 30, who became his second wife (Find a Grave memorial 15969383). Watson prints his writings and the record of his community (Watson, pp. 111ff.). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 16 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 35854). In 1881 Davies testified that he had come to Walla Walla from Montana in the fall of 1867 with his family and the James, David Thomas and Sorenson families; Swen O. Hagg put the first party at five families, about forty people. Davies also said that “the association commenced in 1866 in Montana” and that “the doctrine of reincarnation is taught and believed”; a list he put in evidence names forty-three members in March 1881 (Watson, pp. 111ff.; Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). The community dated its era from January 24, 1866. On May 25, 1881, the court gave Cilley, Courtney and Evans judgment against Davies for $3,225; the sheriff sold his livestock and equipment on June 11, and on July 16 the community’s eighty acres, the west half of the northwest quarter of section 34, township 7 north, range 37 east (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). In 1885 the First National Bank of Walla Walla won a default judgment against him and his son over nine notes of 1879, made out to Lewis H. Bowman (First National Bank v. Davies, 1885). A letter of March 4, 1866, from Sven Olson Hagg at Deer Lodge City says that the first in the Deer Lodge Valley to receive “this power” of the Spirit was “his servant William D.”, president of the Aaronic priesthood, standing “in Abel’s place” by birthright (MS 31876, folder 22; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). It is the earliest known record of his spiritual claims. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJ8-9RQ). Held to bail after the siege as “S. P. Guhl” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Leader of the Council Bluffs group; sustained as Cainan’s first counselor on January 24, 1869, having come to Omaha on January 22 “from Montana, where he had lived some years”; he organized the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations on February 7, 1869, and presided over them until May 30, 1869 (Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876); and sent on a mission to Denmark, where he broke with Cainan (Anderson, pp. 193–94); in October 1869 Williams wrote that “the important request from Denmark for money is altogether against my wishes,” and that Guhl “likes to take some other way,” to which Williams consented only because of “his often importunities” (Williams to the Omaha church, October 13, 1869, MS 31876); Cainan had written ahead to Deer Lodge to receive him on his way to Scandinavia (Anderson, p. 187), and later named him among the “traitors” (Anderson, p. 204). He died at Council Bluffs, Iowa, in 1883. In a letter of November 24, 1874, from 678 14th Street, Omaha, to William James and the Saints in Montana, Guhl wrote that Cainan had ordered him and “Bro. Poulsen” to organize the church at Omaha and had told him, in a letter of October 3, 1874, that his mission stood “under his especial direction” and not under Deer Lodge. The Spirit Prevails names the second woman shot at the surrender on June 15, 1862, after Isabella Bowman, as “Mrs. O’Hagg” (p. 8), and Alexander Dow’s affidavit calls her a Danish woman (Anderson, p. 148); she may have been Anna, but the identification has not been checked. The 1870 U.S. census lists Swen Hagg, 37, farming in Walla Walla County, Washington Territory, with John, 10; as Swen O. Hagg he proved up a homestead of 170.62 acres there, patented July 24, 1890 (BLM General Land Office records, accession SER-WAWWAA 016765). In June 1880 “Swin O. Hagg”, 48, born in Sweden, a laborer and a widower, was living in William W. Davies’s dwelling at Walla Walla, with an Ole Hagg, 72, born in Sweden, two houses away (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c). Testifying for Davies in 1881, Swen O. Hagg said he had known him “ever since the fall of 1861,” had joined his association in 1866, and had come to Walla Walla in the fall of 1867 with the first members, five families of about forty people; in Davies’s teaching he was the central figure of the second of the circles around the Trinity. Ola Hagg, 73, who had come to the camp in July 1868 and also testified for Davies, was probably his father (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). His own letters survive in the Montana church’s records. On March 4, 1866, he wrote from Deer Lodge City that he had wintered there with his little son in the house of L. C. Larsen, which he had helped build and where the Morrisites now held their meetings; the first to receive the Spirit there, he said, was “William D.” (Davies). On January 22, 1869, he wrote from 926 Washington Street, San Francisco, as a missionary. He had left “Israels Camp” on December 19, 1868. His father lived at its “Hovedquarter” (headquarters) with his sister and her husband Jens Mortensen (the James Mortensen of Davies’s camp), his own son was in their care, and “Israels Standard” (Davies) cared for them all; David M. Thomas was then on a mission at Portland, Oregon (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 22; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). On the roll Beck, Niels R., in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born February 26, 1823, Tørring, Skanderborg, Denmark, son of Rasmus Nielsen and Anne Nielsdatter (Family Tree) Died July 21, 1888, Deer Lodge, Montana; buried at Deer Lodge (Family Tree) Wife Maria Simonsen Thompson (1834–1898), married February 3, 1851, at Tønning, Skanderborg, Denmark (Family Tree) Children Four in Family Tree: Erastus (1853–1914), Simon Thomsen (1855–1926), Margaret Anna (1857–1942) and Annie Serena (1859–1940) June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “N. R. Beck” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term Later path Stayed with the Morrisites. Family Tree describes him as a Morrisite; died at Deer Lodge, Montana, in 1888. June 1862After the siege of Kington Fort he is among the men brought before Judge Kinney and held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term of court. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) 1866–78A “Neil A. [or R.?] Beck of Montana” sends gifts by letter and money order to William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, the first of them toward the purchase of its eighty acres; a list of donations filed in a lawsuit against Davies credits “Neils R. Beck” with $4,839 over these years, and Davies testified that he had received “over $1500 from Mr. Beck to pay for land,” $300 for a printing press and more than $3,000 besides, adding that “Mr. Beck is not a member.” Probably the same man. (Cilley v. Davies, 1880–81) 1870Farming in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, as “Nelson Beck,” 48, born in Denmark (real estate $550, personal property $1,350), next to the households of Ole Olsen and Lars C. Hansen, both also on the roll. The household is Ellen C., 49, Chris, 11, and Anna, 8, the children born in Utah. (1870 U.S. census) 1 May 1871Receives the patent for 160 acres in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, secs. 34–35), a preemption cash entry at the Helena land office (certificate 230). It is the earliest Morrisite land patent found in the valley. Lars C. Hansen patented land in the same section in 1873. (BLM General Land Office records) 1880Farming alone at Cottonwood Creek in the Deer Lodge Valley, aged 57, the first household on the census page. His neighbors include Lars C. Hansen and his family and Lars C. Larson, whose children were born in Idaho in 1864 and in Montana from 1866, the path of the Morrisites from Soda Springs to the Deer Lodge Valley. (1880 U.S. census) 21 Jul 1888Dies at Deer Lodge, Montana, and is buried there. (Family Tree) A household that does not match Family Tree gives Niels a wife, Maria (born 1834), and four children born between 1853 and 1859; the 1860 census at Moroni agrees, with Maria and four children. The 1870 census in the Deer Lodge Valley lists a different household: Ellen C., aged 49, and two children, Chris, 11, and Anna, 8. Ellen may be a second wife, or the enumerator may have taken the names down wrongly. Neither Ellen nor Chris appears in Family Tree, and where Maria was in 1870 is not known. By 1880 Niels was living alone. The later Becks of the valley In 1884 an eighteen-year-old Dane, Soren R. Beck, born July 9, 1866, the son of Anders and Annie (Sorenson) Beck, came alone to Deer Lodge and for three years worked on “a ranch belonging to Nels R. Beck, adjoining the city of Deer Lodge.” In 1889 he leased land on the Little Blackfoot and went on to raise horses, cattle and sheep (Progressive Men of the State of Montana, 1902, p. 1637). The biography does not say how the two were related. Family Tree makes Soren (FamilySearch 9MKM-NJF) a son of Anders Rasmusen Beck (1830–1905), whom it lists as Niels’s younger brother, both children of Rasmus Nielsen and Anne Nielsdatter of the Tørring area; if so, Soren was Niels’s nephew, which would explain why he came to work on his ranch. A third Beck family, Nels Jensen Beck and Maria Helena (Hansen) Beck, who came from Denmark in 1872, is distinct from both. What the family accounts say A family history held at the Church History Library, as summarized by Julie A. Wright, says that Niels was baptized a Latter-day Saint in Denmark in 1851 and came to Utah with his wife in 1855; that she accepted plural marriage, which he could not; and that when he left the church and joined the Morrisites she would not leave Utah with him. It adds that he became a wealthy cattle rancher in Montana and left most of his estate to the Latter-day Saint church he had left (Eva and Evelyn Sorenson Jacobsen, “Life History of Niels Rasmussen Beck,” cited in Wright, “Mormon Movement to Montana,” 2004, pp. 34–35). The Church History Library catalogs it under Eva Sorensen Jacobsen as an undated photocopied typescript of four leaves (MS 2735 275); its catalog summary describes the same story of conversion in Denmark, joining the Morrisites, the move to Deer Lodge and success as a rancher. The family history itself has not yet been seen for this guide. Henry Hendrickson, interviewed in 1962, remembered from his childhood “another Beck family” besides the Becks of Race Track: an old, rich bachelor with a lot of land, living toward Garrison, whose nephew came when he heard of the estate; he did not give the man’s first name, and the speakers said that family were never Morrisites (interview by Don Cornelius, April 19, 1962, p. 16, OH 018-001, University of Montana). Niels, whose wife stayed in Utah and who lived alone by 1880, could have seemed a bachelor to a child, and Soren R. Beck could have been the nephew, but nothing yet shows that Hendrickson meant him. Neither account of the estate has been checked against the probate record. The Montana church’s own records add a point in that direction. Its membership record, kept from 1874 to 1887, and its council minutes for 1881–1890 name Lars and Mary Beck, baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, in 1871, and Niels J. Beck and Mary Helene Beck, baptized at Deer Lodge in 1878 (his membership slip gives his birthplace as Jernved, Ribe, May 6, 1847, which identifies him as Nels Jensen Beck); Nels Beck voted in the elections of 1883 and 1886 and twice sat on the council. Niels R. Beck does not appear in either record (Church of the Firstborn records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library). That he was left out of a record begun in Montana does not prove he had left the church, but it fits Hendrickson’s memory of a Beck who was not a Morrisite. A head reading A typescript page among the Morrisite papers at Utah State University, a fragment of a letter whose writer and date are lost, says that a prophet living incognito at Cottonwood felt men’s heads “Phrenologically” to tell

(1880 U.S. census) 1882–92Receives four federal land patents near Blackfoot, all in the same township (Boise Meridian, T3S R35E), each under a different law: 158.45 acres by cash entry (January 20, 1882, Oxford land office); a 160-acre homestead (April 18, 1888, Oxford); 200 acres under the Desert Land Act of 1877, which required the claimant to irrigate the land (September 23, 1890, Blackfoot land office); and a Timber Culture Act claim, granted for planting trees (March 17, 1892). (BLM General Land Office records) 9 May 1899Dies at Blackfoot, Idaho. (Family Tree) Thurza, not Martha The roll names John’s wife Thurza, and the 1860 census at Moroni has Thurza, aged 55. The 1870 census in Oneida County gives the wife of “Jno. Garrett” as Martha, aged 50, which raised the question of a second wife. The 1880 census answers it: John Garrett, 65, and his wife Thirza, 75, were living together at Blackfoot. The 1870 “Martha” was most likely the enumerator’s mistake. The land at Blackfoot John’s four patents lie close together in one township near Blackfoot, more than 500 acres in all. Using cash entry, the Homestead Act, the Desert Land Act and the Timber Culture Act together was a common way to put together a larger farm than any one law allowed. A homestead normally needed five years’ residence before final proof, so John was probably living on that land by about 1883, when he was in his late sixties. The case files at the National Archives would show when he made each entry and who witnessed his proofs. Open questions Who is the Jane Garrett on the roll? Did family members help him work the Blackfoot land, or join him there? Where were the Garretts between the siege of 1862 and 1870? Did they go to Soda Springs with the other Morrisites before moving north toward Blackfoot? If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. His land entry file at the National Archives (Carson City land office) should show when he settled on the land. If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. Places Kington Fort South Weber, Utah. The fort at South Weber where Morris gathered his followers in 1861–62, and the siege of June 1862. MO-IMG-001 · Monument, December 2008 Built in 1853 and abandoned in 1858, then reoccupied by the Morrisites. Nothing of the fort survives; a monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site, Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, was erected in August 2006 at 6600 South and 475 East (N 41.14677, W 111.96884), sponsored by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping, with the site designed by Douglas B. Stephens (Barlow, 2022). The fort was named for Bishop Thomas Kington, and “Kington” is the correct spelling. The monument itself notes that the earliest sources (the notebook kept by Kington’s wife, his gravestone, Wilford Woodruff’s journals, and early church records) all spell it that way; recent scholarship such as Holley (2008) follows them. Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts, and some modern references, including the Utah History Encyclopedia and Wikipedia, write “Kingston Fort.” Insiders used both: Forscutt, who lived in the fort, wrote “Kingston’s Fort” and called it “the proper name” of the place (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702). Search under both spellings. Not all the people in the fort were from South Weber. Holley (2008) names eleven men from Slaterville and Marriott, about nine miles to the northwest, among the prisoners of June 1862, and two of the family groups on the roll, Cowan–Bull and Higham, were Slaterville families (see “Families on the roll” on the roll page). A log cabin nearby, which the local historian Ed Cooper, from oral accounts of older South Weber residents, identified as the building Morris used to hold the three departing members whose detention led to the siege, is shown in MO-IMG-046–049; it has been moved from its original site, and the identification rests on local tradition. About 200 yards south, on the west side of the road, in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery, a marker reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021). The name lingered locally. In the early 2000s, while the editor was going door to door in South Weber, a woman then in her sixties said that elementary-school classmates had called her “Morrisite” as a taunt because of where in South Weber she lived; she said her family had no Morrisite connection. (Editor’s memorandum of recollection, written November 1, 2026; the conversation was not recorded at the time.) A cannonball from the siege was kept by the family of Al Peek, together with a portrait of Mary Christoffersen Anderson (MO-IMG-051–053; the portrait is MO-IMG-062). VisitThe monument is public. The Pioneer Cemetery appears to lie on private land but is reached by a public easement; stay on the access route. The cabin is on private property. Places on the ground The fort and the siege of June 13–15, 1862, as the sources place them. Nothing of the fort survives, and the ground is now streets, houses and fields. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate (placed from a plan or a written description); the dashed square is the fort as G. Q. Jones drew it. Most of this is private land: the monument is the public place to visit. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. Streets are drawn straight through the monument corner and are approximate. The fort’s outline follows the plan by G. Q. Jones (1996) and the editor’s 2009 overlay of it on an aerial photograph; it is good to perhaps a hundred feet. The Kington Fort–Morrisite War Site monument Located 2006 map Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, at 6600 South and 475 East, erected in August 2006 by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping. It stands within the area of the old fort. Public. Sources: Barlow (2022); see History. Kington Fort Approximate 1853–1862 Built in 1853 by the settlers under Bishop Thomas Kington and abandoned in 1858; a square of about 645 feet with log and later adobe houses along an earth wall, gates on each side and a public square in the middle. The Morrisites reoccupied it in 1861, rebuilt the wall in adobe and built new houses. Jones’s plan places Morris’s tent and an adobe schoolhouse in the southwest part of the fort, and the intersection of today’s 6600 South and 475 East inside it. Sources: G. Q. Jones, “Morrisite Fort – Plan, South Weber, Davis County, Utah,” December 1996 (not reproduced here); the monument text. The bowery, west of the fort Approximate June 13, 1862 map The open-air meeting place in a grove of trees west of the fort. On the morning of June 13, as Morris spoke to his people there, the posse’s cannon fire fell among them, killing two women and wounding Mary Christoffersen. The marker follows Jones’s plan. Sources: Jones plan (1996); see History. The west gate and the surrender Approximate June 15, 1862 map Jones places near the west gate the scene on June 15, after the white flag was raised, in which Joseph Morris and two women were killed and John Banks was fatally wounded. Accounts of how it happened differ; see History and Questions. Sources: Jones plan (1996). The south gate and the slough Approximate June 15, 1862 map Jones’s plan marks a slough just outside the south gate, where a road crossed it, and notes that on June 15 an armored battery made from the rear of a wagon was rolled toward the fort, caught a wheel in the mud and tipped over, and that its crew retreated under musket fire. Jones gives no source for this. Anderson describes a rolling battery of willows and wagon wheels pushed up to the fort wall the same day, so the accounts differ. See MO-IMG-032 under Images. Places Morristown Soda Springs, Idaho. The settlement at Soda Springs founded in May 1863 under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor. MO-IMG-061 · Anderson gravestone, October 2018 The Morrisites were among the founders of Soda Springs, one of the oldest towns in Idaho. Connor reported bringing 160 settlers (53 families, seven single men, and four widows), who arrived May 20, 1863, and were given building lots on a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River, beside the military reservation of Camp Connor (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). A later marker describes a 200-acre survey west of Soda Creek, lots of 25 by 130 feet, and one-room log homes with dirt floors. The Morrisite “Lower Town” stood below the military “Upper Town”; Soda Springs was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. After the troops left in 1865, hard winters and failed crops thinned the settlement. Many Morrisites moved on, some north to the Blackfoot area, and others sold to miners and to Latter-day Saint settlers, whose new town site dates from Brigham Young’s visit of 1870–71. Most of the old town now lies under Alexander Reservoir. Those who stayed, led by Niels Anderson, carried their quarrel with the Mormon hierarchy into territorial politics; the Niels Anderson Homestead marker credits his anti-polygamy campaign with helping deny Mormons the vote in Idaho. Accounts differ on some details: most give 160 settlers (one popular account says about 325), Camp Connor’s founding is dated May 20 or May 23, and the National Park Service marker wrongly calls Morris Welsh-born. Markers stand in town, including the Park Service’s Morrisite settlement marker in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse (HMDB), the state’s Camp Connor marker (HMDB), and “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor’s probable site near the hospital (HMDB). Descendants held a reunion in Soda Springs on August 3, 2013. Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson, married at Morristown on July 20, 1863 (the date on their gravestone; some accounts give July 30), are buried in Fairview Cemetery at Soda Springs. Their gravestone carries a long bronze inscription giving a Morrisite account of the 1862 siege, in which Mary, then fourteen, lost her jaw to the first cannon shot fired into the fort. Forscutt, who was present, described her lower jaw “hanging only by a narrow strip of skin,” with two women dead beside her (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702; MO-IMG-061, with transcription; MO-IMG-062; HMDB; see also the Niels Anderson Homestead marker). VisitThe markers and the Anderson gravestone in Fairview Cemetery are publicly accessible. The townsite is largely under Alexander Reservoir. Places on the ground The 1863 settlement and the land the Morrisite families later took up. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate; squares are land patents, drawn at the quarter-section or smaller part they name. Most of the old town lies under Alexander Reservoir. Public. Sources: Historical Marker Database, 106709, 106710, 106726. The Park Service panel says it is believed to have stood near the Caribou Memorial Hospital, just south of the markers; a settler recalled that Connor later moved the fort a little farther east, on the hill. Places Carson City & California Nevada · California. The western congregations in Carson Valley and San Francisco, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails. The western congregations, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails and led the California church after 1882. In May 1863 Connor gave 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City in an empty quartermaster’s train bound there for stores (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). VisitNo surviving sites identified for this guide. Information welcome. In the chronology May 1863Many Morrisites leave Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, commanding the District of Utah. On May 5 a party of 160 (53 families, seven single men, and four widows) sets out with a company of California Volunteers; it reaches Soda Springs on May 20, where Connor has a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River beside a new military post, Camp Connor (established by order of May 23). The Morrisites call their town Morristown. Connor also gives 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City, Nevada, in an empty supply train. Others settle in California. (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 1, 226–29.) 1860s–Some Morrisites return to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, in Utah and elsewhere. The 2006 monument at South Weber notes that a few were rebaptized and remained there. Others find a home in the Reorganized Church (RLDS): the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt joins it in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear (Johann Lebrecht Bär, 1838–1919), a Swiss convert from Affoltern am Albis who emigrated from Zürich in 1860 and lost his wife and child at Kington Fort, later serves as an RLDS missionary to Switzerland and Germany, dies in Independence, Missouri, and publishes his autobiography in the RLDS Journal of History. In 1865 RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptize several people who appear on the roll. Others join only after years in the Morrisite groups: Erick and Caroline Eliason are baptized together at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870; Margaretta Cook leaves the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and is baptized RLDS in 1873; and Lena Hanson, at Soda Springs and then Deer Lodge, in 1895 (see the roll). 1869George Williams leaves Utah for England, passing through Omaha from January 18 to February 5, where the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations are organized on his authority (see Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places); a year later he writes from Loughborough that it was “now one year since I left the continent of America”; his wife and children stay in Salt Lake City, and he asks the Montana members to send help for “my little ones” (Williams to the Saints of the Most High in Montana, January 10 [?], 1870, Church History Library, MS 31876). By June he is at Ashwicken, near King’s Lynn, Norfolk, writing to the Saints at Omaha and Council Bluffs, where Rasmus Rasmussen is “the presiding Bishop.” George Thompson is with him at Ashwicken that summer, and William P. Thomas and a Brother James come to England too: Thompson writes on July 29, 1869, to “Beloved Brethren W. P. and D. J.,” one at Llanybyther in Wales and the other at Derby. The Omaha minutebook names him: on June 2, 1869, Guhl left for Denmark with “2 Welsh brethren, William P. Thomas, a High Priest, and an Aaronic Priest Daniel James,” called “to go to Wales on mission.” In March 1870 Williams writes that “Bro Thomas & Bro James,” having “attended the heavenly call,” are “now permitted to return to their families in Montana” by way of Omaha. In September 1870 he gives his own account of Almerin Grow, who had walked from California to Salt Lake on hearing of him, was told of “his mission to the Sultan & Priesthood of Mahommet,” and was later “sent to Constantinople & Jerusalem,” returning “without my consent” (Williams to the Omaha church and to Andrew Hendrikson, 1869–70; George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869; and the Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876). Danish-language congregations keep membership and account books in Omaha, Nebraska, and Council Bluffs, Iowa. 1873The Montana council minutes, kept in English this year, show the church at Warm Springs while its leaders are away. William James is on “his Mission in Nevada.” Williams calls William P. Thomas “on a Mission to Salt Lake,” and he appoints Andrew Hendrikson by letter “to take the Presidency, assisted by the Bishop and his Counselors,” while both are absent (May 5, 1873). In March a committee of four tries a quarrel between Thomas and Daniel James over the line between their lands and Daniel James’s cattle, set on by dogs as they passed Thomas’s place. It tells the two to forgive each other, but Thomas rejects the ruling as “Develish talke.” In July, Damander, who had hosted the Council Bluffs councils, turns against Williams, saying “Cainan was a Man like Brigham Young to lead the People astray.” James takes back the presidency on July 20. In September the council meets privately at Rasmus Rasmussen’s house to keep Thomas out and agrees to report him to Williams; Thomas, Williams’s appointed first counselor and “our second man in authority,” is to be left alone until Williams answers. In December the sisters in the town of Deer Lodge complain that Margaret Thomas did not invite them to the sisters’ feast at Warm Springs (council minutes, March–December 1873 and January 12, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876). In California the same year, George Dove, who with his father James had followed Williams and then Davies, begins receiving communications and organizes a Church of the Firstborn of about thirty people (Watson, p. 198). 1882–83Williams dies in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 year,” after about two years of great pain from “an enlargement of the bone” in his shoulder joint; George Thompson, who had done his writing for him, still knew of no one “appointed to fill his place” in August 1883 (Thompson to William P.
