Places Omaha & Council Bluffs Nebraska · Iowa. Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive. Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive in translation. Their own minutebook, written up at Omaha in May 1871, tells how they began. Jens Jacob Poulsen, “a High Priest of the Weber House,” was sent ahead by George Williams to gather the scattered Morrisites, and spent about a year there. Williams himself arrived in Omaha on January 18, 1869, “from his home in South Cottonwood in Utah,” on his way to England, held meetings in Omaha and Council Bluffs, and left on February 5 with Poulsen and a Brother Mortensen, who went on to Denmark. On February 7, 1869, at Council Bluffs, S. P. Guhl, newly come from Montana, organized the church on Williams’s authority: Council Bluffs City Congregation No. 1, under Carlton Fellows, with Hans Nielsen over the Scandinavians at Crescent City, since the Danes “were not satisfied” to have an American president; and Omaha City Congregation No. 2, for all the Saints west of the Missouri, under Jens Jensen, with a district at Florence under Niels Jensen. Rasmus Rasmussen became the first bishop. A conference at Omaha on April 6, 1869, sustained “George Williams, called of the Lord Cainan,” as “our Prophet, Seer and Revelator,” and on May 30, as Guhl left on a mission to Denmark, Andrew Hendrikson was appointed to preside, with Jens Jensen and Hans Nielsen as counselors (minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In March 1871 the church gave up its yearly conferences, which Hendrikson said Guhl had brought in “in likeness with the Mormons’ custom” and Williams had never commanded, and met instead in councils in members’ houses and in “social gatherings.” That May one of its leaders, Sister Marie Mortensen, joined the Reorganized Church, and Hendrikson had the early records copied into a book, “for many of us must be called hence and go to other places.” The last entry is dated June 4, 1871, at Jens Jensen’s house in Omaha. Most of the congregation moved to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1871–72. VisitNo sites identified; the record survives in documents only. Places on the ground The two congregations organized at Council Bluffs on February 7, 1869, and their districts, as the Omaha minutebook names them. All the markers are approximate: they show the towns, not buildings. No meeting place has yet been located. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. Towns are placed at their old centres. The river is drawn roughly along its present course; it has moved since the 1870s (the Carter Lake bend was cut off by the flood of 1877), so its exact line then is not shown. The minutebook made the river the boundary: Omaha City Congregation No. 2 took in “all the Saints west of the Missouri.” The inset at upper left shows where Fremont and Lincoln lie, beyond this map; its rivers are drawn only roughly. Council Bluffs: Congregation No. 1 Approximate 1869–1872 map Council Bluffs City Congregation No. 1, organized on February 7, 1869, at a conference held in Council Bluffs, with the High Priest Carlton Fellows as president. The Danish members “were not satisfied” with an American president, so Fellows was kept as president “for the English” and the Scandinavians were given their own district (see Crescent City). Councils met in Brother Damander’s house, and in 1871 Williams wrote to Andrew Hendrikson in care of Damander at P.O. Box 610, Council Bluffs. The house has not been located. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; Williams’s envelopes, MS 31876, folders 11–12. Crescent City: the Scandinavian district Approximate 1869–1870 map A district of Congregation No. 1 for the Scandinavian Saints at Crescent City and round about, under Hans Nielsen from February 1869 and, after he stopped holding meetings, under Peder Staffanson from March 1870. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library. Omaha: Congregation No. 2 Approximate 1869–1872 map Omaha City Congregation No. 2, for “all the Saints west of the Missouri,” organized on February 7, 1869, under the High Priest Jens Jensen. Its conferences were held in Omaha, among them the one of April 6, 1869, that sustained Williams as prophet. Rasmus Rasmussen, the first bishop, had his post office box here (P.O. Box 40). The minutebook was written up at Omaha in May 1871. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; Williams’s envelope to Rasmussen, June 1869, MS 31876, folder 10. Florence: a district of No. 2 Approximate 1869–1870 map A district of Congregation No. 2 for the Saints at Florence and round about, under Niels Jensen “from Florence.” Florence, now part of north Omaha, was the site of the Latter-day Saints’ Winter Quarters of 1846–48 and a later outfitting point for emigrants to Utah. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library. Fremont, Nebraska: a branch Approximate 1870–1873 map Niels Jensen “from Fremont” testified at the Omaha conference of October 16, 1870. By November 30, 1871, Fremont had a branch of its own: a council met that evening in Andrew Peterson’s house, with Andrew Hendrikson, Niels Jensen, Peter A. Just, J. Helstrøm and S. Jensen. In March 1873 Peterson wrote to Hendrikson in Montana that the Fremont members hoped to follow that summer and were trying to sell their place. About 30 miles northwest of Omaha, beyond this map. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; council minutes, Fremont, November 30, 1871, and Andrew Peterson to Hendrikson, March 1873, MS 31876, folders 37–38. t: Deer Lodge Valley, Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana
s: Places Deer Lodge Valley Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana. The longest-lived center of the movement, and the Lord’s House at Racetrack, the last Morrisite church standing. MO-IMG-014 · Racetrack church, November 2018 The longest-lived center of the movement. The wood-frame Morrisite church, built in 1878–79, still stands on private land at Racetrack, about 8 miles south of Deer Lodge: on the north side of Dempsey Road, just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (Exit 195; about 46.29° N, 112.75° W; NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County; until 1901 this was Deer Lodge County, the county named in older records and in this guide’s photograph captions). The county lists it as a frame building of 18 by 36 feet (Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026). It was last photographed for this guide in August 2020. Called the Lord’s House, as the panel over its doors reads, it was the church’s meeting place: George Thompson was elected president of the church there in 1886, and Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954) presided over the Montana church from it. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive, and its condition has worsened markedly since 2009. See the condition record under Images. The Deer Lodge paper, the New North-West, spoke well of its Morrisite neighbors. In June 1878 it reported that the post office at Gwendale, Deer Lodge County, had been renamed Morristown, and that “as many of the people are Morrisites” they would likely take to the name. In 1883 it called the settlements on Warm Springs Creek and the upper Deer Lodge River “largely composed” of Morrisites and praised them as industrious, hospitable and law-abiding; in 1885 it noted “a large number of Morrisites in this valley” (New North-West, June 7, 1878, p. 3; April 13, 1883, p. 2; October 30, 1885, p. 3; see Newspapers). The paper’s notices place Gwendale in the upper Deer Lodge valley, near Warm Springs and Lost Creek. It was school district No. 6; in April 1875 “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” met at the Gwendale school house on the railroad question, with Morgan Evans in the chair and a W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee; Gwendale primaries were held at Wier’s store; and a smelter there began work in August 1877 (New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2; June 18, 1875, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3). Morgan Evans, whose land later became Anaconda, gave Gwendale as his address. By 1883 the same school district, No. 6, was called Willow Glen, with Peter Jessen, a Gwendale man since the 1870s, as a trustee and J. I. Eardley as clerk (New North-West, May 4, 1883, p. 3). In March 1880 the land office listed Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims were held up while it decided whether the ground was mineral land; among them were Daniel James and William P. Thomas, on Warm Springs Creek east of where Anaconda was built (secs. 33 and 34, T5N R10W), and Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen, in sec. 9, T4N R10W, near today’s Opportunity (New North-West, April 30, 1880, p. 4); all four claims were patented as homesteads in 1880–81. In January 1882 the paper reported that John R. Eardley, formerly of San Francisco, had built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and that the neighborhood had petitioned for a post office there “to be called Willow Glen”; in March it reported his appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was” (New North-West, January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3). Gwendale, renamed Morristown in 1878, and Willow Glen were thus successive post offices for the same neighborhood, between Anaconda, Opportunity and Warm Springs. The exact site of the Gwendale school house is still not known. View onlyThe church is privately owned, unsafe and not open to the public. View it from Dempsey Road or the frontage road; do not enter the property. Places on the ground Sites named in the sources, with how precisely each can be placed. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate; squares are land patents, drawn at the quarter-section or section the patent names. Sites not yet located are listed without a marker. Most of these places are private land today. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. “Willow Glen Ranch” near Opportunity, shown in gray, is the later company stock farm of that name (burned in 1963), not the Willow Glen of 1882. The Lord’s House, Racetrack Located 1878–1969 map The church of the Montana Morrisites, built in 1878–79 and dedicated on August 9, 1879, on the north side of Dempsey Road just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County). George Thompson was elected president of the church here on May 10, 1886. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive. Don Cornelius, who saw it in 1962, dated it to 1878 and described a building of planed lumber, once painted white, with “THE LORD’S HOUSE” lettered above its double doors, standing in a pasture; Julie A. Wright gives its dedication as 1879. Privately owned and unsafe: view it from the road only. Sources: Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026; Anderson, Revisited; Don Cornelius, “Mormonism in Montana, 1847–1898” (M.A. thesis, Montana State University [now the University of Montana], 1962), pp. 63–64; Julie A. Wright, “Mormon Movement to Montana” (M.A. thesis, University of Montana, 2004), p. 37. See the photographs under Images. Homesteads and land entries, Racetrack to Deer Lodge Located 1871–1905 Federal land patents to Morrisite families cluster along the river between Racetrack and the town of Deer Lodge (T6N–T9N, R8W–R9W). The earliest is Niels R. Beck’s preemption entry, patented in 1871. On the map each patent is a square at the quarter-section or section it names: that locates the land, not the house. Most of it is privately owned today. Niels R.

s: Places Kingdom of Heaven Walla Walla, Washington. William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. William W. Davies's commune near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. Its site lay on the west side of Mormon Grade Road, a few hundred yards south of Scenic Loop Road, near Russell Creek (Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). An interpretive sign that Walla Walla 2020 put up at the corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. The road name and Davies’s grave in Lyons Cemetery remain. VisitLyons Cemetery is public. The colony site is not marked. Places on the ground Sites of Davies’s community, 1867–1881, and of what remains of it. Solid markers and tracts are located; outlined markers are approximate; sites not yet located are listed without a marker. The colony land is private today. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. Tracts are drawn from their legal descriptions on the BLM section grid. The corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads is from OpenStreetMap. The colony’s eighty acres Located 1867–1881 map After the 1881 judgment against Davies, the sheriff levied on his land, “the W½ NW¼ sec. 34, T7N R37E,” less one acre, and sold it at the courthouse door on July 16, 1881, for $1,975. A witness in the case spoke of the eighty acres “where he resides,” so this was almost certainly the camp. The tract lies on the west side of Mormon Grade Road just south of its corner with Scenic Loop Road, which matches Dan Clark’s placing of the site near Russell Creek. Private land; the site is not marked. Sources: Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, Walla Walla Frontier Justice, case 2373 (WAL-3153); Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026; section lines from the BLM National PLSS dataset. Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads Located today map The road named for the colony. Walla Walla 2020 put an interpretive sign about Davies’s community at this corner; it was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. Sources: Walla Walla 2020; OpenStreetMap. Swen O. Hagg’s homestead Located patented 1890 map Swen O. Hagg (the roll’s Svend Hegg), who came to Walla Walla with the first five families in 1867 and was living in Davies’s house in 1880, patented a 170-acre homestead about three miles east-southeast of the camp in 1890 (S½ SE¼ sec. 1, T6N R37E, and lots in sec. 6, T6N R38E). The square shows the part in section 1. Sources: Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov); section lines from the BLM National PLSS dataset. The Davies cabin, Fort Walla Walla Museum Located today map A cabin in which Davies and his family lived has been moved to the grounds of the Fort Walla Walla Museum. Public, during museum hours. Sources: Wikipedia, “William W. Davies”; OpenStreetMap. Davies’s other land Not yet located 1870s A witness in 1881 listed 160 acres on Mill Creek, 160 acres “on the mountains” in Oregon or near the line, and 40 to 80 acres more. These tracts have not yet been found in the land records. Sources: Deposition of V. D. Lambert, case 2373. Davies’s grave, Lyons Cemetery Not yet located 1906 Davies died in 1906 and is buried in Lyons Cemetery, north of Mill Creek Road. Public. Its position is not yet on this map. Sources: Wikipedia, “William W. Davies.” In the chronology 1867–1881William W. Davies, who in an 1867 pamphlet declared that a third dispensation had been opened through him on January 24, 1866, setting baptism aside for a covenant vow (Watson, p. 124), leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of Heaven, near Walla Walla, Washington. He declares his infant son Arthur to be Christ returned, the “Walla Walla Jesus.” Lawsuits by former members end the community: in 1881 a court awards three of them $3,225, and the sheriff sells the community’s livestock and its eighty acres to satisfy the judgment.
